en: The Scripture of the Questions of the Brahma Viśeṣacintin, Volume One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat...

The Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of sixty-four thousand bhikṣus and seventy-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. All of them were renowned by the wise; they had attained the perfection of dhāraṇīs, possessed the unhindered eloquence of *pratibhāna*, had attained various *samādhis*, and had acquired great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They moved with unimpeded vigor, had ultimately attained fearlessness, thoroughly understood the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, and had attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.

Their names were: Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Ratnapāṇi Kumārabhūta, Ratnamudrāhasta Kumārabhūta, Ratnaśrī Kumārabhūta, Gaganagañja Kumārabhūta, Cittotpādadharmacakrapravartana Kumārabhūta, Jālinīprabha Kumārabhūta, Vikrīḍita Kumārabhūta, Guṇagañja Kumārabhūta, Sarvadharmaparityāga Kumārabhūta, Padmavyūha Kumārabhūta, Siṃha Kumārabhūta, Candraprabha Kumārabhūta, Candrāvabhāsa Kumārabhūta, Varasammati Kumārabhūta, and Sarvavyūha Kumārabhūta.
Led by Bhadrapāla and others, there were sixteen great virtuous men, whose names were:

the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Suparikīrtitanāmadheya, the Bodhisattva Mahādeva, the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa, the Bodhisattva Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍita, the Bodhisattva Indradhvajaprabhāsaśrī, the Bodhisattva Uttaramati, the Bodhisattva Jayamati, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva Susthitamati, the Bodhisattva Supravāraṇa, the Bodhisattva Anantamati, the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara. Such were the seventy-two thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

The Four Heavenly Kings, with Śakra, King of Devas, as their chief; the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; as well as the Brahma Kings and other Brahmā deities; together with immeasurable other devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all gathered there in great numbers.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of hundreds of thousands of millions of people, who gathered with reverence as he preached the Dharma for them.

Then, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha rose from his seat, adjusted his robes to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, shook this trichiliocosm and surveyed all sentient beings within it, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to ask a few questions; if the Buddha permits me, I shall venture to consult you.
The Buddha said, "Jālinīprabha!"
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it so as to gladden your heart.
Thereupon, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, having received this permission, was filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body surpass the radiance of hundreds of thousands of millions of suns and moons; I reflect to myself:
"If there are sentient beings who are able to see the Buddha’s body and contemplate it, that is truly rare."
I further reflected:
"If there are sentient beings who are able to see the Buddha's body and contemplate it, this is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata. The Buddha said:
“Jālinīprabha! It is so, it is so.

Just as you have said, if the Buddha-Tathāgata did not apply his majestic spiritual power (adhiṣṭhāna), no sentient being would be able to see the Buddha’s body or contemplate it, nor would there be anyone able to question the Tathāgata.”
Why is this? "Jālinīprabha!

The Tathāgata has a light named 'Tranquil Adornment. If this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it are able to see the Buddha’s body, contemplate the Buddha’s body, and do not impair their faculty of sight."

“Jālinīprabha! The Tathāgata possesses a light called ‘Fearless Eloquence. If this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it will be able to question the Tathāgata with inexhaustible eloquence.”

“Jālinīprabha! The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Gathering All Roots of Virtue. If this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it will be able to ask the Tathāgata about the causes and conditions for the deeds of a universal wheel-turning monarch.”

The Tathāgata possesses a light named Pure Adornment; if this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the karmic causes and conditions of Śakra, King of the Devas.

“The Tathāgata possesses a light named Sovereignty; if this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the karmic causes and conditions of the Great Brahmā King.”

The Tathāgata has a light named "Free from Affliction"; if this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it are able to ask the Tathāgata about the path practiced by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

“The Tathāgata has a light named ‘Skillful Detachment. If this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it will be able to ask the Tathāgata about the path practiced by those of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.”

The Tathāgata possesses a light named "Benefiting All Wisdom and Knowledge. If this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the supreme Buddha-vehicle, the Mahāyāna path.

“The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Benefiting Those Who Go. When he comes or goes, light radiates from beneath his feet; if this light touches sentient beings, those who encounter it will, at the end of their lives, be reborn in the heavens.”

“The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘All-Adorned. When the Buddha enters a city and emits this radiance, sentient beings who encounter it attain joy and gladness, and all manner of ornaments adorn that city.”
“The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Dispersion’; if this light touches various worlds, immeasurable and boundless worlds tremble.
The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Producing Joy’; if this light touches sentient beings, it can extinguish the suffering and affliction of beings in the hells.”
“The Tathāgata has a light named ‘Supreme Compassion’; if this light touches sentient beings, it can cause animals not to kill or harm one another.
The Tathāgata has a light named ‘Cool Refreshment’; if this light touches sentient beings, it can extinguish the hunger, thirst, and feverish afflictions of the hungry ghosts.”
“The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Luminous Purity’; if this light touches sentient beings, it can cause the blind to regain their sight.
The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Audiency of Hearing’; if this light touches sentient beings, it can cause the deaf to regain their hearing and perceive sounds.”

“The Tathāgata possesses a light called ‘Cessation’; if this light touches sentient beings, those who abide in the ten unwholesome paths of action will be enabled to dwell securely in the ten wholesome paths of action.”
“The Tathāgata possesses a light called ‘Shame and Modesty’; if this light touches sentient beings, it can cause those who are insane to all regain right mindfulness.
The Tathāgata possesses a light called ‘Departing from Evil’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those with wrong views to all attain right view.”
“The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Able to Relinquish. If this light touches sentient beings, it can cause those who are stingy to break their hearts of avarice and practice generosity.”
“The Tathāgata has a light named ‘Free from Regret and Heat’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who have violated the precepts to all come to uphold them.
The Tathāgata has a light named ‘Beneficial and Peaceful’; if this light touches sentient beings, it enables those who are prone to anger to all practice patience.”
“The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Diligent Cultivation’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who are indolent to practice diligence.
The Tathāgata possesses a light named ‘Single-Mindedness’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who have lost mindfulness to attain meditative concentration.”
“The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Able to Resolve’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who are ignorant and deluded to all attain wisdom.
The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Stainless Purity’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who lack faith to all attain right faith.”
“The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Able to Sustain’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who have heard little to become widely learned.
The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Dignified Conduct’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those who lack a sense of shame and remorse to attain shame and remorse.”
“The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Peaceful Security’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those with excessive desire to sever their lustful cravings.
The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Joyful Delight’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those with excessive anger to sever their hatred.”

“The Tathāgata possesses a light named Illumination; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those with much delusion to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby sever their ignorance.”

“The Tathāgata has a light called ‘Pervasive Movement’; if this light touches sentient beings, it causes those with equal proportions [of the defilements] to eliminate those equal proportions. Jālinīprabha!

The Tathāgata possesses a light called "Manifesting All Kinds of Colors. If this light touches sentient beings, it enables all who encounter it to see the Buddha’s body in various distinct colors, immeasurable kinds of colors, and more than hundreds of thousands of millions of colors.

“Jālinīprabha! You should know that whether for a single kalpa or for the remainder of the kalpas, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma based upon the light of the Tathāgata can never be exhausted.”
"Therefore, the merit of the light of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible.
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata manifests immeasurable and boundless bodily radiance and adornments, inconceivable, teaching the Dharma in accordance with skillful means.
World-Honored One!
"I have not heard these names of the various radiances,
World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, World-Honored One!"

If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing the names of these various radiances, are able to give rise to pure faith and a mind of reverence, those sentient beings will ultimately and certainly attain such a body of radiance as that of the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!

We pray that you will now emit the light that summons the bodhisattvas to awaken all bodhisattvas, so that those bodhisattvas from other regions who are skilled in posing difficult questions may all become aware [of this]. Once they have become aware, may they resolve to come to this Sahā world; having arrived here, may they question the Tathāgata, make offerings to the Tathāgata, and engage in dialogue with the Tathāgata.

At that time, having accepted the request of Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a radiance that illuminated the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of other directions.
Thereupon, immeasurable bodhisattvas from all directions, having been touched by the light of the Buddha upon their bodies, all came to this Sahā world.
At that time, to the east, beyond as many buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in seventy-two Ganges Rivers, there was a buddha-land named Pure and Clean.

In that world-system there is a Buddha named Candraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently lives, exists, and abides, teaching only the Dharma of purity for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

In that buddha-field, there was a bodhisattva brahmā named Viśeṣacintin who dwelt in the wheel of non-retrogression. Having been touched by the Buddha’s light upon his body, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this great radiance appeared in this world?
The Buddha Candraprabha replied, "Brahmā!"
To the west, passing from here through as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in seventy-two Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Sahā.
In it dwells a Buddha, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently lives, exists, and remains, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
"This light emitted from the body of that Buddha is for the purpose of gathering the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the ten directions.
Brahmā said, "World-Honored One!"

I now wish to go to the Sahā world to behold that Buddha, to make offerings to him, to pay homage, to attend upon him, and to engage in deep and subtle inquiry through questions and answers; that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, likewise desires to see me.
That Buddha said to him:
"Go then, Brahmā! Now is the very time."

"In that land, there are currently many thousands of billions of great bodhisattvas gathered before you. Brahmā! You should now travel to that world with ten kinds of pure and firm minds, namely: because your mind neither increases nor decreases in the face of blame or praise;

because you maintain a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) upon hearing both good and evil; because you maintain a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) toward both the ignorant and the wise; because your intention is always equanimous toward all classes of sentient beings—superior, middling, and inferior; because your mind remains free from duality whether receiving contempt or offerings; because you do not perceive the merits or faults of others; because you see all various vehicles as being of one single flavor; because your mind is not startled or terrified upon hearing of the three evil realms; because you conceive the thought of the World-Honored One toward all bodhisattvas; and because you conceive the thought of something rare and marvelous at the appearance of a Buddha in the five turbidities."
"Brahmā! You should dwell in those worlds by relying upon these ten kinds of pure and firm minds.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed his Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
However, I do not dare to utter a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata; what I am capable of practicing, the Buddha himself knows.
At that time, the other bodhisattvas in the land of the Tathāgata Candraprabha addressed their Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have attained great benefit, for I was not born in such a land, nor among such evil sentient beings.
The Buddha told him:
“O sons of good family!
Do not speak such words. Why is this?

If a bodhisattva were to practice the pure conduct of brahmacarya for a full hundred thousand kalpas in this land, it would not equal the merit of one who, in that Sahā world, maintains a mind free from anger and obstruction from morning until noon; the latter's merit is superior.
Why is this? Because that world is full of defilements and many hardships, and its sentient beings are full of defilements and much strife.
At that moment, there were twelve thousand bodhisattvas in that land who wished to set out together with the Brahma-deva Viśeṣacintin, saying:

"The Tathāgata knows our practice of the bodhisattva path; we too wish to travel through the Sahā world with these ten minds and a single mind, to see Śākyamuni Buddha, pay him homage, and make offerings to him, while traveling through that land with a single-minded concentration."

At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, prostrated themselves before the Buddha Candraprabha, and suddenly vanished from that land. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm—in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta—they arrived at the Sahā world where the Buddha Śākyamuni was. They prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, saying:
"Jālinīprabha! Do you see the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin coming?"
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
Indeed, I have seen it.”
The Buddha said:
"Jālinīprabha! Among all those who correctly question bodhisattvas, this Brahmā Viśeṣacintin is the foremost."
Among all bodhisattvas who skillfully preach the Dharma as they see fit, he is the foremost;
among all bodhisattvas with exquisite voices, he is the foremost;
among all bodhisattvas with exquisite speech, he is the foremost.
Among all Bodhisattvas who first inquire after others' welfare with their minds, he is the foremost;
among all Bodhisattvas who should offer worship through speech, he is the foremost;
among all Bodhisattvas whose speech is unobstructed, he is the foremost.
Among all bodhisattvas regarding intentional speech, he is the foremost;
among all bodhisattvas regarding a mind free from malice, he is the foremost;
among all bodhisattvas practicing loving-kindness, he is the foremost.
Among all bodhisattvas who practice with a mind of compassion, he is the foremost;
among all bodhisattvas who practice with a mind of sympathetic joy, he is the foremost;
among all bodhisattvas who practice with a mind of equanimity, he is the foremost.
"Among all Bodhisattvas who inquire with a mind of doubt regarding all things wholesome, he is the foremost.

At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, together with twelve thousand Bodhisattvas, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse and requested:
"The World-Honored One of great and supreme fame Is universally heard throughout the ten directions."
All the Tathāgatas wherever they may be have none who do not praise you.
There are other pure lands where even the names of the three evil realms do not exist;
yet you have forsaken such wondrous lands to be born here out of compassion.
The Buddha is named Wisdom Without Diminution, equal to all Tathāgatas;
by virtue of his great compassion and original vow, he dwells in this defiled and evil land.
If a person were to practice the Brahma-conduct in a pure land for the full duration of one kalpa, [their merit would not equal that of one who practices here].
In this land, for even a brief moment, practicing loving-kindness is supreme.
If a person in this land has committed offenses of body, speech,
or mind that would cause them to fall into the three evil realms, they shall be purified and removed in this very life.
Bodhisattvas born in this land Should not harbor grief or distress;
Even if they have offenses leading to evil realms, Their headaches shall be relieved.
If the bodhisattvas of this land Are able to protect the Dharma, [they shall attain liberation].
In every place of birth throughout successive lives, one shall not lose right mindfulness.
If a person wishes to sever their bonds, extinguish afflictions, karma, and transgressions,
protect the Dharma in this land, and increase all-encompassing wisdom.
Though one may uphold the pure precepts for many billions of kalpas in the Land of Purity,
it is more excellent to do so from dawn until noon here in this Sahā world.
I have seen the Land of Peace and Bliss, the realm of Amitāyus Buddha.
One who neither experiences suffering nor even the name of suffering, and whose performance of merit is not considered extraordinary—
yet who, amidst these very afflictions, is able to endure what is unbearable and teaches this Dharma to others— their merit is the most supreme.
I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Greatly Compassionate Savior from Suffering,
who is able to endure wicked sentient beings and whose preaching of the Dharma is exceedingly difficult.
The Buddha has gathered from the worlds of the ten directions all those Bodhisattvas of renowned fame.
To those who listen to the Dharma without weariness, he extensively expounds the Buddha-way.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and all the devas, nāgas, and spirits—all desire to seek the Dharma; may he preach according to their faith and joy.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as laymen and laywomen of pure faith—
may these four assemblies gather together, and you, O World-Honored One, please expound the Dharma for them at this time.
There are those who delight in the Buddha-vehicle, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha, knowing their profound intent, willed that all their doubts be severed.
Those who do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas are able to give birth to the Triple Gem;
for the sake of these bodhisattvas, I now entreat the Dharma King.
Your fame spreads everywhere; Bodhisattvas from the ten directions have heard it and have all gathered together. We pray that you will expound the unsurpassed Way.
This Dharma is not the realm of the two vehicles, yet we enter it through the power of faith.
Inconceivable wisdom is the domain of the Buddha alone.
I now have a request: I repent before the World-Honored One.
Since the Tathāgata never tires, I pray that you will explain the path to bodhi.
At that time, after the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin had praised him with verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva’s mind is firm and does not grow weary?”
How does a bodhisattva ensure that what they say is definitive and free from subsequent regret?
How does a bodhisattva increase all roots of goodness?
How does a bodhisattva remain free from fear and maintain unshakable dignified conduct?
How does a bodhisattva increase all wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*)?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know how to proceed from one stage (*bhūmi*) to the next?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the expedient means (*upāya*) for teaching and transforming sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva accord with all sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva not lose the bodhicitta?
How is a bodhisattva able to unify the mind so that it is not distracted?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully seek the Dharma?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully eliminate the transgression of violating the precepts?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully sever all afflictions?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully enter among the great assemblies?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully open the gift of Dharma?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the power of prior causes so as not to lose their roots of goodness?
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to practice the six pāramitās by themselves without relying on the instruction of others?
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to relinquish meditative concentration and intentionally take rebirth in the desire realm?
"How does a bodhisattva attain non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas?
How does a bodhisattva practice according to reality so as not to sever the lineage of the Buddhas?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Brahmā! Excellent!”
Brahmā! You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning. Brahmā!
"Listen now with a sincere mind; I shall speak for you.
Mahābrahmā said, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, "Brahmā!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas, whereby their minds are firm and they do not grow weary. What are these four?
First, because they give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Second, because they are diligent and never slacken;
third, because they believe and understand that birth and death are like a dream;
fourth, because they correctly contemplate the unequaled wisdom of the Buddha.
"Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish these four dharmas; thus their minds are firm and they do not grow weary. Brahmā!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas, such that what they say is definitive and they do not later regret it. What are these four?
First, they definitively teach that all phenomena are without self.
Second, because he definitively teaches that there is no happiness in any place of rebirth;
third, because he definitively and constantly praises the Mahāyāna;
fourth, because he definitively teaches that the karmic results of transgressions and merits are never lost.
"Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish these four dharmas, such that what they say is definitive and they never regret it midway. Brahmā!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas that cause all roots of goodness to increase. What are these four?
First, because they uphold the precepts;...
Second, because of extensive learning;
third, because of practicing generosity;
fourth, because of leaving the household life.
These are the four dharmas.
"Brahmā! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished these four dharmas, they are without fear, and their dignified deportment remains unshakable."
What are the four?
First, not fearing the failure to obtain wealth and profit;
second, not fearing defamation and humiliation.
Third, not fearing an evil reputation;
fourth, not fearing suffering and affliction.
These are the four dharmas.
“Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas that cause all white dharmas to increase. What are these four?
First, because they teach all sentient beings to practice for great enlightenment;
second, because they practice giving without seeking karmic retribution;
third, because they protect and uphold the true Dharma.
Fourth, because they teach wisdom to all bodhisattvas;
these are the four dharmas. "Brahmā!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and thus skillfully know how to proceed from one stage to the next. What are these four?
First, the accumulation of all roots of goodness.
Second, because they are far removed from all faults;
third, because they skillfully know the dedication of merit through expedient means;
fourth, because they are constantly diligent and energetic.
These are the four dharmas.
"Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and thus skillfully know the expedient means for teaching and transforming sentient beings."
What are the four? First, because of acting in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings;
second, because of giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the merits of others.
Third, because of repenting of transgressions to eliminate offenses;
fourth, because of exhorting and requesting all Buddhas;
these are the four dharmas.
“Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas to accord with all sentient beings.
What are these four?
First, because they constantly seek the benefit and peace of all sentient beings;
second, because they personally renounce their own happiness;
third, because their minds are harmonious and patient.
Fourth, because of abandoning arrogance;
these are the four dharmas. "Brahmā!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and do not lose the bodhicitta. What are these four?
First, they constantly recollect the Buddha.
Second, because the roots of goodness they cultivate are never separated from the bodhicitta;
third, because they draw near to spiritual friends;
fourth, because they praise the Mahāyāna.
These are the four dharmas.
"Brahmā! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished these four dharmas, they are able to unify their minds so that they do not become distracted."
What are the four?
First, because of being far removed from the mind of a śrāvaka;
second, because of relinquishing the mental inclinations of a pratyekabuddha.
Third, because they seek the Dharma without weariness;
fourth, because they extensively expound for others the Dharma as they have heard it.
These are the four dharmas.
“Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and thus skillfully seek the Dharma.
What are these four?
First, one should conceive of the Dharma as a precious jewel because it is difficult to obtain;
second, one should conceive of the Dharma as a sublime medicine because it cures all ailments;
third, one should conceive of the Dharma as wealth and profit because it is never lost.
Fourth, because one gives rise to the perception of suffering regarding the arising and ceasing of phenomena until reaching nirvāṇa;
these are the four dharmas. "Brahmā!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and are thus well able to emerge from the transgression of violating the precepts.
What are these four? First, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through internal contemplation of all phenomena.
Second, they attain the patience of non-extinction because all phenomena have no departure;
third, they attain the patience of causes and conditions by contemplating the causal conditions of all phenomena;
fourth, they attain the patience of non-abiding because there is neither new nor old.
These are the four dharmas.
"Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who ultimately accomplish these four dharmas thoroughly sever all afflictions."
What are the four? First, through correct observation;
second, by distancing oneself from all future obstacles and increasing all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Third, because of attaining the power of wholesome dharmas;
fourth, because of dwelling alone in seclusion.
These are the four dharmas.
“Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and thus skillfully enter among the great assemblies.
What are these four?
First, seeking the Dharma without seeking victory;
second, possessing a respectful mind free from arrogance;
third, seeking only the Dharma without seeking self-exaltation.
Fourth, teaching others the wholesome Dharma without seeking fame or profit;
these are the four dharmas. "Brahmā!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and are thus skilled in opening up the gift of Dharma. What are these four?
First, they guard and protect the Dharma.
Second, because one benefits oneself with wisdom and also benefits others;
third, because one practices the dharma of virtuous persons;
fourth, because one demonstrates to others both defilement and purity.
These are the four dharmas.
"Brahmā! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished these four dharmas, they obtain the power of prior causes and do not lose their roots of goodness."
What are the four? First, not seeing the faults of others' shortcomings;
second, constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness toward those who are angry.
Third, constantly teaching the causes and conditions of all phenomena;
fourth, constantly recollecting bodhi—
these are the four dharmas.
“Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas by which they are able to practice the six pāramitās on their own, without relying on the instruction of others.”
What are the four? First, leading others through the practice of giving;
second, not speaking of the faults of others who have violated the precepts.
Third, skillfully knowing how to gather beings through the Dharma for their transformation;
fourth, attaining a thorough understanding of the profound Dharma.
These are the four dharmas.
“Brahmā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas by which they are able to relinquish their meditative concentrations and be reborn in the desire realm.
What are these four?
First, because their minds are supple;
second, because they have attained the power of all roots of goodness;
third, because they have skillfully cultivated the power of wisdom and expedient means.
Fourth, because they do not abandon any sentient beings;
these are the four dharmas. "Brahmā!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish four dharmas and thereby attain non-retrogression from all Buddha-dharmas. What are these four?
First, they are able to endure immeasurable birth and death.
Second, because they make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
third, because they practice immeasurable great loving-kindness;
fourth, because they practice immeasurable great compassion.
These are the four dharmas.
"Brahmā! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished these four dharmas, they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas and practice according to reality."
What are the four?
First, because they do not retreat from their original vows;
second, because they practice according to reality.
Third, because of great desire and diligence toward all wholesome dharmas;
fourth, because of practicing the Buddha-way with a profound mind. Brahmā!
"When all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished these four dharmas, they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas and practice according to reality.

While these and other such sets of four dharmas were being taught, twenty-two thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and five thousand Bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions came to make offerings to the Buddha; the celestial flowers they scattered pervaded the trichiliocosm, accumulating until they reached the height of the knees.
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha asked the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin:
"Brahmā, the Buddha has declared you to be the foremost among all bodhisattvas who ask correct questions. In what way is a bodhisattva’s inquiry considered a correct question?"
Brahmā said: "Jālinīprabha!
If a bodhisattva asks because he perceives a self, it is called an erroneous question, not a correct one."
To ask questions out of a desire to see others is called an erroneous question, not a correct one;
to ask questions that differentiate between phenomena is called an erroneous question, not a correct one.
Jālinīprabha!
If a bodhisattva asks questions without the view of self, without the view of another, and without the view of phenomena, this is called a correct question and not a perverse question.
"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!..."

If a bodhisattva asks about arising, it is called an erroneous question; if they ask about cessation, it is called an erroneous question; if they ask about what is possible and what is impossible, it is called an erroneous question.
Jālinīprabha!

If a bodhisattva does not inquire from the perspective of arising, does not inquire from the perspective of cessation, and does not inquire from the perspective of what is possible or impossible, this is called a correct inquiry.

"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha! If a bodhisattva asks for the sake of defilement, it is called an improper question; if they ask for the sake of purification, it is called an improper question; if they ask for the sake of birth-and-death, it is called an improper question; if they ask for the sake of transcending birth-and-death, it is called an improper question; and if they ask for the sake of nirvana, it is called an improper question."
Jālinīprabha!

If a bodhisattva does not inquire for the sake of defilement or purification, does not inquire for the sake of birth-and-death or emerging from birth-and-death, and does not inquire for the sake of nirvāṇa, this is called a correct inquiry.
Why is this? Because within the station of dharmas, there is neither defilement nor purity, neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!

If a bodhisattva asks for the sake of acquisition, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of grasping, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of realization, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of discrimination, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of knowledge, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of reliance, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of cultivation, it is not a correct question; if they ask for the sake of cultivating views, it is not a correct question.
Therefore, Jālinīprabha!

To ask by way of that which is without attainment, without grasping, without realization, without discrimination, without knowledge, without reliance, without cultivation, and without the view of cultivation—this is the correct question.

"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha! If a bodhisattva [discerns] that this is a wholesome dharma and that is an unwholesome dharma; that this is a dharma with outflows and that is a dharma without outflows; that this is a faulty dharma and that is a faultless dharma; that this is a conditioned dharma and that is an unconditioned dharma; and that this is a mundane dharma and that is a supramundane dharma."
Jālinīprabha!
To ask about these two dharmas according to their respective bases is called an erroneous question.
Jālinīprabha!
If a bodhisattva perceives neither duality nor non-duality, and practices with equanimity regarding the signless and the signless, this is called a correct question.
"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!..."

If a bodhisattva discriminates when asking about the Buddha, it is called a wrong question; if they discriminate when asking about the Dharma, it is called a wrong question; if they discriminate when asking about the Saṅgha, it is called a wrong question; if they discriminate when asking about the Buddha-lands, it is called a wrong question; if they discriminate when asking about sentient beings, it is called a wrong question; if they discriminate when asking about the vehicles (yāna), it is called a wrong question.
Jālinīprabha!
If a bodhisattva does not pose questions regarding phenomena in terms of unity or difference, this is called a correct question.
"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!"
"All dharmas are correct; all dharmas are erroneous!
Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said, "Brahmā!..."
"What is the correctness of all dharmas?
What is the deviance of all dharmas? Brahmā said:
“Jālinīprabha! Because all phenomena are inconceivable, all phenomena are called ‘correct.
If one conceives of that which is inconceivable, all phenomena are called ‘erroneous.’”
The tranquility of all phenomena is called right reflection; if one does not have faith in or understand this tranquility, that is to conceptually differentiate all phenomena.
To differentiate all phenomena is to enter into overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and whatever is conceptually differentiated by one who has entered overweening pride is termed a false inquiry.
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
“Brahmā, what is called the true nature of all phenomena?”
Brahmā said: "Jālinīprabha!
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and reach the limit of detachment; this is called the 'Right Nature' (samyaktva)."
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
"Brahmā! There are few sentient beings who are able to understand the true nature of all such phenomena."
The Brahmā said:
"This true nature of phenomena is neither one nor many,
O Jālinīprabha!"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who can thus know the true nature of all phenomena—whether they have known it, are now knowing it, or will know it in the future—such persons have no phenomenon already attained, no phenomenon being attained now, and no phenomenon to be attained in the future.
Why is this? The Buddha has taught that non-attainment and non-discrimination are called the mark of one who has completed what was to be done.
Jālinīprabha!
If there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard this true nature of all phenomena, practice with diligent effort, this is called practicing according to reality.
That person does not engage in conceptual play with any phenomena; if one does not engage in conceptual play with any phenomena, that person has no attainment of any phenomenon.
If there is no attainment of any phenomenon, that person dwells neither in the world nor in nirvāṇa.
"Why is this? Because the Buddhas neither attain birth-and-death nor attain nirvana.
Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
“Brahmā! Does the Tathāgata not preach the Dharma for the sake of crossing over birth and death? Brahmā replied:
“Is there a teaching shown by the Buddha that brings about the transcendence of birth and death? He replied: “There is not.”
“The Tathāgata does not cause sentient beings to leave the world, nor does he cause sentient beings to attain nirvāṇa.
Brahmā said: “Good son!...”

For this reason, you should know that the Tathāgata does not cause sentient beings to emerge from birth-and-death and enter into nirvāṇa; rather, he merely acts to transform and deliver those who falsely discriminate between the two marks of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa. Within this, there is in reality no one who emerges from birth-and-death and reaches nirvāṇa.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are equal; in reality, there is no person who comes and goes within birth and death, nor is there any person who enters into nirvana, for they are neither defiled nor pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O Brahmā!"
Excellent, Brahmā!
If anyone wishes to speak of the true nature of all phenomena, they should do so as you have spoken.
When this Dharma was being taught, two thousand bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any phenomena, attained the exhaustion of outflows and their minds were liberated.
The Tathāgata again addressed the Great Brahmā, saying: “Brahmā!
I do not apprehend birth-and-death, nor do I apprehend nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Although the Tathāgata speaks of birth-and-death, in reality there is no person who comes and goes within birth-and-death.
Although nirvāṇa is spoken of, in reality there is no one who attains nirvāṇa.
If there is one who enters such a dharma-gate, you should know that this person possesses neither the marks of birth-and-death nor the marks of nirvāṇa.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus in the assembly rose from their seats and spoke these words:
"If there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, then we have practiced the holy life in vain."
"For what purpose do they practice the right path, the various dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"World-Honored One, if there are those who give rise to views of arising or views of cessation regarding the Dharma, such persons do not transcend birth and death; for them, the Buddha has not appeared in the world."
World-Honored One!
If there were one who held a fixed view regarding nirvāṇa, that person would neither transcend birth and death nor attain nirvāṇa. Why is this?
The World-Honored One said:
"Nirvana is called the eradication of all marks, because it is far removed from all movement, all notions of self, all impulses, and all conceptual play."
"World-Honored One!

These bhikṣus have already left the household life within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, yet they have now fallen into the heterodox views of non-Buddhists, seeking a definitive mark within the bliss of nirvāṇa—just as one extracts oil from sesame seeds or butter from curd."
"World-Honored One!
If there are those who seek nirvana within the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena, I declare that such people are heterodox practitioners of overweening pride and false views."
“World-Honored One!
For one who practices the Path correctly, regarding the dharma of quiescence, they do not conceive the mark of arising nor the mark of cessation; there is neither attainment nor fruit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, Prince of Dharma, asked the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin:

"How may I employ various skillful means to guide the minds of these five hundred bhikṣus who have risen from their seats and departed, leading them into this Dharma-door so that they may attain faith and understanding, and be freed from evil and false views?"
Brahmā said: “Good son!
Even if one were to go to as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, one could not find such a Dharma-gate.”
It is like a foolish person who, fearing empty space, abandons it and flees; yet wherever he goes, he does not leave empty space behind.

These bhikṣus are just the same: though they travel far away, they do not transcend the mark of emptiness, they do not transcend the mark of signlessness, and they do not transcend the mark of wishlessness.
Furthermore, it is like a person who seeks empty space, running back and forth while saying,
"I wish to obtain space; I wish to obtain space," yet though he moves through the midst of space, he does not see space.
These bhikṣus are also like this: desiring to seek nirvāṇa, they practice within nirvāṇa yet do not attain nirvāṇa.
Why is this? That which is called "nirvāṇa" exists only as a name; just as space exists only as a name and cannot be grasped, so too is nirvāṇa: it exists only as a name and cannot be attained.

At that time, having heard this teaching, five hundred bhikṣus did not grasp at any phenomena; their outflows were exhausted and their minds attained liberation. Having attained the supernormal powers, they spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
If a person seeks nirvana within the state of ultimate quiescence of all phenomena, for that person, the Buddha has not appeared in the world.
World-Honored One!
We who are now here are neither ordinary beings, nor those in training (*śaikṣa*), nor those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), nor Arhats; we do not abide in the world, nor do we abide in nirvana.
Why is this? Because it is through being free from all movement, all notions of self, all impulses, and all conceptual play that it is called the appearance of the Buddhas in the world.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the bhikṣus:
"Are you now truly śramaṇas, such that all that was to be done for your own benefit has been fully accomplished?"
The bhikṣus said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
We have now become defiled by various afflictions; we have done what should not be done."
Śāriputra said: "Venerable elders, for what reason do you speak thus?"
The bhikṣus said: "Śāriputra!
We understand the characteristics of all afflictions; therefore we say that one who is defiled by afflictions performs what should not be done."
"Śāriputra! It is with this intention that I have spoken thus: 'I have already attained all the defilements of affliction;
I do what ought not to be done. Śāriputra said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
You who now abide as fields of merit are able to consume offerings.”
The bhikṣus said: “Śāriputra!
Even our Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, cannot yet digest such offerings; how much less can we digest them?”
Śāriputra asked, "For what reason do you speak thus?
The bhikṣus replied:
“Śāriputra! The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, knows and perceives the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), for that nature is eternally pure.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Who is it that should receive offerings from the world?
The Buddha said:
"Brahmā! One who is not led away by worldly dharmas.
Thus spoke the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin.
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to digest these offerings?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā, it refers to one who does not grasp at or cling to any phenomena. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
Who is pure enough to serve as a field of merit and capable of receiving offerings?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! It refers to those who do not destroy the bodhicitta. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
Who is the true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
"Brahmā! It means not abandoning a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
Who knows how to repay the Buddha’s kindness?
The Buddha said:
"Brahmā! It refers to those who do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
How does one make offerings to the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! It is because of penetrating the limit of non-arising. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to draw near to the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! Even at the cost of losing one’s life, one shall not violate the prohibitions.
“World-Honored One!”
"Who is able to pay reverence to the Buddha?
The Buddha said,
"One who well guards the six sense faculties."
“World-Honored One!
Who in the world is said to possess wealth?
The Buddha said:
"One who has accomplished the seven riches.
"World-Honored One!
Who is called 'one who is content'?"
The Buddha said,
“One who has attained supramundane, supreme prajñā.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"Who is it that practices detachment?
The Buddha said:
"One who has no aspirations within the three realms."
“World-Honored One!
Who is it that is free from all unwholesome conduct in the world?
The Buddha said:
"One who is able to sever all fetters and taints.
"World-Honored One,
who is called a person of pleasure?"
The Buddha said,
“There is no attachment.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"Who is able to reach the other shore?
The Buddha said,
"One who is able to relinquish the six sense bases."
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to abide on the other shore?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! You have reached the path of equality.
“World-Honored One!”
"How do bodhisattvas increase their giving?
The Buddha said,
"Because bodhisattvas can explain the mind of omniscience to sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
How can bodhisattvas uphold the precepts?
The Buddha said:
“Because they are always able to never abandon the bodhicitta.
“World-Honored One,
how are the bodhisattvas able to practice patience?”
The Buddha said:
"Because one perceives that the mind of omniscience is inexhaustible. [The interlocutor asked:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice diligence?
The Buddha said:
"Because they do not apprehend the mind of omniscience through observation."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice meditative concentration?
The Buddha said:
“Because they are able to awaken to the fact that the intrinsic nature of the mind of omniscience is pure.
“World-Honored One!
How is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice prajñā?”
The Buddha said:
“Because there is no conceptual proliferation regarding any phenomena.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"How is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice a mind of loving-kindness?
The Buddha said,
"Because they do not give rise to the perception of sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice compassion?
The Buddha said:
“Because they do not give rise to the notion of dharmas.
“World-Honored One,
how is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice the mind of sympathetic joy?”
The Buddha said,
“Because they do not give rise to the notion of a self.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"How is it that bodhisattvas are able to practice the mind of equanimity?
The Buddha said,
"Because they do not give rise to the notions of 'self' and 'other'."
“World-Honored One!
How do the bodhisattvas abide in faith?
The Buddha said:
“Because one has faith that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression.
“World-Honored One,
how do bodhisattvas abide in the wisdom derived from hearing?”
The Buddha said,
“Because they do not cling to any phenomena characterized by names.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"How do the bodhisattvas abide in a state of having a sense of shame?
The Buddha said,
"Because they know and see internal phenomena."
“World-Honored One!
How do the bodhisattvas abide in a sense of shame?
The Buddha said:
“Because of relinquishing the external sense bases.
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a bodhisattva’s universal practice in all places of merit?”
The Buddha said:
"One can purify the actions of body, speech, and mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The body is pure and free from all evils; the speech is pure and free from false words;
the mind is pure and detached from all defilements—this is the universal conduct of the Bodhisattva.
Contemplating impurity, they are free from greed; practicing loving-kindness, they are free from hatred."
Because they practice wisdom, they are free from delusion; this is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
Whether in a village, a wilderness, or amidst a great assembly, their dignified demeanor never falters; this is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
Faithfully knowing that the Dharma is the Buddha, faithfully knowing that detachment is the Dharma,
and faithfully knowing that the unconditioned is the Sangha— this is the universal practice of the Bodhisattva.
Knowing the conduct of those with much desire, and the conduct of those with much hatred and delusion,
Skillfully knowing how to transform this practice is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
Not relying on the desire realm, not dwelling in the form or formless realms,
practicing such meditative concentration is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
Knowing that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless,
yet not exhausting the outflows— this is the universal practice of the bodhisattva.
Skillfully knowing the vehicle of the śrāvakas, as well as the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,
Thoroughly penetrating the Buddha-vehicle— this is the universal practice of the bodhisattva.
Clearly understanding all phenomena, without doubting what is the path and what is not the path,
and maintaining equanimity toward love and hatred— this is the universal practice of the bodhisattva.
"In the past, the future, and the present age, there is no conceptual discrimination whatsoever; this is the universal conduct of the bodhisattva.
— *The Scripture of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*, Fascicle One.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Brahma Viśeṣacintin, Volume Two.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the Brahma Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva transcend..."
How does one dwell amidst worldly phenomena while remaining untainted by those worldly phenomena?
How does one truly and skillfully know all worldly phenomena according to worldly phenomena, yet remain untainted by worldly phenomena?
"How does one teach and transform sentient beings so that they leave the world behind, yet attain the equality of worldly dharmas and act within the world without destroying worldly dharmas?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Brahmā in verse:
"I say that the aggregates (skandhas) are the world, The basis upon which the world depends."
Not relying on the five aggregates, one attains liberation from worldly dharmas.
The Bodhisattva possesses wisdom; knowing the true nature of the world, although associated with the five aggregates, he is not defiled by them.
Gain and loss, praise and blame, Censure and honor, suffering and pleasure—
These eight worldly dharmas Constantly drag the world along.
The Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom Knows these worldly phenomena as they truly are.
Seeing the signs of the world’s decay, he remains unmoved within it;
gaining profit, his mind does not exult; losing profit, his mind does not sink.
His mind is firm and unshakable, following no worldly ways.
Gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—
regarding these eight worldly dharmas, his mind remains ever equanimous.
Knowing that the world is illusory and arises from the two inversions, he dwells in detachment.
The wise Bodhisattva does not follow the worldly path.
He fully understands all the paths that exist in the world;
therefore, he is able to deliver sentient beings from their suffering within the world.
Though they act within the world, they remain unstained like a lotus;
yet they do not destroy worldly conventions, for they have thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Moving through the world while in the world, they do not perceive it as "the world."
The Bodhisattva moves through the world, clearly understanding the characteristics of the world.
The world has the characteristic of emptiness, and emptiness itself is without characteristic;
knowing this, the Bodhisattva is not defiled by the world.
Just as the world is known, so it is explained according to that knowledge;
because one knows the nature of the world, one does not destroy the world.
The five aggregates have no intrinsic nature; this is precisely the nature of the world.
If a person does not know this, they remain bound within the world;
if they see and know the five aggregates to be neither arising nor ceasing,
such a person moves through the world without relying upon it.
Ordinary people do not know the Dharma; they give rise to disputes in the world, contending over what is real and what is unreal, dwelling within these two extremes.
I am never at variance with the world, nor do I engage in such matters of dispute.
Because they have fully realized the true nature of the world,
all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas are entirely free from dispute;
for they know the world to be equal, these teachings are neither real nor false.
If the Buddha-dharma were fixed, such that there were both truth and falsehood,
it would constitute attachment, no different from the teachings of the non-Buddhists.
But within the Buddha-dharma now, there is neither truth nor falsehood.
Therefore, I have always taught that the supramundane dharma is non-dual.
If a person knows the true nature of the world in this way,
they will not grasp at these evil views regarding what is real or what is false.
One who thus knows the world to be as pure as space is a person of great renown, illuminating the world like the sun.
If a person sees the world as I see it, [they shall likewise attain this state].
Such persons as these are able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
All phenomena arise from conditions; they possess no inherent nature of their own.
If one understands this principle of dependent origination, one will penetrate the true reality of all phenomena.
If one knows the true nature of phenomena, one then knows the characteristic of emptiness;
if one can know the characteristic of emptiness, one sees the Teacher.
If there are those who hear such a description of the nature of the world, [they shall attain liberation].
Though one acts within the world, one does not dwell in the world.
Those who rely on various views cannot reach this matter:
how can one act in the world without relying upon the world?
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are those who delight in this patience,
the Buddha will always appear before them in the world.
If a person understands and realizes this, they shall protect my Dharma.
They also make offerings to me; they too are teachers of the world.
If a person, for even a brief moment, understands that the nature of the world is thus, that person will never provide an opportunity for the evil Māra to gain the upper hand.
If one can penetrate this meaning, they possess great wisdom;
such a person is truly wealthy, a patron who bestows the riches of the Dharma.
If one understands the world in this way, they are likewise endowed with the precepts.
With the strength of patience, courageous and firm, advancing with great diligence,
he is fully endowed with all meditative concentrations and has attained the great supernormal powers;
through wisdom, he knows the paths of all worlds as they truly are.
If one can practice in this way, they will accomplish samādhi;
delighting in a place of tranquility, they will give rise to prajñā.
Wherever this Dharma is heard, there the Buddha is not in vain.
Such bodhisattvas will, before long, sit at the site of enlightenment.
If one possesses deep knowledge and vision of the nature of this world,
then they can subdue all Māras and swiftly attain the unsurpassed path.
The Tathāgata further addressed the Brahmā Śikhin: “Brahmā, the Tathāgata, having transcended the world,
teaches the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.”

Brahmā! As for what is called "the world," I say that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are named the world; attachment to the five aggregates is named the origin of the world; the exhaustion of the five aggregates is named the cessation of the world; and observing the five aggregates without perceiving two distinct phenomena is named the path to the cessation of the world.

Furthermore, Brahmā! As for what are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the five aggregates are merely verbal designations. Within them, grasping at linguistic expressions and false views is called the world; not abandoning these views is called the origin of the world; seeing the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of these views is called the cessation of the world; and by whatever path one does not grasp these views, that is called the path leading to the cessation of the world.
Brahmā! This is my intention;
therefore, within this very fathom-high body of mine, I now teach the suffering of the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the Four Noble Truths spoken of by the Buddha, I do not yet know which among them are the true Noble Truths.”
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! That which is called the Truth of Suffering is not, in reality, a Noble Truth.”
Brahmā! That which is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering is not, in reality, a noble truth. Brahmā!
That which is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering is not a real noble truth,
Brahmā! That which is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is not a real noble truth.
“Brahmā! If that suffering were a true noble truth, then all cattle, swine, and other such animals would also possess a true truth. Why is this?
Because they all undergo various kinds of suffering,
for this reason, suffering is not a true reality. "Brahmā!
If that accumulation were a truly real noble truth, then sentient beings of the six realms would possess a truly real truth.
Why is this? Because it is due to that cause of accumulation that they are born into the various destinies.
For this reason, accumulation is not a true noble truth.

"Brahmā! If that cessation were a true noble truth, then all the world would fall into the false view of annihilationism, and those who speak of the dharma of cessation would possess a true noble truth."
Why is this? Because they teach that the cessation of phenomena is nirvana; for this reason, cessation is not a real truth. "Brahmā!
If that path were a truly real noble truth, then all paths conditioned by the conditioned would likewise have to be real truths.
Why? Because they rely upon conditioned phenomena while seeking liberation from conditioned phenomena.
For this reason, the Path is not a true reality.
"Brahmā! Therefore, you should know that the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path are not true noble truths."
Brahmā! That which is the true noble truth consists in knowing that suffering is non-arising; this is called the true noble truth of suffering.
Knowing that the origin of suffering is non-conjunction; this is called the true noble truth of the origin of suffering.
Within the dharma of ultimate cessation, knowing there is neither arising nor ceasing is called the noble truth of the reality of cessation;
regarding all dharmas with equanimity and attaining the Way through the non-dual dharma is called the noble truth of the reality of the path.
“Brahmā! That which is the true noble truth is neither false speech nor true speech. Brahmā!”
What is false speech?

It refers to attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, attachment to a life-principle, attachment to a person, and attachment to an individual; attachment to the view of eternalism, attachment to the view of nihilism; attachment to the view of existence, attachment to the view of non-existence; attachment to the view of arising, attachment to the view of cessation; and attachment to the view of saṃsāra, attachment to the view of nirvāṇa.
Brahmā! This is called false speech. Brahmā!
If one does not adhere to such views, does not come into contact with such views, and does not grasp such views, this is called speaking the truth.
"Brahmā! If a practitioner says, 'I know suffering,' this is called false speech."
If a practitioner says, "I have abandoned the origin [of suffering]," this is called false speech.
If a practitioner says, "I have realized cessation," this is called false speech.
If a practitioner says, "I am cultivating the path," this is called false speech.
Why is this? Because it does not accord with the mindfulness permitted by the Buddha, it is called false speech. "Brahmā!
What is the mindfulness approved by the Buddha?
It is the non-recollection of all phenomena.
If one does not recollect any phenomena, this is called the mindfulness approved by the Buddha.
If a practitioner dwells within this mindfulness, they do not dwell in any signs;
if they do not dwell in any signs, they dwell in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
if they dwell in the limit of reality, this is called the non-dwelling mind.
If one does not dwell in the mind, such a person is called neither a speaker of true words nor a speaker of false words. Brahmā!
Therefore, you should know that one who is neither a speaker of true words nor a speaker of false words is called a noble one and possesses the noble truth.

“Brahmā! That which is called ‘the real’ is so because it has been real from antiquity to the present. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is always thus; the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is eternally thus; and the world and nirvāṇa are likewise eternally thus. Because it is thus, it is called the Real Noble Truth.”
Why is this? It is not that being apart from birth and death is called a Noble Truth, nor is it that causing one to grasp at nirvāṇa is called a Noble Truth. “Brahmā!
If a person realizes these Four Noble Truths in this manner, they are called one who speaks the truth. Brahmā!

In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom. Such persons will say that the characteristic of arising is the Truth of Suffering; the harmony of various conditions is the Truth of Origination; the cessation of phenomena is the Truth of Cessation; and seeking characteristics by means of the non-dual dharma is the Truth of the Path.

"Brahmā! I say that those foolish people are followers of external paths who have fallen into evil realms; I am not their teacher, and they are not my śrāvaka disciples. Because such people follow external, heterodox paths and have destroyed and lost the Dharma, they claim that there are truths."
“Brahmā! Observe this:

when I sat at the site of enlightenment, I did not find even a single dharma that was either real or false speech. If a Buddha does not find any dharma, could there possibly be any verbal expression, any formal discussion, or any teaching among the assembly regarding such a dharma?”
The Brahmā said: “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!
Because all phenomena are unattainable and because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, my awakening is characterized by the absence of craving.”
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata has no attainment regarding any dharma, for what reason is it said that the Tathāgata sitting at the site of enlightenment is called a Buddha?"
“By realizing what dharma, O Brahmā, is the Tathāgata called ‘the One Worthy of Offerings, Truly and Fully Enlightened’? The Buddha said: “Brahmā!”
What do you think? Are the dharmas I have taught conditioned or unconditioned?
Are these dharmas real?
"Is it false? Brahmā said, "World-Honored One!"
"These dharmas are false and not real,
Sugata! These dharmas are false and not real."
The Buddha said, “Brahmā! What do you think?”
“If a dharma is illusory and not real, does that dharma exist or does it not exist?
Brahmā replied:
“World-Honored One!
If a dharma is illusory, that dharma should neither be said to exist nor should it be said not to exist.
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! What do you think? If a dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, can that dharma be apprehended?”
Brahmā said: “World-Honored One!
If a dharma is non-existent, that dharma cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist.”
The Buddha said,
“Brahmā! If a phenomenon is neither existent nor non-existent, how can that phenomenon be realized?”
The Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
That dharma is not realized.”
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!

When the Tathāgata sat at the site of enlightenment, he knew only that all afflictions and defilements arising from false and inverted perceptions are ultimately non-arising; he attained this through non-attainment, and he knew this through non-knowing.”
"Why is this? "Brahmā!

The Dharma I have attained cannot be seen, cannot be heard, cannot be perceived, cannot be cognized, cannot be remembered, cannot be grasped, cannot be clung to, cannot be spoken, and cannot be challenged. It transcends all spheres of experience; it is without speech or expression, without activity or seeking, without letters, and beyond the path of language. It is not a sphere of consciousness, being without characters and unspeakable by words."
"Brahmā! That Dharma is thus, just like empty space; do you then wish to attain realization within such a Dharma? Brahmā replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are truly most rare;

they have accomplished inconceivable and unprecedented dharmas, have deeply entered great kindness and great compassion, and having attained such a dharma of the mark of cessation, they teach others through words and language so that they may attain it as well."
World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this Dharma, are able to believe and understand it, one should know that these people have not come from meager merit. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe. Why is this?
"Because the world cannot believe in such a Dharma. The Buddha said, "Brahmā!"
"How is it that this Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe? Brahmā said,
"World-Honored One!"
The world is attached to truth, yet this Dharma is not like that; this Dharma is neither real nor false.
The world is attached to dharmas, yet this Dharma is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma.
The world is attached to nirvana, yet this Dharma has neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
The world is attached to wholesome dharmas, yet these dharmas are neither wholesome nor unwholesome;
the world is attached to pleasure, yet these dharmas are neither suffering nor pleasure;
the world is attached to the appearance of a Buddha in the world, yet these dharmas involve neither the appearance of a Buddha nor nirvāṇa.
Although there is the teaching of the Dharma, this Dharma is not of a nature that can be expressed;
although the Sangha is praised, the Sangha is itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
for this reason, this Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe.
“World-Honored One!

For example, just as it is difficult to believe that fire could emerge from water or water could emerge from fire, so too is it difficult to believe that bodhi exists within afflictions and afflictions exist within bodhi.”

Why is this? The Tathāgata has realized the nature of these illusory afflictions; there is no dharma to be realized, and though he teaches the Dharma, it cannot be seen. Although he possesses knowledge, he is free from discrimination; although he has realized nirvāṇa, there is nothing known. Although he cultivates all practices, he does not produce dualistic marks; although there is a dharma realized, there is nothing attained; and although he extinguishes all hindrances, there is nothing extinguished.
“World-Honored One!

If a good man or a good woman is able to have faith and understanding in the meaning of such a Dharma, you should know that this person has attained liberation from all views; you should know that this person makes offerings to all Buddhas.”
Because they have personally attended upon immeasurable Buddhas, it should be known that such persons receive the protection of virtuous people.
Because they are protected and mindful of by all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), it should be known that such persons have faith in the Great and Sublime Dharma.
Because they have attained supremacy through sublime roots of goodness, it should be known that such persons have well acquired the great and wondrous treasury of the wealth of the Dharma.
Because they are able to guard the treasury of the Buddha-Dharma, it should be known that such persons act in accordance with their karmic tasks.
Because they are able to skillfully perform their duties, one should know that such persons are of noble lineage.
Because they have been born into the family of the Tathāgata, one should know that such persons are capable of practicing great relinquishment.
Because they have abandoned all afflictions, it should be known that this person attains the power of ethical discipline.
Because they do not give rise to a mind that violates the Dharma of precepts, it should be known that this person attains the power of patience.
Because such a person is able to relinquish body and life, one should know that this person has attained the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).
Because the mind of such a person does not grow weary, one should know that this person has attained the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*).
Because they have burned away all unwholesome dharmas, one should know that such a person attains the power of wisdom.
Because they are free from all views of evil conduct, one should know that such a person cannot be defeated by others.
Because they have transcended all realms of Māra, one should know that such persons cannot be overcome by enemies.
Because they are free from all adversaries, one should know that such persons do not deceive the world.
Because they do not deceive the Tathāgatas, you should know that such a person is a speaker of truth.
Because they are well able to explain the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, you should know that such a person is a speaker of reality.
Because they explain the true characteristics of dharmas according to the ultimate meaning, it should be known that such persons receive excellent protection and mindfulness.
Because they are protected and mindful of by all Tathāgatas, it should be known that such persons are gentle, compliant, and virtuous.
Because they dwell together in excellent peace and happiness, one should know that such a person is called "greatly wealthy.
Because this person possesses the wealth of the noble Dharma, one should know that this person is always able to be content.
Because they fully practice the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), it should be known that such persons are easy to satisfy and easy to support.
Because such persons are free from craving for food, it should be known that they have attained the power of patience (kṣānti).
"Because such a person has reached the other shore, one should know that this person is a savior.
Because this person can deliver those who have not yet been delivered, one should know that this person is a liberator."
Because this person is able to resolve what has not yet been resolved, one should know that this person is one who can bring peace.
Because this person is able to pacify what has not yet been pacified, one should know that this person is one who can bring cessation.
Because they cause those who have not yet attained liberation to attain it, one should know that such a person is a guide.
Because they are able to show the right path to others, one should know that such a person is a knower of the right path.
Because this person can liberate those who have not yet been liberated, one should know that this person is a great king of physicians.
Because they are well-versed in the medicines of all dharmas, one should know that this person is like an excellent medicine.
Because they treat the disease of the afflictions of sentient beings, one should know that such a person possesses great power.
Because such a person possesses the power of wisdom, one should know that such a person possesses the power of non-retrogression.
Because they possess the firm and ultimate Dharma, one should know that this person has the power of diligence.
Because they constantly practice without relying on others, one should know that this person is like a lion.
Because they are free from fear, such as the bristling of body hair, one should know that such a person is like a great dragon.
Because their minds are well-tamed and supple, one should know that such a person is like a great elephant.
Because they are well able to subdue their own minds, one should know that such a person is like a bull-king.
Because they are well able to lead the great assembly, one should know that such a person is greatly courageous and valiant.
Because they are able to destroy all demonic adversaries, one should know that such a person is fearless.
Because they have attained freedom from the fear of the great assembly, one should know that such a person has nothing to dread.
Because this person has attained the dharma of fearlessness, one should know that this person has nothing to dread or avoid.
Because this person is able to expound the Dharma of Truth, one should know that this person is like the bright moon.
Because they have attained fulfillment in all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), one should know that such a person illuminates like the sun.
Because they are able to illuminate with the light of wisdom, one should know that such a person is like the wick of a lamp.
Because they have departed from all darkness and obscurity, one should know that this person’s mind is as firm as the earth.
Because they have attained freedom from both hatred and attachment, one should know that this person is as impartial as the earth.
Because they are able to accommodate all sentient beings, one should know that such persons do not abide like the wind.
Because they are unattached to all phenomena, one should know that such persons are as pure as water.
Because they sweep away all defilements of affliction, one should know that such persons are like fierce fires.
Because they incinerate all flickering thoughts, one should know that such persons are like Mount Sumeru.
Because they are firm and immovable, one should know that such persons are as adamantine and solid as the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
Because they cannot be destroyed and their minds are firm, one should know that such persons are invincible.
