Because no enemy can subdue them, one should know that such persons are immeasurable.
Because they cannot be measured by those of the two vehicles, one should know that such persons abound in treasures like the ocean.
Because they abound in the treasures of the True Dharma, one should know that such persons are like the great ocean.
Because they have exhausted all afflictions, one should know that such persons are never satiated.
Because they constantly seek the Dharma without weariness or satiety, one should know that such a person is one who has attained fulfillment.
Because they possess wisdom and the Dharma of contentment, one should know that such a person is like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
Because such a person is able to turn the wheel of Dharma, one should know that this person is like King Śakra.
Because such a person sustains and maintains form, one should know that this person is like Brahmā, the Heavenly King.
"Because such a person has attained mastery, one should know that this person brings down a great rain.
Because this person can rain down the rain of Dharma, one should know that this person brings down ambrosia."
Because they cause sentient beings to receive the Dharma-rain of ambrosia, one should know that such persons are able to increase themselves.
Because they have attained the powers of the faculties and the factors of enlightenment, one should know that such persons have reached the other shore.
Because they are able to transcend the drowning of the world, it should be known that such persons have entered the further shore.
Because they are able to enter the wisdom of the Buddha, it should be known that such persons are close to arrival.
Because they have attained proximity to the Buddha’s bodhi, one should know that such a person is peerless.
Because their wisdom is supremely fulfilled, one should know that such a person is equal to the unequaled.
Because their wisdom derived from hearing is peerless, one should know that such a person cannot be measured.
Because they have transcended all measures and are not subject to measurement, one should know that such a person is without obstruction.
Because their eloquence in joyful exposition is unhindered and unattached, one should know that this person’s mindfulness is firm and stable.
Because they have attained the power of fully retaining what they have heard, one should know that this person is able to proceed.
Because these people attain the meaning in accordance with reality, it should be known that they have attained a wholesome mind.
Because they are able to contemplate and enter the True Dharma, it should be known that these people well understand sentient beings.
"Because this person has attained the minds of sentient beings, one should know that this person practices with diligent vigor.
Because they act for the benefit and peace of all the world, one should know that this person has already transcended the world."
Because this person’s mind transcends the world, one should know that this person cannot be defiled.
Because the mind is unstained like a lotus flower, one should know that this person is not obscured.
Because they are not obscured by the eight worldly dharmas, one should know that such persons have attained delightful love.
Because they are loved by all the wise, one should know that such persons are worthy of honor.
Because they possess the wisdom of extensive learning which is worthy of esteem, one should know that such persons are to be honored by others.
Because they are known by those who possess wisdom, one should know that such persons are worthy of offerings.
Because they are honored by devas and humans, one should know that such persons are worthy of taking refuge;
because all sentient beings take refuge in them, one should know that such persons are esteemed by the virtuous.
Because they are those to whom all noble ones (ārya) turn for refuge and pay homage, one should know that such persons are worthy of being sought after.
Because they are those who receive offerings from those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), one should know that such persons have distanced themselves from what is to be sought.
Because they have departed from all practices of the two vehicles, one should know that such a person is free from flattery and crookedness.
Because they are devoid of the defiled qualities of flattery and crookedness, one should know that such a person is upright and handsome.
"Because they are fully endowed with and have perfected the majestic deportments, one should know that such persons are most lovable.
Because they have transcended all worldly forms, one should know that such persons are those upon whom one may rely."
Because they possess majesty and virtue in their full perfection, one should know that such persons are fully adorned.
Because they possess the various marks that adorn the body, one should know that such persons have their bodies interspersed with these features.
Because they possess the eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana), one should know that such persons are able to protect.
Because such persons are able to protect the lineage of the Buddha (buddhagotra), one should know that such persons are able to gather [it].
Because they have attained the non-interruption of the lineage of the Buddha-dharma, it should be known that such persons are able to obstruct all evils.

Because they are constantly able to protect the noble Saṃgha, these persons are seen by all Buddhas; these persons have attained the Dharma-eye; these persons receive the prediction of the Buddha-wisdom from all Buddhas; these persons fulfill the three patiences; these persons fulfill the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); these persons are able to subdue all Māras; these persons have already attained omniscience (sarvajñatā); these persons are able to turn the wheel of Dharma; and these persons are able to perform the deeds performed by Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!

If there are good men or good women who hear such profound meanings of the Dharma, and having heard them, are not startled, not excessively startled, and not supremely startled, these people shall obtain such merit.”
"Bhagavān! Even if I were to spend an eon or the remainder of an eon speaking of the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family, I would still not be able to exhaust it."

If one can believe, accept, receive, and uphold the enlightenment of the Buddhas—which is thus difficult to know, difficult to see, and difficult to realize—and can read, recite, and extensively explain such teachings as these for others; having established oneself therein, one further causes others to abide within these teachings.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying: "Brahmā!
You have praised those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas based on only a small portion of their physical forms and merits."
As the Buddha knows, because I am fully endowed with the unobstructed wisdom of a Buddha, Brahmā!
Those sons and daughters of good family possess such immeasurable merits as these, and even more immeasurable ones beyond these.

If there are those who can understand the profound Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata—understanding its meaning, its phrases, and its syllables—they will be able to realize that profound intent; they will accord with it without contradiction, being in harmony rather than discordant, and they will be able to understand its true meaning rather than merely following the literal names.
In this way, the bodhisattva knows the teachings spoken: by relying on what kind of language does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma?
By relying on what kind of intention does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma?
By relying on what skillful means does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma?
By relying on what entry does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma?
By relying on what great compassion does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma?
"Brahmā! If there is a bodhisattva who knows this wisdom of the five powers of the Tathāgata, that bodhisattva performs the work of sustaining all sentient beings. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the five powers of practice?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! First is the teaching of the Dharma through speech;
second is the teaching of the Dharma through the mind.”
Third, teaching the Dharma through skillful means;
fourth, teaching the Dharma through entry [into the world];
fifth, teaching the Dharma through entry into great compassion.

"Brahmā! These are called the five types of power and knowledge employed by the Tathāgata; they are not within the cognitive domain of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others regarding this profound Dharma."
The Brahmā said: “World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva know the Tathāgata’s speech and his preaching of the Dharma?”
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!

The Tathāgata speaks of past dharmas, speaks of future dharmas, and speaks of present dharmas; he speaks of defiled dharmas and pure dharmas, speaks of wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas, speaks of mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas, speaks of outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas, speaks of blameworthy dharmas and blameless dharmas, speaks of conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas, speaks of the dharmas of self, sentient beings, persons, and individuals, speaks of the dharmas of realization, and speaks of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.”
Brahmā! You should know that these various expressions are like descriptions of illusory phenomena, for they lack any fixed determination;
they are like descriptions of dream-like phenomena, for they are false perceptions.
Speech is like an echo, for it issues from empty sound;
speech is like a shadow, for it arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
speech is like a seal, for it does not undergo transmigration.
That which is spoken of is like a mirage because it arises from inverted views;
it is like space because it is neither born nor extinguished;
and there is nothing that can be spoken of, for one should know that this is due to the absence of verbal expression.

“Brahmā! If a bodhisattva can understand all such teachings on the Dharma in this way, then although that bodhisattva employs all manner of speech to teach the Dharma, they have nothing at all to say regarding any phenomena. Because they do not crave or cling to phenomena, they attain the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). By means of this eloquence, even for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, they may teach the Dharma in various ways without exhaustion or obstruction; for whatever they say does not depart from the *dharmadhātu*, nor do they grasp at the marks of differentiation.”
"Brahmā! This is called the Tathāgata’s verbal teaching of the Dharma. Brahmā!"
How does a bodhisattva understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means of teaching the Dharma through his profound intentional power? O Brahmā!
The Tathāgata may speak of defiled phenomena as pure, or speak of pure phenomena as defiled; regarding this, the bodhisattva should understand the Tathāgata’s profound intention in such a way.
Brahmā! How does the Tathāgata speak of defiled phenomena as pure? Brahmā!
Because the essence of defiled phenomena is not perceived, the Tathāgata thus describes defiled phenomena as pure.
Brahmā, how does the Tathāgata describe pure phenomena as defiled?
"Brahmā! Because the essence of pure dharmas is not perceived, the Tathāgata speaks of these pure dharmas as being defiled.
Furthermore, Brahmā!"

I rely upon the teaching of giving to manifest nirvāṇa; yet ordinary people, lacking wisdom, cannot properly understand the meaning of what I have spoken according to their own inclinations. Only the bodhisattvas well understand my intention; they should thus believe in the profound and virtuous intent of the Dharma and reflect: "One who practices giving will attain great wealth and honor in future lives."
Within this Dharma, there is not a single phenomenon that can pass from one moment to the next and transition into a future life, because Nirvana is not a phenomenon subject to transition.

If there is not a single dharma that can transition from one thought-moment to another and proceed to a future life, this is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas; the true reality of all dharmas is itself nirvāṇa.
Observing the precepts is nirvana, because there is no doing and no arising.
Forbearance is nirvana, because it ceases moment by moment.
Diligence is nirvana, because there is nothing to grasp or reject.
Dhyāna-concentration is nirvāṇa, because it does not crave its flavor.
Prajñā is nirvāṇa, because it does not apprehend signs.
Craving is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no characteristic of desire.
Hatred is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) has no characteristic of hatred.
Delusion is the limit of reality, because the nature of phenomena has no characteristic of delusion.
The world is nirvāṇa, because it is without retrogression and without arising.
Nirvāṇa is the world, because of attachment to it.
Truthful speech is falsehood, because it gives rise to various views.
Falsehood is truthful speech, for the sake of those with overweening pride.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!

Because the Tathāgata acts according to his will, he may say of himself: 'I am one who teaches the extreme of eternalism,' or 'I am one who teaches defilement,' or 'I am one who teaches the extreme of annihilation,' or 'I am one who teaches non-action,' or 'I am one who teaches there is no agent of action,' or 'I am one who holds wrong views,' or 'I am one who lacks faith,' or 'I am one who is ungrateful,' or 'I am a thief,' or 'I am a spitter,' or 'I am one who does not accept [offerings]. Yet, the Tathāgata possesses none of these qualities."
Brahmā! You should know that this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his intentions.
By means of what intention does he enable sentient beings who are arrogant to abandon their conceit? Brahmā!
The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma based on such a profound intention: "Brahmā!

If a bodhisattva knows that the Tathāgata speaks according to the skillful means of his conduct, then upon hearing that a Buddha has appeared in the world, they will be able to believe and accept it, because [the Buddha] reveals to sentient beings the physical body as the fruit of virtuous karma."
If they hear that a Buddha does not appear in the world, they believe and accept it, because all Buddhas possess the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
If they hear that a Buddha preaches the Dharma, they also believe and accept it, because he does so for the sake of those sentient beings who delight in words and letters.
If one hears that the Buddha does not preach the Dharma, one still believes and accepts it, because the dharma-nature of all Buddhas is ineffable.
If one hears that there is nirvana, one also believes and accepts it, because it extinguishes the afflictions arising from inversion.
If one hears that there is no nirvāṇa, one also accepts it with faith, because all phenomena possess the characteristic of being neither born nor extinguished.
If one hears that there are sentient beings, one also accepts it with faith, because this enters the gateway of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If one hears that there are no sentient beings and yet believes and accepts it, this is because one has entered the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). O Brahmā!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus well understands the Tathāgata’s skillful means of teaching the Dharma according to circumstances is fearless regarding all spoken words and sounds; you should know that such a person is also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
“Brahmā! How does a bodhisattva know the Tathāgata’s skillful means in preaching the Dharma? Brahmā!”
The Tathāgata teaches generosity to sentient beings so that they may attain great wealth;
he teaches ethical discipline so that they may be reborn in the heavens;
and he teaches patience so that they may attain physical beauty.
Diligence, because it brings about the perfection of wisdom;
meditative concentration, because it brings about tranquility;
and wisdom, because it relinquishes all afflictions.
Through extensive learning, one attains wisdom;
through practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, one achieves the prosperity and happiness of humans and devas;
and through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one attains rebirth in the Brahma world.
Śamatha, because it attains vipaśyanā; the stage of training, because it attains the stage of no-more-learning;
the stage of the pratyekabuddha, because it is pure and consumes all offerings.
The Buddha-ground, because it demonstrates immeasurable wisdom;
Nirvana, because it extinguishes all suffering and affliction. Brahmā!
By means of such skillful expedients, I praise and expound this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

You should know that the Tathāgata truly does not apprehend a self, sentient beings, life-span, or a person; likewise, the Tathāgata does not perceive giving, nor does he perceive the fruit of giving;
he does not perceive stinginess, nor does he perceive the fruit of stinginess.
Nor does one perceive the upholding of precepts, nor the fruit of upholding precepts;
nor does one perceive the violation of precepts, nor the fruit of violating precepts;
nor does one perceive patience, nor the fruit of patience.
Nor does one perceive anger, nor the fruit of anger;
nor does one perceive diligence, nor the fruit of diligence;
nor does one perceive indolence, nor the fruit of indolence.
Nor does one perceive meditative concentration, nor the fruit of meditative concentration;
nor does one perceive a distracted mind, nor the fruit of a distracted mind;
nor does one perceive wisdom, nor the fruit of wisdom.
One does not perceive delusion, nor does one perceive the fruit of delusion;
one does not perceive suffering or pleasure,
nor does one perceive the fruit of suffering or pleasure.
“Furthermore, one does not perceive a stream-enterer, nor does one perceive the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including not perceiving awakening, nor perceiving the fruit of nirvana. O Brahmā!

The Tathāgata constantly teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and these sentient beings, relying upon the Tathāgata’s instructions, practice diligently according to the teachings as they were spoken, cultivating all practices in accordance with reality.
For what reason do sentient beings practice and diligently cultivate those practices, yet fail to attain and fail to realize that Dharma?

That which is called the practice of a srotāpanna, up to the fruit of arhatship, up to not attaining the stage of a pratyekabuddha, not attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and even not attaining nirvāṇa.
For this reason, those sentient beings do not attain nirvāṇa and do not see nirvāṇa.
"Brahmā! This is called the Tathāgata’s skillful means in preaching the Dharma."
"Brahmā! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice so as to cause sentient beings to embrace the sublime Dharma. Brahmā!"
How does a bodhisattva know the Tathāgata’s entry into the teaching of the Dharma? O Brahmā!
The eye is an entrance into the gate of liberation; likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are entrances into the gate of liberation.
Why is this? Because the eye is empty, devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self, for such is its intrinsic nature;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self, for such is their intrinsic nature.

Brahmā! You should know that all sense-bases (*āyatana*) are entrances into the gates of liberation; you should know that because right practice is not deceptive, these forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*) are all entrances into the gates of liberation.

These are what are called the gate of emptiness, the gate of signlessness, the gate of wishlessness, the gate of non-activity, the gate of neither arising nor ceasing, the gate of neither coming nor going, the gate of non-retrogression and non-arising, and the gate of the natural purity and tranquility of self-nature.
"Furthermore, Brahmā! The Tathāgata reveals all names as gateways to liberation. Why is this?
Because all names are neither joined nor functional, and because their intrinsic nature is inert.
Brahmā, you should know that the Tathāgata teaches the Noble Truths within all syllables and letters; you should know that he teaches the gates of liberation within all the dharmas he speaks.
“Brahmā! There is no teaching of the Dharma through names or words; the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not speak of ultimate truth. Brahmā!”

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from any defilement regarding dharmas; within all that he teaches, he reveals the gateways to liberation, causing beings to enter into realized wisdom and to enter into nirvāṇa.
Brahmā! This is called the Tathāgata’s entrance into the dharma-gate of teaching the Dharma. Brahmā!
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study this Dharma.
'Brahmā! How does the Tathāgata, with a heart of great compassion, universally preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings?'"
"Brahmā! The Tathāgata possesses thirty-two kinds of great compassion that are in accord with reality, through which he universally preaches the Dharma for all sentient beings.
What are these thirty-two kinds of great compassion that are in accord with reality?"
"Brahmā! That which is called 'all dharmas are without self,' yet sentient beings do not believe or understand it, reckoning instead that there is a self.

Regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion. All dharmas are without sentient beings, yet sentient beings reckon that there are sentient beings. Regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."
All dharmas are devoid of a life-principle, yet sentient beings falsely conceive of a life-principle; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are devoid of a person (puruṣa), yet sentient beings conceive of there being a person; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
"All dharmas are non-existent, yet sentient beings abide in the view of existence; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."
All phenomena are without abiding, yet sentient beings abide in all phenomena; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena have no place of refuge, yet sentient beings delight in places of refuge; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
"All phenomena are not mine, yet sentient beings are attached to the notion of 'mine'; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."
All phenomena have no point of attachment, yet sentient beings conceive of things as having such attachments; it is toward these sentient beings that the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are devoid of grasped characteristics, yet all sentient beings possess such grasping; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
"All phenomena are unborn, yet sentient beings abide in the state of birth; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."
All phenomena are free from retrogression and rebirth, yet sentient beings abide in retrogression and rebirth; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All dharmas are without defilement, yet sentient beings are stained by and attached to these dharmas; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All dharmas are free from greed, yet all sentient beings possess greed; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are free from hatred, yet all sentient beings possess hatred; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are free from delusion, yet all sentient beings possess delusion; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
"All dharmas come from nowhere, yet sentient beings are attached to where they come from; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."
All dharmas go nowhere; yet sentient beings are attached to future births. Regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are without action, yet sentient beings all engage in action; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

All phenomena are without conceptual proliferation, yet sentient beings engage in various forms of conceptual proliferation; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
"All dharmas are empty, yet sentient beings fall into the view of existence; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All dharmas are signless, yet sentient beings grasp at signs; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."
"All dharmas are wishless, yet all sentient beings possess wishes; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All sentient beings in the world constantly engage in mutual anger, resentment, and strife; regarding these sentient beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion."

All those in the world who hold wrong views and practice perversely upon deviant paths—the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings in order to cause them to abide in the right path.

All the world has fallen into perversion, fallen into peril and difficulty, and dwells upon unrighteous paths; desiring to cause them to enter the true path, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all these sentient beings.

"All sentient beings in the world are constantly bound by stinginess and greed; they do not know contentment and seize the wealth of others. It is for the sake of teaching and transforming them so that they may abide in the noble riches of faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and remorse that the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion toward these sentient beings."

All sentient beings in the world are constantly acting as servants to wealth, property, houses, wives, and children; regarding these fragile and unsubstantial things, they conceive the notion of solidity. Because the Tathāgata desires to cause them to definitively know that all such things are ultimately impermanent, he gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.

"All ordinary beings in the world take their own bodies as enemies and thieves, yet they constantly crave offerings, honor, fame, and praise, regarding them as true friends. Although these beings claim such things are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they are actually evil associates (*pāpamitra*). It is for the sake of acting as true spiritual friends to cause them to ultimately sever all suffering and ultimately attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, that the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all such sentient beings."

"All sentient beings in the world delight in practicing deceitful deeds, sustaining themselves through wrong livelihoods such as farming and real estate; because he teaches the Dharma so that they may practice right livelihood and transcend the triple world, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings."

All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; only through diligent cultivation of all practices can they be brought to fulfillment. Yet sentient beings fall into indolence, and for this reason they are unable to attain noble liberation. In order to cause them to exert themselves so as to obtain the firm dharma of liberation, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion toward these sentient beings.

“Brahmā! Sentient beings abandon the unsurpassed Great Vehicle, the unimpeded supreme Dharma, and the supreme Dharma of Nirvāṇa, yet seek the inferior Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle—namely, the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. For the sake of those sentient beings, so that they may come to know and delight in the Dharma of the Great Vehicle—that is, so that they may know how to observe the Buddha Vehicle—the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion toward all such sentient beings.”
“Brahmā! Thus does the Tathāgata practice the thirty-two forms of great compassion toward all sentient beings; for this reason, the Tathāgata is called ‘the one who practices great compassion.’”

If a bodhisattva is able to constantly cultivate and accumulate these thirty-two forms of great compassion toward sentient beings, that bodhisattva mahāsattva shall be known as a great field of merit; endowed with great majestic power, they attain non-retrogression and should be understood as one who acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.

When this "Chapter on the Dharma-Door of Great Compassion" was being preached, thirty-two thousand people all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and seventy-two thousand sons of gods attained the stainless Dharma-eye.
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
why is it that this Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, upon hearing this teaching corresponding to the Dharma-gate of Great Compassion, does not feel joy?”
Brahmā said: “Good son!
If consciousness dwells in dualistic dharmas, there is joy; if consciousness dwells within the non-dual reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), there is no joy.”
"Good son! It is, for example, like a phantom person created by a Tathāgata who hears the Dharma teachings spoken by the Tathāgata and feels neither joy nor delight.
In this same way, good son!"

"Because one knows that all phenomena are like illusory appearances, one does not give rise to thoughts of superiority toward the Tathāgata, nor does one give rise to thoughts of inferiority toward other sentient beings.
Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha asked the Brahmā: "Good son!..."
Knowing all phenomena, why is it called having the characteristic of being like an illusion? He replied: “Good son!
"If there is a person who discriminates all dharmas and practices in two places, you should question them. He asked: "Brahmā!
"In what place do you travel? He replied,
"O son of good family!"
"Wherever ordinary beings go, there I shall go.
Net-Luminosity Bodhisattva said, "Brahmā!"

Ordinary worldlings walk upon the paths of greed, hatred, and delusion; they pursue the false paths of the view of a self-body, attachment to precepts and rituals, the net of doubt, and the notions of "I" and "mine.
O son of good family!
"How could you possibly proceed in this place?
Brahmā asked, saying,
"O son of good family!"
"Do you wish to obtain the definitive characteristic of the dharmas of an ordinary person? He replied, "Brahmā!"
"I do not even perceive the existence of ordinary worldlings, much less their dharmas! Brahmā asked,
"Virtuous man!..."
"If these dharmas are not determinate, how can your mind possess those defiled states such as greed, hatred,
and delusion? He replied, "There are none."
Brahmā said: "Good son!
All dharmas are free from the characteristics of greed, hatred, and delusion; their mode of activity is likewise so."
"Good son! All the practices of ordinary beings are themselves the practices of the noble ones; they are non-dual and without distinction. Good son!"

If a person practices the path for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, yet within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) there is neither increase nor decrease; therefore, all practices are non-practice.
It is asked: what is meant by "all speech is non-speech"?
"Good son! The Tathāgata explains all dharmas by means of an ineffable characteristic; therefore, every explanation is non-explanation.
What is meant by 'all paths being non-paths'?"
“Good son! Because there is nowhere to which one goes, all paths are non-paths.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Brahmā! Excellent!"
"Brahmā! If you wish to preach the Dharma, you should speak thus.
*The Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*, Fascicle Two.
The Sutra of the Questions of the Brahma God Viśeṣacintī, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Great Brahma God Viśeṣacintī, saying: "Virtuous..."
"O man! You speak of the sphere of activity of all ordinary persons; I perceive the characteristics of practice within those who so practice. Brahmā said:
"Good son! If I were to have a place of birth, there would necessarily be the characteristic of conditioned activity. He asked:
“Brahmā! If you do not arise, how can you teach and transform all sentient beings? Brahmā replied:
“I am born in the same manner as those born through the Buddha’s transformation.
Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva said:
“That which is born from the Buddha’s transformation has no place of birth.”
Brahmā asked, "Can it be seen? He replied:
“Brahmā, it is by the power of the Buddha that they are seen. Brahmā said:
“Good son! My birth is also like this, due to the power of karma.
Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva asked:
“Brahmā! Do you practice within the arising of karma? Brahmā replied:
"I truly do not act within the arising of karma. He asked, "Brahmā!..."
"How can it be that there is no karma, yet one speaks of it by the power of karma? Brahmā replied, "Good son!..."
"As with the power of karma, so it is with this; these two do not transcend suchness.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If one can enter into this teaching spoken by the Great Dragon with intentional meaning, it should be known that such a person attains great merit. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
It is already extremely difficult even to hear the name of such a superior person, let alone to hear what they teach.
World-Honored One!
It is like a tree that does not rest upon the earth, yet manifests its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits in the midst of empty space.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The characteristics of this great person are likewise such: they do not abide in any phenomena, yet they manifest throughout the ten directions.
They display walking, being born, declining, and dying, appearing everywhere in the lands of all Buddhas; and yet, they also possess such wisdom, eloquence, and delight in teaching."
“World-Honored One!
If there were wise sons or daughters of good family who heard of this power of mastery over wisdom, who would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Samantakusuma, who asked the elder Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"Do you realize the nature of phenomena, or do you not?
Yet you are unable to thus expound the Dharma with such vigor of great wisdom.
The Buddha has declared that you, Venerable One, are the foremost among those possessed of wisdom."
"Virtuous One!
Why do you not manifest such power of wisdom, eloquence, and mastery? He replied:
“Good son! According to the power of his wisdom, the Buddha declared that among his śrāvaka disciples who possess wisdom, I am foremost in being able to speak.”
“Venerable Śāriputra! How much is the scope of the realm of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)? He replied:
“There is none. “Venerable Śāriputra!

If the realm of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no measure of more or less, why do you say that according to the power of wisdom, the Buddha declared me to be the foremost among his śrāvaka disciples who are wise and capable of teaching?”
He replied: "Good son! Among the śrāvakas, they speak according to the Dharma they have attained."
“Venerable Śāriputra! Do you perceive that the realm of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has a limited characteristic? He replied:
“There is none. “Venerable Śāriputra!
If that is so, why do you say that you speak according to the Dharma you have attained?”
Venerable Śāriputra!
Just as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has immeasurable characteristics, so too is its realization; and just as its realization is, so too is its teaching. Why is this?
"Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has immeasurable characteristics. Śāriputra said,
"O son of good family!"
“The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not a characteristic that can be realized. “Venerable Śāriputra,
if that nature of phenomena is not a characteristic that can be realized, have you emerged from the nature of phenomena to attain liberation?”
He replied, "No, Venerable Śāriputra. "Venerable Śāriputra! [he continued.]
"Why is that? He replied,
"O son of good family!"
"If one were to attain liberation by departing from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), then one would destroy the nature of phenomena.
The Bodhisattva Samantakusuma said: "Therefore, Śāriputra!"
"As you have realized the Dharma, so too is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Śāriputra said,
"O son of good family!"
"I have come to listen, not to speak. "Venerable Śāriputra! All dharmas enter into the dharma-nature;
within this dharma-nature, could there possibly be one who speaks or one who listens?"
He replied, "No, Venerable Śāriputra. "Venerable Śāriputra! [he continued.]
"If it is so, why do you say that you have come to listen and not to speak?
He replied, "Good son!
The Buddha said that two kinds of people obtain immeasurable merit:
the first is those who single-mindedly and diligently expound the Dharma;
the second is those who listen and receive it with a focused mind.
"For this reason, Puṣpa, you should speak and I should listen and receive it.
"Venerable Śāriputra, can you listen to the Dharma while having entered the meditative absorption of cessation?"
He replied: "Good son!
One who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation does not engage in dualistic activity while listening to the Dharma."
“Venerable Śāriputra! Do you believe that all phenomena possess the characteristic of being extinguished by their very nature? He replied:
“Good son! All such dharmas possess the characteristic of being extinguished by their very nature; I believe this teaching.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Samantakusuma.
"If this were so, then Śāriputra would be unable to hear the Dharma at all times.
Why? Because all dharmas are, by their very nature, characterized by constant cessation."
Śāriputra said: "Noble son! Are you able to preach the Dharma without arising from meditative concentration?"
He asked: "Is there perhaps even a single dharma that is not concentration? He replied:
"No. "Venerable Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that all foolish ordinary beings are always in meditative concentration."
Śāriputra asked, "By means of what concentration do all ordinary beings always remain in concentration?
He replied:
"Because of the samādhi of the indestructible nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Śāriputra said,
"O son of good family!"
"If it were so, there would be no distinction between ordinary persons and noble ones. "Venerable Śāriputra, it is so, it is so!"
I do not wish to create a distinction between ordinary persons and noble ones. Why is this?
Because noble ones do not attain a single dharma, and ordinary persons do not give rise to a single dharma; these two do not transcend the mark of the equality of dharmatā.
Śāriputra said: “Good son! By what means do you define the characteristic of the equality of the nature of all dharmas?”
He said: "It is like the knowledge and vision attained by Śāriputra. Venerable Śāriputra!"
"Have you given birth to the dharmas of the noble ones? He replied, "No!"
“Do you extinguish the dharmas of ordinary persons? He replied, “No.”
“Have you attained the dharmas of the noble ones? He replied, “No.”
“Do you see the dharmas of ordinary beings? He replied, “No.”
“Venerable Śāriputra! If this is so, what knowledge or vision do you possess that leads you to say you have attained the Dharma? He replied:
“Good son! Have you not heard of suchness?
The suchness of ordinary beings who lack wisdom is itself the suchness of the exhaustion of outflows and liberation;
the suchness of the exhaustion of outflows and liberation is itself the suchness of nirvana without remainder.”
The Bodhisattva Samantakusuma said:

"Venerable Śāriputra! Just as suchness is not different from suchness, does not alter suchness, does not change suchness, and does not destroy suchness, so too should one know all phenomena through this suchness."
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Just as a great fire can burn every wick and every flame, so too do these sons of good family, through the nature of the Dharma they teach, burn away all afflictions."
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra! It is as you have said;
the nature of the Dharma taught by these sons of good family is fully capable of incinerating all afflictions."
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha asked the Elder Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra,
the Buddha has declared you to be the foremost among those of great wisdom."
"What is this wisdom, such that Śāriputra is the foremost among those who possess wisdom? He replied:
“Good son! What is called a śrāvaka attains understanding by means of sound; they possess a limited wisdom that reflects upon their own physical characteristics.
Because of this wisdom, the Buddha declared me to be the foremost among his śrāvaka disciples who possess wisdom, but not the foremost in wisdom among bodhisattvas.”
He asked: "Is wisdom a characteristic of conceptual proliferation? He replied:
"No," he replied. [The other] asked:
"Is wisdom not the mark of equality?"
He replied, “It is so. He said:
"Now, Venerable One, you have realized the wisdom of equality; why then do you say that wisdom has limits?
He replied, "Good son!..."
"Because of the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), wisdom is immeasurable; because it enters the nature of phenomena according to its extent, wisdom is measurable.
He asked: "Is there any phenomenon with immeasurable characteristics that is described as having measurable characteristics?"
He replied, "There is none. Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva said:
"If this is so, why does Śāriputra preach the Dharma according to measure?
At that time, Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
Then, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha named ‘Jālinīprabha’?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, saying:

“Good son! Manifest the radiance of the merit accomplished by your own roots of goodness, causing the minds of all devas, humans, and the entire world to rejoice; and may those whose roots of goodness and merit have ripened give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s command, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.

Having spoken these words, he adjusted his robe to bare the right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and immediately from between the fingers of his right hand—adorned with white and red webbing—emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.
Throughout all the infinite worlds in every direction, there were those in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
those who were blind, deaf, hunchbacked, handless, or footless; those suffering from various ailments;
those beings of greedy and evil nature; the ignorant and naked; those tormented by hunger and thirst; and those who were bound, imprisoned, or impoverished.
As for those sentient beings who suffer from various afflictions such as physical form, decrepitude, impending death, and envy;
those possessed of stinginess, greed, broken precepts, malice, laziness, distracted thought, lack of wisdom, lack of faith, meager learning and vision, shamelessness, and lack of remorse;
and those fallen into the net of false views and doubt—all such beings who encounter this light shall [be liberated].

All attained happiness and were filled with joy; not a single sentient being experienced desire, anger, ignorance, pride, sorrow, or affliction, nor was there anyone who did not find happiness or rejoice.

As for the great assembly before the Buddha—consisting of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and śrāvakas, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all these members of the great assembly were of one identical color, golden in hue and without distinction; that is to say, the color of the Tathāgata.

At that time, the entire great assembly was likewise thus: their bodies were filled with bliss and their minds attained joy, no different from when a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of the Adornment Arising from the Food of Joy.

At that time, the entire great assembly attained something rare: each saw the others as being no different from the Buddha, and they no longer perceived the Buddha’s body as superior or their own bodies as inferior.

Furthermore, by the power of the radiance of the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, four bodhisattvas immediately emerged from the earth from the region below; they were named Praṇidhibalotthita, Jayabhadra, Jñānacandraprabha, and Anabhibhūta.
These four bodhisattvas stood with palms joined and thought to themselves,
"Who is the Buddha that we should pay homage to?
Immediately, they heard a voice from the sky saying:
“By the power of the radiance of the Bodhisattva Kumārabhūta Jālinīprabha, this entire assembly has become one golden color, no different from the Buddha.
At that time, the four bodhisattvas gave rise to a sense of rare wonder and spoke these words:
“We now speak the truth: the colors of those in this assembly are no different [from one another], and all dharmas are likewise so.”
He then made this vow:
"If these words of mine are truthful and not false, may the World-Honored One Śākyamuni now manifest a miraculous sign, so that I may behold him, make offerings to him, and pay him homage."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, saying:
“Good son! Cease this display of supernatural power. You have already performed the work of a Buddha; you have already caused immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the path of the Buddha.”
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately ceased his supernormal power and withdrew the manifestation of light.

Once the light was withdrawn, the deportment and physical appearance of the entire assembly returned to their original forms, with no difference between their bodies and speech as before; at that very moment, the Tathāgata’s physical form appeared upon the lion throne, exactly as it had been originally.
At that time, the four bodhisattvas immediately beheld the Tathāgata; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and spoke these words:

“The realm of wisdom of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is inconceivable; and the realm of the merit, roots of goodness, and power of aspiration of the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha is also inconceivable. By virtue of those merits, he is able to bestow such happiness upon sentient beings and cause them to rejoice.”
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
from where have these four bodhisattvas come?”
The four bodhisattvas said,
"We have come from a buddha-world in the direction below. Mahākāśyapa spoke:
“What is the name of that land?
What is the name of the Buddha?
The four bodhisattvas replied:
“The land is named Manifestation of All Jewel Adornments, and the Buddha’s name is Single Jewel Canopy;
he is currently preaching the Dharma. Mahākāśyapa asked, “How far is that Buddha-land from here?”
The four bodhisattvas said,
“The Buddha knows this himself.
Mahākāśyapa then spoke:
“Virtuous ones, for what reason have you come here?

The four bodhisattvas replied, “The radiance of this youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha illuminated that place; we encountered it and immediately heard the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as the name of the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.”
"Therefore, we have now come here to see Śākyamuni Buddha and the superior man Jālinīprabha.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Buddha, how far away from here is the world called Sarvaratnavyūha, where the Buddha Ekaratnacchattra currently resides?
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”
"That land is located beyond seventy-two Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands from here.
Mahākāśyapa said, "World-Honored One!"
"Bhagavān, how long has it been since these four bodhisattvas departed from that land and arrived here?
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
"In the space of a single thought-moment, he vanished from that land and suddenly arrived here. Mahākāśyapa said,
"How rare, World-Honored One!"

Indeed, the distant illumination of the bodhisattvas' radiance and the swiftness of their supernormal powers are most rare; that the radiance of the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha now shines so far, and that these four bodhisattvas have been able to arrive with such speed, is truly marvelous.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa! As you have said,
the power of the supernatural faculties of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is so swift in its activity that it is inconceivable and cannot be matched by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa asked the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha:
"Good son! For what reason and by what causal conditions has your manifestation of light illuminated this great assembly, rendering it all golden in color?"
He replied, “Mahākāśyapa!
You may ask the World-Honored One, and he shall explain it for you.”
Then Mahākāśyapa reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!

When this youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha attains Buddhahood, the great assembly in that gathering shall all be of a uniform golden color, and they shall all together believe in and delight in all-encompassing wisdom.
"In that Buddha-land, there will not even be the names 'śrāvaka' or 'pratyekabuddha'; there will be only a pure assembly of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"One should know that those bodhisattvas born there are like Buddhas.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"As you have said, all those bodhisattvas born there are entirely like Buddhas."
At that time, forty-four thousand people in the assembly, having heard this, all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having thus resolved their minds, they wished to be born in that land and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"When the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha attains Buddhahood, we shall all be reborn in his land.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Blessed One, after how much time will this youth, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
"You should ask him yourself.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa asked the youth Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva: "Noble son!..."
“Virtuous one, when will you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Net-light Bodhisattva said, “Mahākāśyapa!”
If someone were to ask a magically conjured person,
"Virtuous one, when will you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?",
how would that conjured person answer?
He asked: "A person created by illusion has no determinate characteristics; what could possibly be said about them? He replied:
"All dharmas are likewise thus without any fixed characteristic; how can you ask when you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
He asked: "A person created by illusion is devoid of self-characteristics; they have no distinction, no difference, and no aspirations.
Are you, O Benevolent One, also like this? If you are thus, how can you benefit immeasurable sentient beings?"

“Mahākāśyapa! Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is the very nature of all sentient beings; the nature of all sentient beings is the nature of illusion; and the nature of illusion is the nature of all dharmas.”
"In this Dharma, I see no benefit and see no lack of benefit.
Mahākāśyapa said: "Good son!..."
"O Benevolent One, how could you now fail to cause sentient beings to abide in Bodhi?
He replied, "Does the Bodhi of the Buddhas possess any characteristic of abiding?"
He replied, “There is not. “Mahākāśyapa! [the Buddha said.]
"For this reason, I do not cause sentient beings to abide in bodhi, nor do I cause them to abide in the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Mahākāśyapa said,
"O son of good family!"
"Virtuous One, where do you now head? He replied,
"The place I head toward is the heading toward suchness (tathatā)."
He said: "It is as if there were no destination and no turning. He asked:
"Just as there is no going and no turning, all dharmas abide in the mark of suchness (tathatā).
For this reason, I have no going and no turning. Mahākāśyapa said:
“If all dharmas abide in the mark of suchness, being without movement or transition, how do you, O Venerable One, further teach and transform sentient beings?
Net-Luminosity Bodhisattva replied:
“If a person makes a vow, they are unable to teach and transform sentient beings; if a person perceives transition within dharmas, they likewise are unable to teach and transform sentient beings.”
Mahākāśyapa said: “Good son! Can you not turn back sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death in the world?”
“Mahākāśyapa! I do not even attain the world, much less transform sentient beings within it. Mahākāśyapa said:
“Good son! Can you not cause sentient beings to attain nirvana?
“Mahākāśyapa! [he replied.]
“I do not yet even see nirvana myself, much less can I teach and transform sentient beings so that they attain nirvana?
Mahākāśyapa said, “Good son!

If, as you say, the benevolent one neither attains the mundane world nor attains nirvāṇa, for what reason do bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path, practicing toward enlightenment in order to save immeasurable sentient beings?
"Is this not for the sake of bringing sentient beings to extinction? "Mahākāśyapa!

If a bodhisattva perceives nirvana as distinct from the world, and practices the path to enlightenment while grasping at the marks of sentient beings, then such a person should not be called a bodhisattva."
Mahākāśyapa said: "Good son! Where does the venerable one now practice?"
“Mahākāśyapa! I do not practice within the world, nor do I practice within nirvāṇa; furthermore, I do not practice by means of the mark of a sentient being. Mahākāśyapa!”
"In response to what you have asked, O worthy one, where do you now practice?
I practice in the same place as the sphere of activity of a person emanated by the Buddha. Mahākāśyapa said:
"A person conjured by the Buddha has no sphere of activity.
Mahākāśyapa, you should know that the sphere of activity of all sentient beings is likewise characterized in this way."
Mahākāśyapa said: "Good son!
A person manifested by the Buddha is without greed, anger, or delusion. If all sentient beings were to act in such a manner, where would the greed, anger, and delusion of all sentient beings go?"
“Mahākāśyapa! I now ask you; answer me as you see fit. Mahākāśyapa!”
"Do you now still possess greed, hatred,
and delusion? He replied, "I do not."
He asked: "Are these greed, hatred, and delusion completely extinguished? He replied:
"No," he replied. [The Buddha] said:
"If Mahākāśyapa now possesses no greed, hatred, or delusion, yet these are not utterly extinguished, then where do you place his greed, hatred, and delusion?"
He replied: "Good son!

Ordinary persons give rise to greed, anger, and delusion through inverted views that produce false conceptualizations. Because those in the Dharma of the noble ones thoroughly understand the true nature of inversion, they do not give rise to false conceptualizations; therefore, they possess no greed, hatred, or ignorance."
“Mahākāśyapa! What do you think? If a phenomenon arises from perversion, is that phenomenon real or is it false?”
He replied, "Good son! These dharmas are illusory and not real."
He asked: "If a phenomenon is not real, can it be made real? He replied:
"No," he replied. [The Buddha] said:
"If these dharmas are not real, would you, Mahākāśyapa, desire to find greed, hatred, and delusion within them?"
He replied, "No. [The Buddha] asked:
"If that is so, then in what respect can greed, anger, and delusion defile sentient beings? He replied, "Good son!
"If it is so, then all dharmas, from the very beginning, are by their own nature free from the characteristics of greed,
anger, and delusion. Net-Light Bodhisattva said, "Mahākāśyapa!"
"Therefore, I say that the characteristics of all phenomena are like those created by a Buddha through transformation.
When this teaching was spoken, forty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Kumārabhūta Jālinīprabha, those people shall no longer fall into the three evil realms.”
If there are those who behold the body of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, it should be known that all demonic activities will be unable to obstruct or hinder them.
If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma taught by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, those sentient beings shall not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Those sentient beings who are taught and transformed by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha shall never regress from great bodhi.
World-Honored One,
we pray that you will speak of the adornment of the Buddha-field through the roots of goodness and merit of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha."
The Buddha said,
“Kāśyapa! This youth Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva, wherever he travels through the various Buddha-lands, is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.”
“Kāśyapa! Do you see the light emitted by the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha? He replied:
“I have seen it,” [he replied]. The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!

The mustard seeds that would fill a trichiliocosm might still be counted, but the sentient beings who, through the light radiated by the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, have been established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, are beyond counting.

Kāśyapa! You know that the benefit brought about by the light emitted by the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha is already so great; how much more so, then, is the benefit produced by his preaching the Dharma?
Listen attentively now, and I shall briefly describe his meritorious roots and the adornments of his pure Buddha-field.

“Kāśyapa! This youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha shall, after seven hundred and sixty million asaṃkhyeya kalpas, attain Buddhahood, being named Samantaprabhā-viśeṣarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; his world shall be named Saṃcita-guṇa-viśeṣa.”

Kāśyapa! When that Buddha proceeds toward the tree of enlightenment, all the Māras and their retinues, as well as the devas, humans, and people within the land, will all become fixed in their destiny for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Kāśyapa! The ground of that buddha-field is as level as the palm of a hand, soft, supple, and smooth like the ground of the Kalinga region of bliss, and is adorned with all kinds of jewels.”

In that world, even the names of the three evil realms do not exist, nor are there the eight difficulties; that Buddha-land is free from elevations and depressions, tiles, rubble, thorns, soil, stones, and other impurities, being adorned instead with exquisite jewel lotuses.
Those lotuses are all made of genuine jewels and emit exquisite fragrances; that world is vast and expansive.
Kāśyapa, such a collection of supreme merits as these exists in that Buddha-world.

The Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-viśeṣa-rāja has a vast and immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas. All have thoroughly cultivated immeasurable dharma-gates and have attained immeasurable sovereign supernormal powers. Their bodies are all adorned with radiance, and they have attained dhāraṇīs, various supreme samādhis, and unimpeded eloquence, being well-able to expound the Dharma.

The light and spiritual powers of those bodhisattvas penetrate everything without exception; they have fully attained all the superknowledges, fearlessnesses, and eloquence, and are well able to subdue all Māras, enemies, and adversaries.
“Kāśyapa, those bodhisattvas practice mindfulness and wisdom, giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and cultivate their minds with supreme wisdom and all excellent virtues.”

In that Buddha-land, there is not even the name "woman. All its bodhisattvas are born by transformation, sitting cross-legged within precious lotus flowers. They take the joy of meditative concentration as their food, and whatever they require—whether places for walking meditation, dwellings, couches, gardens, or bathing pools—is obtained immediately upon thought.

“Kāśyapa! That Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-viśeṣa-rāja does not preach the Dharma by means of written words; rather, he emits rays of light that illuminate all bodhisattvas, whereby they immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Furthermore, these lights shine throughout the ten directions, penetrating them without obstruction, causing all sentient beings to become free from afflictions. Moreover, from those lights constantly issue thirty-two kinds of pure and wondrous sounds of the Dharma.”
What are these thirty-two? They are:
all phenomena are empty, because they are purified by being free from all views;
all phenomena are signless, because they are free from all conceptualization and that which is conceptualized.
All phenomena are wishless, because they transcend the triple world;
all phenomena are free from desire, because their intrinsic nature is quiescent;
all phenomena are free from hatred, because they lack any characteristic of obstruction.
All phenomena are free from delusion, because they are devoid of darkness;
all phenomena come from nowhere, because they are originally unarisen;
all phenomena have no departure, because they have no destination.
All phenomena are without abiding, because they have nothing upon which to rely;
all phenomena transcend the three periods of time, because the past, future, and present do not exist;
all phenomena are without difference, because their nature is one.
All phenomena are unarisen, because they are free from karmic retribution;
all phenomena have no karmic retribution, because their causes are not perceived;
all phenomena are non-created, because they are not subject to creation.
All dharmas are nameless, because names cannot be apprehended;
all dharmas are without arising, because they are neither born nor extinguished;
all dharmas are unreal, because they are fundamentally unarisen.
All dharmas are real, because they are equal through the gateway of the One Path;
all dharmas are without sentient beings, because no sentient beings are perceived;
all dharmas are without self, because they are subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
All dharmas are dull, because they possess no cognition;
all dharmas are equanimous, because they are free from hatred and love;
all dharmas are free from afflictions, because they are without grasping.
All phenomena are without affliction, because their intrinsic nature is unstained;
all phenomena have a single characteristic, because the limit of reality is equal;
all phenomena are free from characteristics, because they are eternally in tranquil concentration.
All dharmas abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because their nature is indestructible;
all dharmas abide in the aspect of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), because they are fundamentally indestructible;
all dharmas enter into the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), because they penetrate it universally.
All phenomena are without conditions, because various conditions do not conjoin;
all phenomena arise from conditions, because they are fulfilled in equality;
all phenomena are bodhi, because they are seen as they truly are.
"All phenomena are nirvāṇa, because they are unconditioned. Kāśyapa!
From the radiance of that Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-vibhu-rāja, there constantly issue these thirty-two kinds of pure and wondrous sounds of the Dharma."
“Kāśyapa! If there are sentient beings who are born in that land, you should know that such persons are able to perform the work of a Buddha. Kāśyapa!”
The lifespan of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, is immeasurable. Kāśyapa!
In that buddha-land, there are no demonic activities capable of creating obstacles for the bodhisattvas.
The Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is anyone who wishes to attain a pure buddha-field, they should adopt the roots of goodness and the merits of adornment for purifying a buddha-field as practiced by that Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!

Because this youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha has, in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Tathāgatas, made pure vows and fully perfected the adornments of his cultivation of merit, he has attained such a pure buddha-field.”

Therefore, Kāśyapa, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to attain such a pure buddha-field, they should train in the vows and practices cultivated by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha Kumārabhūta.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin said to the youth Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta Bodhisattva:
"Virtuous one! You have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha."
The Bodhisattva Mañjushrīkumārabhūta said:
“Brahmā! All sentient beings have been granted the prediction of enlightenment by the Tathāgata.”
He asked: "In what matter did you receive the prediction of enlightenment? He replied:
"One receives the prediction [of enlightenment] by undergoing retribution according to one's karma. He asked:
"What karma did you perform to receive this prediction?"
He asked: "Brahmā!
If karma is not performed by body, not performed by speech, and not performed by mind, can that karma be demonstrated?"
Brahmā replied, "It cannot be shown. He asked:
“Brahmā! For what reason do you speak thus? Brahmā!”
"Is there any mark that can be made regarding the practice of a bodhisattva? He replied, "No!"
"Because awakening is not characterized by conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). He asked: "Brahmā!..."
"Is awakening characterized by activity? He replied, "No!"
"Because bodhi is unconditioned and does not have the characteristic of being produced through effort. He asked: "Brahmā!..."
"Can one give rise to the mark of conditioned activity and thereby attain unconditioned bodhi? He replied, "No."
Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva said: "Brahmā!

Therefore, you should know that based on this meaning and intent, in whatever state there is no karma and no fruit of karma, and where there is neither doing nor acting—that is bodhi. As it is with bodhi, so it is with its explanation; as it is with the explanation, so it is with the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). One cannot obtain the prediction of enlightenment through the production of conditioned phenomena."
The Brahmā asked, "Good son,
is it that you will receive the prediction of enlightenment only after you have practiced the six pāramitās?"
He replied: "Brahmā! It is as you have said:
a bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment by practicing the six pāramitās."

Brahmā! If a bodhisattva relinquishes all afflictions, this is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā). To have no arising regarding all phenomena is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā). To have no injury toward all phenomena is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā). To be free from signs regarding all phenomena is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā). To have no dwelling place regarding all phenomena is called the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā). To be free from conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
“Brahmā! When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās in this manner, in what place do they practice? Brahmā said:
“Good son, there is no place where one practices.
Why is this? For whatever is practiced is non-practice; if one practices, that is non-practice, and if one does not practice, that is practice.”
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
"Brahmā! For this reason, you should know that non-practice is bodhi."

Regarding what you have asked: that you receive the prediction of enlightenment (bodhivyākaraṇa) is like receiving the prediction through the nature of reality (dharmatā) as suchness (tathatā); I, too, receive the prediction in this same way. Brahmā!
Based on this Dharma, one should know that non-practice is the practice of a bodhisattva. Brahmā!
As you have said, regarding your receiving of the prediction: just as True Suchness and the Dharma-realm receive their prediction, so too do I receive my prediction.
The Brahmā said: "Good son!
There is no such thing as receiving a prediction of enlightenment within the true thusness of the dharma-realm."
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
"Brahmā, such a prediction is like the dharma-realm of true thusness."
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what practice does a bodhisattva receive from the Buddhas the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! If a bodhisattva does not practice the dharma of arising, does not practice the dharma of cessation, and does not practice wholesome dharmas...”
Unwholesome dharmas do not proceed; neither worldly dharmas nor supramundane dharmas proceed;
neither tainted dharmas nor untainted dharmas proceed; neither blameworthy dharmas nor blameless dharmas proceed;
neither conditioned dharmas nor unconditioned dharmas proceed; the path of cultivation does not proceed...
Having severed [all attachments], one does not practice the mundane, nor does one practice nirvāṇa;
one does not practice seeing the Dharma, hearing the Dharma, awakening to the Dharma, or knowing the Dharma;
one does not practice giving, relinquishing, morality, concealment, patience, goodness, or exertion.
They do not practice diligence, they do not practice dhyāna, they do not practice samādhi, they do not practice wisdom;
they do not practice conduct, they do not practice knowledge, and they do not practice attainment.
Brahmā! If a bodhisattva practices in this way, the Buddhas will bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Brahmā! All that is practiced has something to which it clings; that which has no clinging is bodhi.
All that is practiced is conceptual discrimination; that which is free from discrimination is bodhi.
All that is practiced is conditioned activity; the absence of conditioned activity is bodhi.
All that is practiced is conceptual proliferation; the absence of conceptual proliferation is bodhi.
"Brahmā! It is by virtue of this meaning that you should know: if a bodhisattva transcends all spheres of practice, they shall receive the prediction [of enlightenment].
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the World-Honored One calls ‘receiving a prediction’ (vyākaraṇa), by means of what dharma is one said to receive a prediction?
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! To be free from the dual characteristics of all phenomena is called receiving the prediction; to not discriminate between arising and ceasing is called receiving the prediction; to be free from the characteristics of the actions of body, speech, and mind is called receiving the prediction.”
“Brahmā! I recall the past;
at that time there was an eon named Sudarśana, during which I made offerings to seventy-two nayutas of Buddhas, yet none of those Tathāgatas bestowed a prediction upon me.”

Furthermore, after this kalpa, there was a kalpa named "Skillful Transformation" (Suvyūha). During that kalpa, I made offerings to seventy-two billion Buddhas; yet these Tathāgatas also did not bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon me.

Furthermore, after this kalpa, there was a kalpa named Brahmastava; during that kalpa, I made offerings to eighty-eight thousand Buddhas, yet these Tathāgatas likewise did not bestow a prediction of my enlightenment upon me.

Furthermore, after that kalpa, there was a kalpa named "Faultless" (Anavadya). During that kalpa, I made offerings to thirty-two thousand Buddhas; yet these Tathāgatas also did not bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon me.

Furthermore, after that kalpa, there was a kalpa named Adornment; during that kalpa, I made offerings to forty-eight thousand Buddhas, honoring them all with every kind of requisite for worship, yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment.

“Brahmā! In the past, throughout one kalpa and the remaining kalpas, I have already made offerings to various Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them with all my heart; I have purely cultivated the brahma-faring, practiced all forms of giving, maintained all precepts, and observed the dhūta ascetic practices.”
Free from ill-will, with patience and a compassionate mind, they practice diligently according to what has been taught; they are able to receive and uphold everything they have heard.
Dwelling alone in seclusion, they enter various meditative absorptions, and in accordance with the wisdom they have heard, they read, recite, contemplate, and inquire.
These Tathāgatas have likewise not bestowed a prediction upon me.
Why is this? Because I questioned the Buddhas by relying on words and letters; for this reason, the Buddhas have not bestowed a prediction upon me.
Why is this? Because they rely upon what is practiced.
Therefore, one should know that if bodhisattvas transcend all practices, they receive the prediction of enlightenment.
“Brahmā! Thereafter, I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prophecy, saying:”
“Good son! In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, I transcended all conditioned activities and fulfilled the six pāramitās.

Why is this? If a bodhisattva can relinquish all marks, it is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); if they can extinguish all that is grasped and maintained, it is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); if they are not harmed by sense objects, it is called the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*); if they are detached from all modes of practice, it is called the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*); if they do not give rise to recollection of any phenomena, it is called the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*); and because they can endure the non-arising nature of all phenomena, it is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Brahmā! In the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I fulfilled these six pāramitās. Brahmā!"

The giving I have performed since first generating the mind of enlightenment does not equal even one hundredth part of this giving characterized by relinquishment; it does not equal one ten-thousandth, one hundred-millionth, nor one hundred-billionth part, nor can it even be approached by calculation or analogy.

“Brahmā! Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have maintained the precepts and practiced the dhūtas; yet compared to this constant extinction of the precepts, my practice does not equal even one hundredth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.”

“Brahmā! Since first generating the mind of awakening, my gentleness and patience have not approached even one hundredth part of this ultimate dharma of patience; they cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.”

“Brahmā! Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have exerted diligent effort; yet this effort of yours—neither grasping nor rejecting—is not even a hundredth part of mine, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.”

“Brahmā! Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, my practice of meditative concentration in solitary retreat has not been surpassed by this non-abiding meditative concentration even by a hundredth part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.”

“Brahmā! Since first resolving my mind toward enlightenment, the wisdom I have contemplated and deliberated upon does not equal even one hundredth part of this wisdom free from conceptual proliferation; it does not equal one ten-thousandth, one hundred-millionth, one billionth, or even one trillionth part, nor can it be approached by any calculation or analogy.”
"Brahmā! Therefore, you should know that at that time I had already attained fulfillment in the six pāramitās. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘fulfilling the six pāramitās’?”
The Buddha said:

"Brahmā! If one does not think of giving, does not rely on ethical discipline, does not discriminate regarding patience, does not grasp at diligence, does not dwell in meditative concentration, and is non-dual regarding wisdom—Brahmā!"
"This is called fulfilling the six pāramitās. Brahmā said,
"World-Honored One!"
“Having fulfilled the six pāramitās, what dharma can one fulfill?
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!”
"Having fulfilled the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñā (all-knowledge). Brahmā said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that, having fulfilled the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñatā?
The Buddha said, "Brahmā!"

The equality of giving is the equality of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); the equality of ethical discipline is the equality of *sarvajñā*; the equality of patience is the equality of *sarvajñā*; the equality of diligence is the equality of *sarvajñā*; the equality of meditative concentration is the equality of *sarvajñā*; and the equality of wisdom is the equality of *sarvajñā*. Because all phenomena are equal in this way, it is called *sarvajñā*.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!

The fulfillment of the characteristics of giving, the characteristics of ethical discipline, the characteristics of patience, the characteristics of diligence, the characteristics of meditative concentration, and the characteristics of wisdom—this is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
“Brahmā! In this way, by fulfilling the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñatā. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the fulfillment of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! If the eye does not see forms, and so on, up to the mind not cognizing phenomena—Brahmā!
If one observes the six internal and external sense bases in this manner, this is called fulfilling omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).”
