Brahmā! Thus is the fulfillment of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), namely, non-attachment to the eye, and so on, up to non-attachment to the mind. For this reason, it is called the Tathāgata’s unobstructed and unhindered wisdom of sarvajñatā.
“Brahmā! Sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) does not receive anything from dharmas. Why is this?
Because *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) is not a vessel for receiving [the Dharma]. O Brahmā!

That which is called "not a vessel" is termed "non-substantiality" (*avastu*), because it is capable of containing and holding. That which is called "non-substantiality" is termed "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*); this emptiness is identical to space, and this is what is called *sarvajñā*.
For this reason, one cannot receive the Dharma. Brahmā!
It is, for example, as all that is created depends upon space, yet that space has nothing upon which it depends.
"In this way, all such wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) emerges from omniscience, yet omniscience has no basis.
The Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Regarding what was said about *sarvajñā*— what is meant by *sarvajñā*,
and for what reason is it called *sarvajñā*?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! All conditioned phenomena are known by that wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna)—namely, by the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all the world. For this reason, it is called ‘omniscience.’”

Because it possesses the wisdom of equality regarding all that is practiced—knowing all minds, knowing all formations, knowing all forms of compassion, knowing all trainings, and knowing all initiations of practice—it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because it is able to leave behind all marks and able to shatter all discursive thoughts, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because it knows, as they truly are, what is spoken and what is not spoken, and because it knows, as they truly are, the mental activities of all sentient beings, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because it knows all things as they truly are through the wisdom of realization, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Because it knows the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*) exactly as they are—all of which emerge from within *sarvajñā*—it is for this reason called *sarvajñā*.
"Because one knows correctly that all right practices arise from sarvajñā (all-knowledge), it is called sarvajñā.
Because one knows all medicines as they truly are, it is called sarvajñā."
Because it can cause all illnesses to be extinguished, it is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Because it can bring about liberation from all bonds, it is called sarvajñā.
Because it can eliminate all afflictions and their habitual tendencies, it is called sarvajñā.
Because it is always present in all meditative concentrations, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because there is no doubt regarding any phenomenon, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because from that *sarvajñā* all mundane and supramundane wisdoms emerge, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because it knows the characteristics of all wisdom and skillful means, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Brahmā!
Because the skillful means of all dharmas emerge from this dharma, it is called *sarvajñā*.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
The wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is profoundly deep; though their minds have no object of focus, they know the mental activities of every sentient being.”
World-Honored One!
Since *sarvajñatā* possesses such immeasurable merits as these, what wise son or daughter of good family, upon hearing of *sarvajñatā*, would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Scripture of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, Scroll Three.
The Scripture of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the youth Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) out of a desire for the benefits of merit, they cannot be said to have set out upon the Great Vehicle.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas possess no merit or benefit, as they lack any state of counteraction.
World-Honored One!

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should not resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of the benefit of merit; rather, they should resolve upon bodhicitta solely for the sake of great compassion, for the sake of extinguishing the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, for the sake of generating all wholesome dharmas, for the sake of liberating them from all false views, for the sake of eliminating all illnesses, for the sake of abandoning attachment to "mine," for the sake of not regarding likes and dislikes, for the sake of not sinking into worldly dharmas, for the sake of wearying of the conditioned, and for the sake of abiding securely in nirvāṇa.
"World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva should not seek a reward of gratitude from sentient beings, nor should they observe what has been done or left undone; furthermore, their mind should remain unmoved by suffering or pleasure."
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the purification of the various roots of goodness of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness arise in the position of a wheel-turning sage king, they cannot be called pure roots of goodness;
if they arise among the Śakra kings or among the Brahmā kings, they likewise cannot be called pure roots of goodness.”

In whatever place they are born, even among animals, they do not lose their own roots of goodness and also cause sentient beings to give rise to various roots of goodness; this is called the purification of a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness.
"Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!
What is the purity of a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness?
Noble son, the roots of goodness of giving are pure because of the relinquishing of all requisites for life."
The roots of goodness of upholding the precepts are pure, because by removing feverish affliction one attains coolness.
The roots of goodness of patience are pure, because the mind does not engage in discrimination.
The roots of goodness of diligence are purified because of being free from indolence;
the roots of goodness of meditative concentration are purified because of not thinking of other vehicles;
the roots of goodness of wisdom are purified because of being free from all views.
The root of goodness of generosity is purified by means of the vision of equality;
the root of goodness of compassion is purified by means of the purity of the straightforward mind;
the root of goodness of sympathetic joy is purified by means of delighting in all dharmas without giving rise to craving.
The purity of relinquishing the roots of goodness is due to being free from all faults;
the purity of not relinquishing the roots of goodness of the bodhicitta is due to having no craving for the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was present in the great assembly, remaining in silence without speaking anything.
Then, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Bhagavān! This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta is seated in this great assembly; why does he remain silent regarding the Dharma being taught here, without offering any discourse?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
Regarding this teaching you have now spoken, you may briefly explain it further."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of the Dharma realized by the Buddha?”
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! The Dharma realized by a Buddha has no marks or characteristics.”
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
Can that Dharma be spoken, expounded, or discussed?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! That Dharma cannot be spoken, cannot be expounded, and cannot be discussed."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
If that dharma is inexpressible, unexpoundable, and indiscussible, then it cannot be demonstrated.”
At that time, the Brahma Viśeṣacintin addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
Do you not expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?”
Mañjuśrī asked: “Brahmā! Within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), is there perhaps any duality of characteristics?”
He replied, "There is none. Mañjuśrī asked:
“Brahmā! Do not all phenomena enter into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)? He replied:
"So be it," Mañjuśrī said.
"If that dharmatā is the characteristic of non-duality, and all dharmas enter into that dharmatā, how should one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?"
The Brahmā asked: "Is there perhaps a teaching of the Dharma that is also non-dual? He replied:
“Brahmā! If it were certain that there were both a speaker and a listener, then there could be the teaching of the Dharma, yet there would be no duality. Brahmā asked:
“Does the Tathāgata not teach the Dharma? He replied, “Brahmā!
Although the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he does not do so by means of dualistic characteristics. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is without dualistic discourse; although there is that which is taught, it is non-dual.
Brahmā asked: "If all dharmas are non-dual, how is it that ordinary beings take the non-dual and make it dual? He replied:

“Brahmā! Because ordinary people are greedily attached to a self, they differentiate things into duality; yet if there were no duality, there would never be two. Although they may variously differentiate them into two, in their ultimate reality, there are no dual characteristics.”
The Brahmā asked: "How does one recognize the non-dual dharma? He replied:
“Brahmā! If there were no duality to be cognized, then it would not be non-dual. Why is this?
"Brahmā! That which is without dual characteristics cannot be cognized. Brahmā!"
Yet the Tathāgata does not speak of dual dharmas; those dharmas are, as they have been described, not like that. Why is this?
Because those dharmas are devoid of names, words, and phrases.
Brahmā asked: “When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, what dharma does he grasp? He replied:
“Brahmā! When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there is nothing to be grasped. Brahmā asked:
"Is it not the case that one does not attain nirvana through the Dharma taught by the Buddha? He asked, "Brahmā!
"In nirvana, is there taking or rejecting? He replied,
"Nirvana neither goes nor comes."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, Brahmā! The Dharma taught by the Buddha neither goes nor comes."
Brahmā asked: "How should this Dharma be heard? He replied:
“As you have said. Brahmā asked, “In what way is it as you have said?”
He replied: "Brahmā!
Just as one does not recognize or hear, so do I speak in accordance with that which is not recognized or heard."
Brahmā asked: "Who is able to hear such a Dharma as this from the Tathāgata? He replied:
“Brahmā! One who does not cling to and is not defiled by any objective realms. Brahmā asked:
"Who is able to know this Dharma? He replied, "Brahmā!"
"By what kind of person is one not quarrelsome, lacking in discernment,
and not rejoicing [in others' faults]? Brahmā asked,
"In what way is a bhikṣu called 'quarrelsome'?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
If a bhikṣu considers something to be good or bad, or to be appropriate or inappropriate, this is called dispute."

"This is right principle, this is wrong principle"—this is called contention. "This is defilement, this is purity"—this is called contention. "This is wholesome, this is unwholesome"—this is called contention. "This dharma is censurable, this dharma is not censurable; this dharma is with outflows, this dharma is without outflows; this dharma is mundane, this dharma is supramundane; this dharma is conditioned, this dharma is unconditioned; this is observance of the precepts, this is breaking of the precepts; this is what may be done, this is what may not be done; this is attainable, this is unattainable."
"Brahmā! This is called dispute. Brahmā!"
If, within the Dharma, there is any sense of superiority or inferiority, or any attachment and grasping, these are all contentions; the Dharma taught by the Buddha is free from contention. O Brahmā!

Those who delight in frivolous discourse do not refrain from contention; those who delight in contention possess no qualities of a śramaṇa; those who delight in the qualities of a śramaṇa are free from conceptual proliferation.
Brahmā asked: “How does a bhikṣu follow the Buddha’s words and follow the Buddha’s teachings?”
He replied: "Brahmā!
If a bhikṣu’s mind remains unshaken whether he is praised or reviled, this is called following the Buddha's teaching."
Not following after words and language is called following the Buddha’s speech.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu extinguishes all marks of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), this is called following the Buddha’s teaching.
Not contradicting the meaning is called following the Buddha’s speech.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu guards the Dharma, this is called following the Buddha’s teaching.
Not contradicting the Buddha’s words is called following the Buddha’s words. Brahmā asked:
“How does a bhikṣu protect the Dharma? He replied: “Brahmā!
"If a bhikṣu does not contradict equality and does not destroy the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), he is then called one who is able to protect the Dharma. Brahmā asked:
"How does a bhikṣu draw near to the Buddha?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
If a bhikṣu, among all dharmas, does not perceive any dharma as being either near or far, this is called being in close proximity to the Buddha."
Brahmā asked: "In what way does a bhikṣu attend upon the Buddha? He replied:
“Brahmā! If a bhikṣu performs no action of body, speech, or mind, he is called a bhikṣu who serves the Buddha. Brahmā asked:
"Who is able to make offerings to the Buddha? He replied, "Brahmā!
"One does not give rise to sinful karma, nor does one give rise to meritorious karma, nor does one give rise to immovable karma. Brahmā asked,
"Who is able to see the Buddha?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
It is one who does not cling to the fleshly eye, does not cling to the divine eye, does not cling to the wisdom eye, does not cling to the Dharma eye, and does not cling to the Buddha eye."
Brahmā asked, "Who is able to see the Dharma? He replied:
“Brahmā! It is one who does not oppose the dharma of all causes and conditions. Brahmā asked:
“Who is able to correctly perceive all causes and conditions? He replied, “Brahmā!
"One who does not give rise to equanimity, does not perceive equanimity, and neither arises nor ceases. Brahmā asked:
"Who attains true wisdom?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
It is those phenomena that are without outflows (anāsrava-dharma), which are neither born nor extinguished."
Brahmā asked: "Who is able to follow and learn the precepts of the Tathāgata? He replied:
"O Brahmā! That which does not arise, is not received, is not grasped, and is not relinquished. Brahmā asked:
"Who is named Right Practice? He replied: "Brahmā!"
"One who does not follow the three realms. Brahmā asked,
"Who is a virtuous person?"
He replied: "Brahmā! One who does not undergo further rebirth."
The Brahmā asked, "Who is the happy person? He replied:
"Brahmā! One who is without self and without what belongs to a self. Brahmā asked:
"Who has attained liberation? He replied, "Brahmā!"
"One who does not break the bonds.
Brahmā asked, "Who is it that attains deliverance?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
It is one who dwells neither in the world nor in nirvāṇa."
The Brahmā asked: "What has the bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted exhausted? He replied:

"Brahmā! If there were something that could be exhausted, it would not be called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). To know the empty nature of all outflows and to know them in accordance with such knowledge is what is called the exhaustion of outflows. Brahmā asked:
"Who speaks the truth? He replied, "Brahmā!"
"One who has departed from the path of all verbal discourse. Brahmā asked:
"Who is it that enters the path?"
He replied: "Brahmā!

Ordinary persons have an entry into the Path; however, those who practice the noble way know that all conditioned phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere, and thus for them there is no entry into the Path."
Brahmā asked, "Who is able to see the Noble Truths? He replied:
“Brahmā! If one perceives nothing regarding all phenomena, why is that?
"All views whatsoever are false; that which has no view is called the truth.
Brahmā asked: "By not seeing what dharma is one said to have seen the truths?"
He replied: "Brahmā! Not perceiving any phenomena is called the ultimate truth."
Brahmā asked: "In what should such true dharmas be sought? He replied:
“Brahmā! One should seek it within the four inversions. Brahmā asked:
"With what intention do you speak thus? He replied, "Brahmā!
When one seeks the four perversions, one finds no permanence, no pleasure, no self, and no purity. Since permanence is not found because permanence does not exist, this is precisely impermanence;
since pleasure is not found anywhere, this is precisely suffering;
since a self is not found anywhere, this is precisely non-self.
Brahmā! Where there is no purity, that is itself impurity.
That all phenomena are without self is the Noble Truth.
If a person seeks the ultimate truth, that person does not recognize suffering;
if a person abandons the origin, that person does not recognize the origin;
if a person perceives cessation, that person does not recognize cessation.
"If a person seeks the Way, that person does not recognize the Way.
Brahmā asked: "How does one cultivate the Way?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “Brahmā!
If one does not discriminate between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and remains free from these two marks, this is called cultivating the path.”
Because all phenomena cannot be apprehended when sought by means of such a path, it is called the "path.
Such a path neither abides in the world nor abides in nirvana.
"Why is this? Because that which is neither departing nor arriving is what is called the Noble Path.
At that time, the Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra Samatācāra addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, saying:
“Mañjuśrī! How does a lay follower take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha? He replied:
“Good son! If an upāsaka does not give rise to two views, how is it that he does not give rise to two views? It means he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of others;

he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of the Buddha; he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of the Dharma; he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of the Saṅgha. This is called an upāsaka taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.”
"Furthermore, good son!
If an upāsaka does not see the Buddha through form, nor through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is called an upāsaka taking refuge in the Buddha."

"Good son! If an upāsaka does not differentiate among phenomena and does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding phenomena, this is called an upāsaka’s taking refuge in the Dharma. Good son!"

If an upāsaka has faith in the unconditioned Dharma and Saṃgha, yet does not depart from his faith in the conditioned Dharma while having faith in the unconditioned Dharma, this is called an upāsaka’s taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If an upāsaka does not see the Buddha, does not see the Dharma, and does not see the Saṃgha, this is called an upāsaka taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṃgha."
At that time, the brahmin Mahābrahmāputra Samacārin addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
"To where do these bodhisattvas who have resolved upon bodhicitta proceed? He replied: "Good son!
They proceed toward space.
Why is this? Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is identical to space.
The Bodhisattva Samacārin said:
“Mañjuśrī, how is it that a bodhisattva is said to have resolved their mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
He replied: "Good son!

If a bodhisattva knows that all arousals are non-arousals, that all phenomena are non-phenomena, and that all sentient beings are non-sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, the Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra Samacārī Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called a ‘bodhisattva,’ what is meant by the term ‘bodhisattva’?”
"For what reason is one called a Bodhisattva?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

If a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings fixed in error, yet perceives no distinction between them and those fixed in the right, they are therefore called a bodhisattva. Why is this?

"Good son! A bodhisattva does not resolve their mind for the sake of beings fixed in the right path, nor for the sake of beings of indeterminate destiny; rather, it is solely for the sake of liberating beings fixed in the wrong path that they give rise to great compassion and resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, they are called 'bodhisattvas'."
Why is this? Son of good family!
Because a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings fixed in the wrong way and aspires toward great enlightenment, he is called a "bodhisattva."
At that time, the bodhisattva named Bodhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on this: for what reason is one called a ‘bodhisattva’?”
The Buddha said, "Speak then. Bodhi Bodhisattva said:

"Just as if a man or a woman were to receive the eight precepts for one day, observing them without violation or deficiency, so too a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of Buddhahood, constantly cultivates pure conduct throughout that interval; therefore, they are called a 'bodhisattva'."
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, possesses an unshakable mind, they are called a ‘bodhisattva.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind.
“If a bodhisattva accomplishes a profound and firm mind of loving-kindness and constantly keeps sentient beings in mind, he is therefore called a ‘bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Who Delivers Sentient Beings said:

“For example, just as a bridge or a boat ferries people across without weariness and without discrimination, if a bodhisattva possesses such a mind to deliver all sentient beings, he is therefore called a ‘bodhisattva.’”
The Bodhisattva Severing Evil Realms said:
"If, wherever a bodhisattva places the soles of his feet upon the lands of all buddha-fields, all evil realms are immediately extinguished; for this reason, he is called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said:

"If sentient beings who see a bodhisattva immediately attain certainty regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and if they escape from fear and terror by calling upon his name, for these reasons he is called a 'Bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"If a bodhisattva, at the place where his foot touches the ground, causes the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra to tremble, for this reason he is called a 'Bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva A-Parikhinna said:

"If a bodhisattva takes a number of kalpas equal to the sands of the Ganges as one day and night, counts thirty such days as a month, and twelve such months as a year, and if, by this reckoning of years, they pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas before encountering a single Buddha—and if they thus practice all forms of pure conduct (brahmacarya) and cultivate merit under as many Tathāgatas as there are sands in the Ganges—only then do they receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet their mind does not cease and they have no weariness, for this reason they are called 'Bodhisattvas'."
The Bodhisattva Guide said:

"If a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings who have fallen into wrong paths, leading them to enter the right path without seeking any reward for their kindness, he is therefore called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Mahāmeru said:
"If a bodhisattva makes no conceptual distinctions regarding any phenomena, being as singular among all forms as Mount Meru, for this reason they are called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said:
"If a bodhisattva is not destroyed by any afflictions, for that reason he is called a 'bodhisattva'.
The Bodhisattva Cittabala said:
"If a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas with the mind, yet his own body and mind are neither destroyed nor impaired, he is therefore called a 'bodhisattva'.
The Bodhisattva Lion’s Gait Sovereign said:

"If a bodhisattva is neither terrified nor afraid amidst various treatises, attains profound dharma-patience, and is able to cause all Māras and non-Buddhists to be utterly struck with fear, he is therefore called a 'bodhisattva'."

The Bodhisattva Acintya said: "If a bodhisattva knows that both mind and phenomena are inconceivable, such that there is nothing to contemplate and nothing to differentiate, for this reason they are called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Devaputra Śāntiprāpta said:
“If a bodhisattva is able to be born in all celestial palaces, yet remains unstained and does not even apprehend this state of being unstained, for this reason he is called a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Satyavādin said:
"If a bodhisattva always speaks with truth whenever he utters words, and does not even speak falsely even in his dreams, for this reason he is called a 'Bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"If a bodhisattva can see that all forms are the form of the Buddha, he is therefore called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Nityakaruṇā said:

"If a bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings fallen into the suffering and affliction of birth and death, does not cling to any personal pleasures but teaches and transforms sentient beings solely through the joy of the Dharma, he is therefore called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Mind said:
"If a bodhisattva is able to feel neither anger nor obstruction toward any afflictions or maras, they are therefore called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Constant Joy Faculty said:
"If a bodhisattva always fulfills their own vows with the faculty of joy, and likewise fulfills the vows of others so that all tasks are accomplished, they are therefore called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Dispelling Doubt said:
"If a bodhisattva does not give rise to doubt or regret regarding any phenomena, they are therefore called a 'bodhisattva'.
The Bodhisattva Lion Youth said:

"If a bodhisattva possesses neither the male nature nor the female nature, yet manifests all manner of physical forms for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, they are therefore called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Ratnāvatī said:
"If a bodhisattva does not give rise to attachment toward worldly treasures but delights only in the Three Jewels, for this reason they are called a 'bodhisattva'.
The laywoman Viśākhadattā said:

“If a bodhisattva has anything to be attained, there is no bodhi; because they do not attain any dharmas, do not give rise to any dharmas, and do not extinguish any dharmas, they are therefore called a ‘bodhisattva.’”
The great worthy Bhadrapāla said:
"If there are sentient beings who hear the name of a bodhisattva, they immediately attain certainty regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; therefore, one is called a bodhisattva."
The youth Ratnacandra said:

"If a bodhisattva is always able to practice the celibate conduct of a youth, even to the point of not entertaining thoughts of the five desires in the mind, let alone experiencing them with the body, he is therefore called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Māndāravagandhika, a son of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, said:

"If a bodhisattva perfumes the mind with the observance of precepts, such that the fragrance of all wholesome dharmas and merits constantly flows forth, and no other fragrance flows, for this reason he is called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Making Joy said:
"If a bodhisattva delights in three dharmas—namely, making offerings to the Buddha, safeguarding the true Dharma, and teaching and transforming sentient beings—he is therefore called a bodhisattva."
The Brahmā Viśeṣacintin said:
"If a bodhisattva perceives all dharmas as being the Buddha-dharma, for that reason he is called a 'bodhisattva'.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"If a Bodhisattva is one whom sentient beings see and immediately attain entry into the samādhi of great loving-kindness, he is therefore called a 'Bodhisattva'.
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, said:

"If a Bodhisattva, although preaching all dharmas, does not give rise to the notion of dharmas, does not give rise to the notion of self, and does not give rise to the notion of others, he is therefore called a 'Bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Kumārabhūta Jālinīprabha said:
“If the radiance of a bodhisattva can extinguish the darkness of all afflictions of all sentient beings, for this reason he is called a ‘bodhisattva.’”
The Bodhisattva Samantakusuma said:
"If a bodhisattva perceives the blossoming of various flowers throughout the Buddha-worlds filling the ten directions, he is therefore called a 'bodhisattva'.
Thus, each of these bodhisattvas, according to their own eloquence of inspired speech (*pratibhāna*), spoke their respective words.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇa Samatācāra, saying: "Good son!

If a bodhisattva can undergo all manner of suffering and affliction on behalf of all sentient beings, and can likewise relinquish all meritorious deeds to give them to all sentient beings, he is therefore called a 'bodhisattva'."
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin asked the Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra Samatācārin: "Good son,
by what practice do you now practice?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
I practice in such a way that all conditioned phenomena and the practices of all sentient beings are my own practice."
Brahmā asked: "By what do all sentient beings practice all conditioned phenomena? He replied:
“Brahmā! That which is the practice of all Buddhas is the practice of all conditioned phenomena and of all sentient beings. Brahmā asked:
“What do the Buddhas take as their practice? He replied: “Brahmā!...”
"The Buddhas take the emptiness of the ultimate truth as their practice. Brahmā asked, "Good man!..."
"If all ordinary beings practice in this way, and the Buddhas also practice in this same way, what difference is there between a Buddha and sentient beings?
The Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra, the Brahmā of Equal Practice, said: "Brahmā!..."
"O Benevolent One, do you wish for there to be distinctions within empty space? He replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī asked the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin: "Brahmā,
does the Tathāgata not teach that all phenomena are empty?"
He replied, “It is so. Mañjuśrī said:
"Therefore, Brahmā! All dharmas are without distinction;

these characteristics of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are likewise without the characteristic of distinction. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not say that dharmas possess various distinct characteristics."
The Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra Samatācāra addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
Regarding the practices described by various words, what is meant by ‘practice’?”
He replied, "Good son!
That place wherein the four right practices exist is called the 'sphere of practice' for that person."
“Brahmā! By what kind of person are the four brahma-vihāras practiced such that the practice of that person is not considered brahma-vihāra?
By what kind of practice are the four brahma-vihāras practiced such that that person is said to have accomplished the brahma-vihāras?”

“Good son! Although one may travel through empty and vast wildernesses, if one is devoid of the holy life (brahmacarya), that person is not said to have accomplished the holy life, nor is he skillfully proficient in knowing the holy life.”

"Good son! Furthermore, there are those who, even while amidst multi-storied pavilions, halls, towers, and gabled buildings, and upon gold and silver couches with exquisite coverlets and bedding, practice and accomplish the holy life (*brahmacarya*) therein; such persons truly accomplish the holy life and are indeed skillful in knowing the holy life."
He asked: "If one perceives the view of self, is that not a non-wise perception? He replied:
“Good son! It is so, it is so. Good son!”
If one perceives a self, that is not the vision of wisdom.
Son of good family!
It is like a person who, by knowing the nature of gold as it truly is, then knows what is malleable and what is not.
"Seeing it in this way is what I call the purification of wisdom.
[The interlocutor] asked: "What do you mean by 'the view of self'?"
He replied: "Good son! It is the essence of the dharma of non-self that is eternal."
"Good son! The self is eternally without substance and fundamentally unestablished; because it is thus ultimately and definitively so, it is called 'self. He asked:
"As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī, to see me is to see the Buddha.
Why is this? Because there is no distinction between my essence and the essence of the Buddha."
Mañjuśrī asked: "What kind of person is able to see the Tathāgata? He replied:
“Good son! If one is unable to alter the characteristics of the view of self, why is this? Because—”
"I see the Dharma, I see the Buddha, and these views are equal.
He asked: "Is there perhaps a state of non-practice that is called 'right practice'?"
He replied, "There is, son of good family!"
"If one does not engage in any conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), this is called right practice.
He asked: "How is it that practicing in such a way is called right practice?"
He replied: “Good son!
If one practices not for the sake of knowing, not for the sake of abandoning, not for the sake of realizing, and not for the sake of cultivating, this is called right practice.”
He asked: "Is there anyone who has not seen the Buddha, yet whose eye of wisdom is pure? He replied:
"Yes, noble son! Since the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, do not perceive dualistic marks, that person possesses the pure, holy eye."
He asked, "What kind of dharmas does the wisdom-eye see? He replied:
“Good son! If one perceives even a single dharma, it cannot be called the wisdom-eye. Good son!”
The eye of wisdom does not perceive conditioned phenomena, nor does it perceive unconditioned phenomena.
Why is this? Because that prajñā is free from conceptual discrimination.

For this reason, Prajñā does not perceive conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); those unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) also transcend the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and for this reason they are not perceived.
He asked: “Is it possible for a bhikṣu of correct practice not to attain the fruits of the path?”
He replied, "There is, noble son!"
Within right practice, there is no fruit, no attainment, and no right practice; nor is there the cultivation of even a single dharma therein.
Son of good family!
Furthermore, in that place, no fruit can be obtained, because it is free from conceptual discrimination.
"Good son! If one does not attain even a single dharma, that is called 'attainment. Good son!"

If one discriminates by saying, "I have attained something," that person possesses pride; for within right practice there is no overweening pride, and because there is no overweening pride, there is neither realization nor attainment.
He asked: "By attaining what dharma is one said to have 'attained the Way'? He replied:
“Good son! By what dharma is there non-arising—being originally unarisen and not arising even later—for the sake of attaining that dharma, I speak of the true dharma.”
He asked: "If dharmas are unarisen, what dharma is realized? He replied:
“Good son! If one knows that which is non-arising, that very knowledge is called the realization of the Dharma.
To see that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are fundamentally non-arising is what is called attaining the realization of right concentration.”
He asked, "By what is one said to have realized right concentration? He replied:
“Good son! I and nirvāṇa are equal and non-dual, without any distinction; therefore, it is called ‘realizing right concentration.
Because one accords with right concentration, it is called ‘realizing right concentration.’”
Because one ultimately attains the dharma of equality, it is called "right concentration.
Furthermore, because it enables the realization of the definitive meaning, it is called "right concentration.
Because it is free from conceptual proliferation regarding all samādhis, it is called "right concentration."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Mañjuśrī! You have spoken these words well; it is exactly as you have said. It is so, Mañjuśrī!

When you preached this Dharma, seven thousand bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any phenomena, attained the exhaustion of outflows and their minds were liberated; thirty-two thousand devas became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; ten thousand people became free from desire and attained meditative concentration; two hundred people resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and five hundred bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Brahma-deva Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī is able to perform the work of a Buddha, bringing great benefit to sentient beings, and causing immeasurable sentient beings to enter into nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! You, too, have benefited immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to enter nirvana."
Mañjuśrī asked, “Brahmā! Do you think that sentient beings have a numerical measure?”
He replied, "No. He asked again:
“Brahmā! Has the Tathāgata ever spoken of the existence of sentient beings?
Furthermore, do sentient beings possess the substantial essence of a sentient being?”
He replied, "There is none. He asked:
“Brahmā! What do you think? Do you consider that the Tathāgata has birth and cessation?”
He replied, “No. He asked again:
“Brahmā! If this is so, what kind of sentient beings does the Tathāgata cause to enter nirvāṇa? Brahmā replied:
“By means of what dharma-nature does the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī teach the Dharma in this way— that there is neither world nor nirvāṇa?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Brahmā!”
"It is so, it is so. The Tathāgata perceives neither the world nor nirvāṇa. Brahmā!
Even those śrāvaka disciples who have been transformed by the Tathāgata likewise perceive neither the world nor nirvāṇa."
Brahmā! What is called "nirvāṇa" is merely a verbal expression; yet there is no person who travels through the world, nor is there any person who travels toward nirvāṇa.
Brahmā asked: "Regarding all the words of dispute and contention that are spoken—what dharma do such words describe? He replied:
“Brahmā! This is mere conceptual proliferation; it does not speak of sentient beings. Brahmā!”
If there were conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then there would be no eternal absence of the conceit "I am.
For this reason, one engages in conceptual proliferation regarding that which is non-existent.
Because one knows that conceptual proliferation lacks true reality, one does not perceive conceptual proliferation.

If one does not perceive conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), that person does not course in the world; if one does not course in the world, there is no divergent view; and because there is no divergent view, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Brahmā asked: "Mañjuśrī, regarding what is called 'entering nirvāṇa,' by means of what antidote do you speak of nirvāṇa?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
For one who has entered nirvāṇa, these causes and conditions do not come together; ignorance does not arise, nor do worldly formations arise."

If one does not give rise to formative activities (*saṃskāra*), then there is no birth; that which is unborn is called *nirvāṇa*. Not giving rise to various activities is termed "quiescence" (*śānti*); that dharma is called the realization of the Noble Path. Because it is eternally unborn, this is what is called the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, the Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra Samacārin addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
"Are all that you have spoken, O Benevolent One, truly real? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O son of good family!"
"All verbal expressions are entirely true.
He asked: "Are even false verbal expressions true?"
He replied, “It is so. For what reason?
"Good son! All these verbal expressions are false and illusory, having neither location nor direction;
if a dharma is false and has neither location nor direction, that is itself reality."
For this reason, all speech is entirely true. Good son!
All the words of Devadatta are no different and no distinct from the words of the Tathāgata.

Why is this? All verbal expressions whatsoever are the verbal expressions of the Tathāgata, for they do not transcend suchness. Regarding all matters expressed through speech, everything is expressed precisely because there is nothing to be expressed; therefore, all verbal expressions are equal, for their characters are identical and those characters are empty.
He asked: "Does the Tathāgata not speak both the language of ordinary people and the language of the noble ones? Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is, noble son! Just as the Noble Ones teach the Dharma through words and speech, do not ordinary people also speak by means of written characters and phrases?"
He replied, "It is so. He said:

"Is there any distinction in words and speech such that one can say, 'These are the words and speech of ordinary persons' and 'These are the words and speech of noble ones'? He replied, "There is not."
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son! Just as those words, names, and phrases are neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized, so too all noble ones are free from all conceptualization."

Therefore, the Sage has no teaching by means of names; that which the Sage practices is not characterized by language, nor by the characteristics of dharmas, nor by the characteristics of sentient beings. It is like the sound produced when various conditions such as a drum or a conch shell come together: these sounds possess no conceptual discrimination.
In this way, noble son!
Because all noble and holy ones thoroughly understand all causes and conditions, they regard all verbal expressions as entirely equal and without any discrimination.
The Bodhisattva Samacārin said: "Mañjuśrī!
As the Buddha has taught, when a great assembly gathers, one should practice two things: either preaching the Dharma according to reality, or noble silence."
Mañjuśrī! What is the teaching of the Dharma according to reality? What is noble silence?
He replied: "Good son!
If one preaches the Dharma without contradicting the Buddha, without contradicting the Dharma, and without contradicting the Sangha, this is called preaching the Dharma according to reality."
“If one knows that phenomena are themselves the Buddha, that being free from marks is itself the Dharma, and that the unconditioned is itself the Sangha, this is called the noble silence.
Furthermore, son of good family!”
If one speaks based on the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;
if one has no recollections regarding any phenomena, this is called noble silence.
If one speaks based on the four right efforts, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;
if one does not treat equality as equality, nor fails to treat it as equality, this is called noble silence.
If one speaks based on the four bases of psychic power, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;
if one does not abandon body, speech, and mind, this is called noble silence.
If one speaks based on the five faculties and the five powers, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;

if one has faith that does not follow the words of others, and for the sake of neither grasping nor rejecting discriminates among all phenomena, dwelling with single-minded concentration in the state of non-conceptualization, and if one believes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure and free from all conceptual proliferation and causal activity, this is called noble silence.
"If there is any teaching based on the seven factors of enlightenment, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;
if one constantly practices equanimity without discrimination, neither increasing nor decreasing, this is called noble silence."
If one speaks based on the Eightfold Noble Path, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;

if one knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are like the parable of the raft—neither relying on the practice of the Dharma nor relying on the practice of non-Dharma—this is called noble silence.

“Good son! Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), if one can establish, reveal, distinguish, and expound them through speech, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality; because it is taught according to reality, it is called teaching the Dharma according to reality.

If one realizes these dharmas through the body, yet does not perceive dharmas apart from the body, nor perceive the body apart from dharmas—within this contemplation, seeing neither duality nor non-duality—and thus sees while not seeing before one’s eyes, this is called noble silence (*ārya-tūṣṇīmbhāva*).”
"Furthermore, noble son!

If one does not falsely conceptualize and cling to a self, nor falsely conceptualize and cling to another, nor falsely conceptualize and cling to dharmas, non-dharmas, or the false conceptualization of neither-dharma-nor-non-dharma, yet speaks, this is called teaching the Dharma according to reality.

If one attains the perception of the ineffable Dharma, is able to transcend all names, words, sounds, and voices, and attains the unmoving state by entering a mind free from conditioned activity, this is called the noble silence."
"Furthermore, noble son!
If one teaches the Dharma to all sentient beings by knowing their faculties and powers in this way, it is called teaching the Dharma according to reality;
if one constantly abides in meditative concentration with an undistracted mind, it is called noble silence."
At that time, the brahmin Mahābrahmāputra Samacaryā Brahmā addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!..."

As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī, among all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, there is none who speaks the Dharma in accordance with reality, nor is there any noble silence.
Why is this? Because they are unable to discern the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, nor are they able to remain constantly in meditative concentration. Mañjuśrī!
If someone in the world were to ask with words of truth:
"Who in the world speaks the Dharma according to reality?
Who in the world dwells in noble silence?"
"One should say that it refers to the Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī! One should correctly state that it refers to the Buddhas."

"Why is this? Because all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, possess the powers of the faculties and skillfully know whether the faculties of sentient beings are sharp or dull, for they always abide in meditative concentration.
The Buddha addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"So it is, so it is! Just as this good man Samacārin has said, only the Tathāgatas possess these two dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have personally heard this from the Buddha and received it directly from the Buddha: ‘When you assemble, you should practice two things: either preach the Dharma in accordance with reality, or maintain noble silence.’”
World-Honored One!
If śrāvakas are unable to practice these, why does the Tathāgata command the bhikṣus to practice the teaching of reality as it is and to practice noble silence?
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, what do you think?”
“If a śrāvaka were not to hear it from another, could he teach the Dharma as it truly is and remain in noble silence?
Subhūti replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One! The Buddha said: “Subhūti!
"Therefore, you should know that among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, none possess the teaching of the Dharma as it truly is, nor do they possess noble silence.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī asked the Elder Subhūti: "Elder Subhūti!"
The Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the eighty-four thousand mental dispositions of sentient beings; do you know this?
Within this regard, are you able to exercise wisdom and preach the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each?
He replied, "I cannot. Mañjuśrī said:

“Subhūti, are you now able to enter the samādhi that contemplates the minds of all sentient beings, penetrating the mental activities of every being’s mind and mental factors, without any obstruction regarding your own mind or the minds of others?”
He replied, “I cannot. Mañjuśrī said:

“The Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the eighty-four thousand mental activities of sentient beings and administers the medicine of the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each. Furthermore, while always abiding in the state of meditative concentration characterized by equanimity, his mind remains unshaken; yet he constantly penetrates the mental activities of all sentient beings without conceptualizing them, being free from obstruction and hindrance.”
"Is Subhūti able to do so now? He replied, "I am not."

Mañjuśrī said: “The Tathāgata, as it truly is, understands the eighty-four thousand mental activities of sentient beings; he preaches the medicine of the Dharma according to reality while remaining constantly in meditative absorption. Within the state of equanimity, his mind does not waver, and he also perpetually penetrates the mental activities of every sentient being’s mind without conceptualization, unobstructed and unhindered.”
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess this as their domain. Subhūti!
There may be sentient beings who have much lust and attain liberation by contemplating the pure rather than the impure; only a Buddha can know this.
There may be sentient beings who have much anger and attain liberation by contemplating faults rather than through a mind of loving-kindness; only a Buddha can know this.

There may be sentient beings who possess great ignorance and attain liberation through not being addressed with speech, rather than through the preaching of the Dharma; this alone the Buddha can know.

There may be sentient beings whose faculties are balanced (samabhāga) and who attain liberation neither through the contemplation of purity, nor through the contemplation of impurity, nor through the contemplation of faults, nor through loving-kindness, nor through not being addressed with speech, nor through the preaching of the Dharma; for them, the Buddha preaches the Dharma by means of the equality of all phenomena according to their specific faculties and natures so that they may attain liberation—this alone the Buddha can know.
Therefore, Subhūti, among those who speak according to reality, the Buddha is the foremost; among those who maintain noble silence, he is the foremost.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!

If those who are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot thus preach the Dharma according to reality, nor can they thus maintain noble silence, then do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the ability to accomplish such merit as preaching the Dharma according to reality and maintaining noble silence?”
He replied, "Only the Buddha should know this.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Elder Subhūti, saying:
“Subhūti! There is a samādhi called ‘Entering All Languages with an Undistracted Mind. If bodhisattvas are able to accomplish this samādhi, they shall all obtain such merit as this.”
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin, saying:

"Good son! For the sake of the eighty-four thousand types of conduct of all sentient beings, one preaches eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma; this is called preaching the Dharma according to reality."
To always abide in all meditative absorptions that extinguish sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is called the noble silence. Good son!

If I were to spend an eon, or even the remainder of an eon, speaking on these two meanings—the characteristics of the Dharma as it truly is and the noble silence—I could not reach their end; yet my eloquence in expounding the Dharma would likewise never be exhausted.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin, saying: "Good son!

In the distant past, immeasurable and boundless, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Pūrvaprabhāsa Tathāgata, up to and including Buddha Bhagavān. The kalpa was named Yaśas, and the land was named Priyadarśana."

That world of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, named Priyadarśana, is adorned with the seven precious jewels; it is prosperous, peaceful, and secure, free from all fears. Gods and humans abound there, and its ground is entirely embellished with various treasures.
“Good son! In that land of Sudarśana, there are four hundred billion sets of four continents; each individual continent measures eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth.”
The various cities therein were equal in length and breadth, each measuring one yojana, and were all adorned with a multitude of precious jewels.
Each and every city was surrounded by twenty-five thousand villages, and within each village dwelt and resided an immeasurable number of hundreds of thousands of millions of people.

When people behold the physical forms and images, their hearts are filled with joy and they feel no aversion; furthermore, they all attain the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). For this reason, the land is named "Joyful Vision" (Sudarśana).
If bodhisattvas come from other worlds, they all obtain happiness, whereas it is not so in other lands. "Good son!

That Buddha Samantaraśmi teaches the Dharma to his disciples by means of the three vehicles; he also frequently and extensively expounds such Dharma discourses as the teaching of reality as it is, or noble silence."
“Good son! At that time, in the land of the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja in the zenith, there were two bodhisattvas:
one named Akṣayamati;”
The second was named Yi-yi (Beneficial Mind).

He went to the land of Xijian (Joyful Vision) to the abode of the Buddha Puguang (Universal Radiance), prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and, with palms joined in reverence, withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha Universal Radiance extensively analyzed and explained the Samādhi of Pure Clarity for the two bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons,
for what reason is it called the Samādhi of Pure Clarity?"

"Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who enters this samādhi, he immediately becomes free from all afflictions and attains pure radiance regarding all Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Pure Radiance'."

Furthermore, all phenomena are pure in the past, all phenomena are pure in the future, and all phenomena are pure in the present; these phenomena of the three periods of time are ultimately pure because they are eternally pure by virtue of that purity. Therefore, it is said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure and eternally pure.
"What is meant by the intrinsic purity of all phenomena?
It means that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness, because they are free from the apprehension of anything within all phenomena.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is signlessness, because they are free from all conceptual discriminations regarding all phenomena."

All phenomena are by nature wishless (*apraṇihita*), because all phenomena are neither grasped nor rejected, are without seeking or desire, and because the ultimate nature of all phenomena is detached; this is called the eternal purity of the nature of all phenomena.
By whatever nature the world exists, nirvāṇa is likewise, sharing that same dharmatā;
by whatever nature nirvāṇa exists, all phenomena likewise share that same nature.
For this reason, it is said that the self-nature of all phenomena is intrinsically pure.
“Good son! For example, it is impossible for space to be defiled; likewise, it is impossible for the nature of the mind to be defiled.”
Good son! For example, although the void may be obscured by smoke, dust, clouds, and mist, becoming neither bright nor pure, it cannot defile the nature of space.

"Good son! If the nature of space were subject to defilement, it could never be called pure. Since that space is truly incapable of being defiled, it is therefore called 'space'; such is the nature of space."

“Good son! Although all sentient beings who engage in conditioned activities give rise to various afflictions through improper mindfulness, the intrinsic nature of their minds is pure and cannot be defiled.”
If it were defiled, it would be perpetually stained and could never be purified; because it is not defiled, the mind is pure by its very nature and attains liberation.
"Good son! This is called entering the gate of the Samādhi of Pure Radiance. Good son!"

That Buddha Samantaprabha taught this Dharma for the sake of those two bodhisattvas; having heard this samādhi, those two bodhisattvas attained the light of the inconceivable Dharma among all phenomena.
The Scripture of the Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, Scroll Four;
The Scripture of the Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa, saying: "World-Honored One!
We have already heard of the entrance into the Samādhi of Pure Radiance; by what practices should we practice this Dharma-gate?"
At that time, the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying:
"Good son! There are two practices which you should perform: [text continues]"
"Either preach the Dharma as it truly is, or remain in noble silence.

Then the two bodhisattvas, having received the instruction from the Buddha, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. They went to a grove containing a wondrous pond, where they used their supernormal powers to manifest jeweled pavilions and practiced therein.

At that time, there was a Brahmā named Subhāṣita who, together with seventy-two thousand other Brahmās, came to where [the two bodhisattvas] were, prostrated his head at their feet, and addressed the two bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

The Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa spoke these words: "You sons of good family, you who have gathered here in this great assembly, should practice two things: either preaching the Dharma according to reality, or noble silence."
Good son! What is meant by preaching the Dharma according to reality?
What is meant by noble silence?
The two bodhisattvas said:
"Brahmā! Now listen with a sincere mind; we shall explain it to you in brief."
"As you have asked, only a Tathāgata can fully comprehend this.
Thereupon, the two bodhisattvas extensively analyzed and explained these two points of meaning for the assembly of Brahmās.

At that time, seventy-two thousand members of the Brahma assembly all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the Brahma Heaven Subtle Light attained the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.

During those seventy-six thousand years, the two Bodhisattvas, by means of their power of eloquence and unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), answered the questions posed to them; they taught the Dharma according to reality or maintained noble silence, tirelessly and without ceasing distinguishing between the two phrases as they questioned and answered one another, never reaching an end.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha spoke these words from mid-air: "Good sons!
Do not give rise to disputes over written characters or spoken words; for all speech is empty like an echo, and the same is true of questions and answers."
Both of you have attained unimpeded eloquence and the inexhaustible dhāraṇī; even if one were to speak for an eon or a hundred eons, one could never exhaust the eloquence of these two phrases.

"Good son! The Dharma of all Buddhas is the ultimate meaning of the characteristic of quiescence. Within this, there is stillness and ultimate stillness; it is without words and without meaning, and cannot be expressed in speech. All verbal expressions are ultimately without meaning."
"Therefore, you sons of good family, you should rely upon the meaning and not rely upon the words.
When the two bodhisattvas had heard the Buddha's instruction, they remained silent.

“Good son! For this reason, you should know that if a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma through their eloquence, it could not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, or even beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.”
"Good son! What do you think?
Could those two bodhisattvas possibly be anyone else?"
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati is none other than the present Mañjuśrī;
the Bodhisattva Upakūṭa is you yourself;
and the Brahmā Prabhāsa is Viśeṣacintin.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samacārin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The bodhi of all Buddhas brings great benefit to those sentient beings who are diligent; those who practice according to what is taught shall attain bodhi.”
World-Honored One!

Sentient beings are indolent; those who are unable to practice according to the teaching cannot achieve anything, even if they encounter hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas. Therefore, one should know that Bodhi is attained through diligent vigor.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the brahmin youth Mahābrahmā Samacārin: "Noble son,
do you know how a bodhisattva practices that which is called 'diligent vigor'?"
He replied: "Mañjuśrī!
If a bodhisattva is able to attain the noble path, this is called diligent vigor."
He asked: "By what kind of practice can one attain the Noble Path? He replied:
"If one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena, such a practitioner can attain the Noble Path.
He asked: "What is meant by 'having attained the Noble Path'?"
He replied:
"If a practitioner perceives all phenomena as equal within the state of equality, this is called having attained the Noble Path. He asked:
“Good son! Can that which is called ‘equality’ be seen? He replied:
"No, it is not so. Why is this? Mañjuśrī!..."
If the dharma of equality could be seen, it would not be equality. Mañjuśrī!
If one is able not to see the equality of all dharmas, this is called seeing equality.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, "Noble son,
can the equality of all dharmas be perceived?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
It cannot be seen; if one sees equality, that is not seeing equality."
Brahmā said: "Mañjuśrī!
If a practitioner does not perceive any phenomena within the state of the equal nature of all phenomena, this is called having attained the Noble Path."
He asked, "Brahmā! For what reason do you not see it?"
Brahmā replied: “Because they are free from dualistic characteristics,
they are not seen, Mañjuśrī!”
"Not seeing in this way is itself right view. He asked: "Brahmā!"
"Who in the world is able to see with equanimity?
Brahmā replied, "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."
He asked: "Brahmā! How is it possible to see?"
Brahmā replied: “Mañjuśrī!
Just as the suchness of form is not produced differently, so too the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not produced differently.”
"Mañjuśrī! Just as the equality of the five aggregates is called the vision of equality. He asked:
“Brahmā! What is this world? Brahmā replied:
"Extinction is the world. He asked: "Brahmā!"
"If that extinction were the world, would the characteristics of the world not be exhausted? Brahmā replied,
"The characteristics of the world cannot be exhausted."
He asked: "Brahmā! For what reason do you say that the world has the characteristic of extinction?"
Brahmā replied: "The world is ultimately characterized by cessation; for this reason, its characteristics cannot be exhausted. Why is that?"
"Because this is exhausted, it is not exhausted again. He asked: "Brahmā!..."
"Would the Buddha not say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have the characteristic of exhaustion?

Brahmā replied, "The characteristic of the phenomenon of exhaustion is itself eternally inexhaustible; therefore, the Buddha says that the characteristics of all conditioned things are inexhaustible."
He asked: "Brahmā! For what reason are they frequently called 'conditioned phenomena' (saṃskṛta-dharma)?"
Brahmā replied, "They are called conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) because they are subject to exhaustion. He asked:
“Brahmā, in what do conditioned phenomena abide? Brahmā replied:
"Conditioned phenomena abide within the nature of the unconditioned. He asked, "Brahmā!..."
"If this is so, what difference is there between conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Brahmā replied, "Between conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena, there is only a difference in words and verbal expressions."

Why is this? Because words and speech are themselves both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). If one seeks the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, there is no distinction between them, for those characteristics are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
He asked: "Brahmā! Upon what dharma do these words exist?"
Brahmā replied: "One who has attained the unconditioned dharma does not engage in verbal proliferation regarding dharmas. He asked:
"Brahmā! What kind of speech is called 'meaning'? Brahmā replied:
"What is meant by speaking words for others so that their minds grasp at signs? Why is this?
All letters and syllables are called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); yet the Buddha-Tathāgata does not dwell in conceptual proliferation, nor does he rely upon or speak it."
Mañjuśrī! All speech is fundamentally not speech; therefore, the Buddha says that all dharmas are ineffable. Why is this?
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not derive their names from those words. He asked, "Brahmā!..."
"How do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, receive their names?
Brahmā replied, "The Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, do not receive their names by way of form, nor by way of marks, nor by way of dharmas."
He asked: "Brahmā! Can the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, be named apart from the phenomena of form?"
He replied, “No, Mañjuśrī!”
Why is this? Because the suchness of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the suchness of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), these two suchnesses of phenomena are neither identical nor different.
It is in this way that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, receive their name; they are named "Tathāgata" because they are the true suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is.
"If the Buddha-Tathāgata is named according to reality, then he does not lose it. He asked: "Brahmā!..."
“By attaining what dharma do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
receive the title ‘Buddha’? Brahmā replied, “Mañjuśrī!...”
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have realized the purity of the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena through thorough penetration; they realize it exactly as that true suchness is.
It is by virtue of this that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, receive their name and are thus titled "Those of Right and Universal Knowledge" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
At that time, the Brahmin Mahābrāhmaṇaputra Samacārin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dwelling within the Great Vehicle, speaks of ‘dwelling’?”
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“The Bodhisattva does not destroy form, but abides in the bodhicitta;
knowing that form is like bodhi— such is the wise Bodhisattva.”
Just as form is bodhi, so too does one enter the mark of suchness with equanimity;
without destroying the nature of all phenomena, such a one is a wise bodhisattva.
Not destroying the meaning of bodhi is itself the meaning of bodhi.
Within the meaning of bodhi, there is likewise no bodhi;
practicing correctly according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is called abiding in bodhi.
The wise Bodhisattva understands bodhi in this way.
The foolish seek awakening within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
yet the aggregates and so forth are themselves awakening—there is no awakening apart from them.
Wise bodhisattvas, regarding phenomena as superior, middling, or inferior, [perceive them as such].
Neither grasping nor abandoning—this is called abiding in bodhi.
The wise do not discriminate between dharma and non-dharma as two;
nor do they perceive them as non-dual—this is called practicing bodhi.
If there are two, they are conditioned; if there are not two, they are unconditioned.
To be free from these two extremes is called practicing bodhi.
Such a person transcends the level of ordinary beings, yet does not enter the stage of the dharmas.
One who has not yet attained the fruit is called a noble one; such a person is a field of merit for the world.
Observing the phenomena of the world, they remain in the midst like a lotus flower;
practicing the supreme path, they are said to abide in bodhi.
Wherever the world moves, there the Bodhisattva moves;
whatever phenomena all the worlds are submerged in,
the wise one knows them as they truly are and attains liberation therein.
The wise have no fear; though submerged in the abyss of the world, they possess neither timidity nor a base mind as they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
These wise bodhisattvas skillfully know the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Therefore, one does not discriminate between what is dharma and what is non-dharma.
This is the practice of the wise Bodhisattva: there is no dharma to be abandoned, nor is there any dharma to be produced; this is called the characteristic of bodhi.
All phenomena are signless, like the nature of empty space;
the wise do not conceive of signs or that which is characterized by signs.
The Bodhisattva constantly protects the Dharma by abiding in equanimity.
Equanimity is itself the Dharma, for it does not discriminate among dharmas.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, all dharmas are empty;
wise Bodhisattvas do not abandon that essential nature of the Dharma.
Manifestly perceiving all dharmas of the Buddha and the essential characteristics of all phenomena,
he speaks for the sake of sentient beings because he abides in *tathatā*.
No māras can disturb him, for all his practices are profoundly deep.
The wise do not grasp at dharmas, for they have fully known all dharmas;
seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, they do not abide therein.
Wisdom has no place of abiding, yet it does not abide elsewhere.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is unimpeded; they do not cling to what is dharma or non-dharma.
If one can remain unattached to these, one will ultimately attain bodhi.
Those people who delight in goodness, through their generosity, become increasingly exalted and honored.
Having relinquished all that one possesses, the mind remains unshaken.
All phenomena cannot be relinquished, nor can they be grasped;
as for all worldly dharmas, they were originally unobtainable by me.
Knowing all phenomena as they truly are— neither bound nor liberated—
the Buddha calls such a person a donor, because they perceive no phenomena.
These bodhisattvas do not conceive of a self or what belongs to a self.
Therefore, when practicing giving, do not give rise to thoughts of greed or attachment;
dedicate all acts of giving toward the Buddha-way.
Regarding both giving and bodhi, do not dwell upon these two characteristics.
The precept of non-action and non-arising abides eternally within the dharma of the precepts;
nor does one harbor the thought, "I abide in this observance of the precepts.
One who possesses wisdom knows the characteristics of the precepts: they neither arise nor are they produced.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva precepts are as pure as space.
One views the body as a reflection in a mirror, speech as an echo, and the mind as a magical illusion;
thus, one does not exalt oneself on account of the precepts.
Their minds are always supple, dwelling securely in the nature of quiescence;
they extinguish all evils and penetrate the wholesome dharmas.
Regarding both the observance and the violation of precepts, they perceive neither of these two characteristics.
Seeing the nature of phenomena in this way, one maintains the untainted precepts.
Having reached the shore of patience, one is able to endure all evils;
regarding all dharmas, the mind remains ever equanimous.
All phenomena perish moment by moment; their nature never abides.
Within them there is no reviling, nor is there any honor.
Even if one's body were dismembered limb by limb, the mind would ultimately remain unmoved.
Knowing that the mind is neither within nor without,
and that the body, enemies, and weapons all arise from the four great elements—
one who perceives this clearly with wisdom is called a person of patience.
Regarding earth, water, fire, and wind, he has never been harmed or injured;
having attained mastery in these matters, he constantly practices the dharma of patience.
When a bodhisattva acts in this way, sentient beings cannot move him.
Courageous and diligent in their exertion, they remain steadfastly established in the Mahāyāna.
Such persons have no point of reliance within body or mind;
though they know the origin of birth and death, its limit cannot be apprehended.
For the sake of a single sentient being, You have adorned yourself with great vows.
The Dharma is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; Where, then, could there be any characteristic of extinction?
The primordial limit is unattainable; It is through inverted views that arising and ceasing are perceived.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally thus abiding; therefore, it is inconceivable.
If one can understand it in this way, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
When Bodhisattvas contemplate sentient beings, they see that these beings do not understand the characteristics of phenomena.
Exerting oneself with diligent vigor, one causes others to be free from inversion.
Not perceiving even the Buddhas as having the definitive characteristics of sentient beings,
yet never abandoning the resolve for enlightenment— this is called a person of vigor.
Contemplating all phenomena, one knows they are all like illusions and transformations;
wisdom finds no solidity, for one views phenomena as empty space.
From false conceptualization, attachment gives rise to defilement.
For this purpose, I open this gateway of Dharma, enabling beings to enter Nirvana.
For their sake, I practice diligence so as not to destroy the Dharma;
because I am free from both dharma and non-dharma, I constantly practice true diligence.
These practitioners practice seclusion; having attained the concentration of non-contention, they dwell neither in solitude nor in bustle.
Always fearing the world, they delight in dwelling in quietude, like the single horn of a rhinoceros.
Sporting in various meditative concentrations, He clearly realizes all supernormal powers.
His mind always abides in equanimity, Regarding empty spaces and villages as equal;
Being impartial and free from discrimination, This constant state is called tranquility.
Always understanding and knowing tranquility, Untainted and non-conceptual;
through faith in the Dharma one attains liberation, And is therefore said to be "tranquil.
Coming and going are both equal, For that which is eternally abiding is equality itself.
Not extinguished within equality, one is therefore said to abide in equality.
Abiding personally in the dharma of equality, by means of this path, sentient beings do not contravene the practice of equality;
therefore, it is said that they dwell eternally in composure.
With constant firmness of resolve, never forgetting the bodhicitta, they are able to transform sentient beings; therefore, they are said to be always in samādhi.
Always mindful of all Buddhas and their true dharmatā-kāya,
Distant from the marks of the physical body, he is therefore called one who is constantly in meditative concentration.
Constantly practicing all dharmas according to the true nature of dharmas,
yet without any recollection or thought, he is therefore called one who is constantly in meditative concentration.
Always never abandoning mindfulness of the Saṃgha, Knowing that the Saṃgha is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
free from calculation and tranquil, With skillful reflection and wise discernment,
One perceives all the Buddhas throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Within the eye and forms, they never give rise to dualistic characteristics.
They are able to hear and receive all the teachings expounded by the Buddhas;
yet within the ear and sounds, they likewise do not give rise to dualistic characteristics.
Within a single moment of mind, they know the minds of all sentient beings;
their own mind and the minds of others—these two are not distinguished.
They recollect the limits of the past, as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
They do not discriminate between what comes before and what comes after;
they are able to reach the immeasurable and inconceivable abodes of the Buddhas,
yet within their bodies and minds, there is no sign of weariness.
Discerning and knowing all phenomena, with inexhaustible eloquence in joyful exposition,
they reveal the characteristics of the nature of dharmas throughout incalculable eons.
Having reached the other shore of wisdom, they understand the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
He constantly speaks for the sake of sentient beings, Free from grasping and conceptual proliferation.
Skilled in knowing the dharma of causes and conditions, He remains far removed from the characteristics of the two extremes.
Knowing this to be the cause of affliction, And also knowing it to be the cause of purification.
One who has faith and understanding in the law of dependent origination is free from all false views;
for all phenomena belong to causes and conditions, and possess no fixed essence.
One of wisdom is free from the view of self, as well as the view of a Buddha and the view of emptiness.
Regarding views of the world and nirvāṇa, there are none such as these.
By the light of wisdom, one knows the nature of all phenomena;
without darkness and without obstruction—this is the path traveled by the wise.
This karma is called the Mahāyāna, the inconceivable Buddha-vehicle;
