it fully accommodates all sentient beings—this is the Bodhi of the Mahāyāna.
Among all vehicles, this vehicle is the foremost.
This Great Vehicle is able to give birth to the other vehicles;
the other vehicles have limitations and cannot accommodate all beings,
whereas only this Unsurpassed Vehicle can fully embrace all sentient beings.
If one practices this immeasurable Great Vehicle of space,
one will harbor no mind of stinginess toward any sentient being.
The wise who dwell in this stainless Great Vehicle—
This vehicle is like space, Colorless and impossible to point out.
If there are sentient beings Who ride upon this Great Vehicle, They should contemplate the characteristics of this vehicle: It is vast and expansive, capable of containing much.
Even if one were to speak for immeasurable and incalculable eons of the merits of the Mahāyāna,
as well as the merits of those who ride this vehicle, they could not be exhausted.
If one dwells in this Mahāyāna, that person will be free from all calamities.
Having encountered freedom from all calamities, such a person is one of wisdom.
Having heard this sublime sūtra, even as little as a four-line verse,
they shall not fall into the evil realms but shall reach a place of peace and security.
Those who love and revere this sutra, whether they be devas or humans,
shall, after casting off this body, be constantly reborn among humans and devas.
In future evil ages, if one should hear this sutra, [one will likewise attain such merit].
I bestow upon them all the prophecy that they shall ultimately attain the path of Buddhahood.
If, in future evil times, one holds this wondrous scripture in hand,
they abide in the true Dharma and are able to turn this wheel of the Dharma.
If a person upholds this sutra, they can transform immeasurable kalpas of coming and going through the realms of birth and death, and draw near to the path of the Buddha.
If one can uphold this sutra, their wisdom will be great and their diligence vast.
This person is extremely courageous, capable of subduing all Māras.
Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me the prediction that I would attain the patience of non-arising;
likewise, I bestow a prediction upon those who love and delight in this sūtra.
"If a Buddha does not appear in the world, and there is no time for the deliverance of sentient beings, those who love and delight in this sutra shall perform the work of a Buddha.

When this verse was spoken, five thousand devaputras all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*); ten thousand bhikṣus, through the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), attained liberation of mind by no longer grasping at any dharmas; and thirty-two thousand people became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all dharmas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if there is anyone who gives rise to the vow for bodhi, this constitutes a false vow.”
Why is this? Because if there is any apprehension of all dharmas as being obtainable, it is entirely erroneous.
If there is anyone who conceives of attaining bodhi and makes a vow based on that, all such actions performed by such a person are erroneous practices.

Why is this? Because that bodhi does not abide in the desire realm, does not abide in the form realm, and likewise does not abide in the formless realm; since that bodhi has no place of abiding, one should not make a vow.
“World-Honored One!
Suppose there were a person who wished to obtain empty space; would that person ever be able to obtain empty space?
The Buddha said:
"No. "In this way, World-Honored One! It is the same for a bodhisattva:

when they give rise to the vow for enlightenment characterized by emptiness, you should know that this is precisely giving rise to a vow of emptiness. This enlightenment is without vows; it transcends the three periods of time and is not a state of grasping at characteristics. If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of enlightenment based on dualistic characteristics, forming such a thought as 'enlightenment is distinct from birth-and-death' or 'nirvana is distinct from enlightenment,' then that bodhisattva is not practicing the conduct of enlightenment."
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī: “Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the conduct of awakening?”
He replied, "Brahmā!
If a bodhisattva practices all dharmas, yet practices nothing within those dharmas, this is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice the bodhisattva path."
Why is this? Brahmā! To transcend all spheres of activity is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the bodhisattva path.
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva’s practice which transcends all practices is the practice of the path to enlightenment?"
He replied: "Brahmā!

To remain far removed from all signs of objective reference, and to be free from the signs of the conditions of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—this is called the Bodhisattva’s practice that transcends all realms of experience."
He asked again: “Mañjuśrī, for what intention do you say that it ‘transcends’?”
He replied: "Brahmā! It does not transcend equality."
Why is this? Brahmā! The equality of all phenomena is itself bodhi.
Again he asked: "How does a bodhisattva give rise to the vow for enlightenment? He replied:
"Brahmā! It should be understood as that very bodhi. He asked again:
"What is enlightenment? He replied, "Brahmā!..."
Bodhi is neither past, nor future, nor present; therefore, the Bodhisattva, through the pure contemplation of the three periods of time, gives rise to the vow for bodhi. O Brahmā!

Just as all phenomena of the past, future, and present are fundamentally unarisen, if they are fundamentally unarisen, there is no practice; to form a vow in such a manner, that person has no basis from which to generate a vow.
"Why is this? Because by making such vows and practicing the conduct of enlightenment, one attains all-aspect omniscience. He asked again:
“What is the meaning of ‘the wisdom of all-knowledge’? He replied, “Brahmā!...”
"One knows all things; therefore, it is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
He asked again: "By what dharma is this 'knowledge of all' constituted?"
He replied, "Brahmā! There are no distinct characteristics."
"In what sense is it that where there is no mark of a sentient being, one knows those sentient beings as they truly are? For this reason, it is called 'the mark of non-distinction.
He asked again: "In what sense is it called 'no sentient being'?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
What is called 'sentient beings' exists only as a name. Apart from the nature of names, there are no sentient beings; apart from those sentient beings, there are no names."
Therefore, names are not different from sentient beings, and the nature of sentient beings is not different from names.

If there were a bodhi distinct from sentient beings, there would have to be two separate characteristics; however, since sentient beings are just as they are—just like bodhi—for this reason, there is no bodhi that exists apart from sentient beings.
Because they are non-different, awakening is equal; because awakening is equal, the self is equal. Attaining awakening through such equality, those dharmas are without distinction.
For this reason, there is no difference between them.

My constant equanimity is like that non-self; therefore, non-self is not different from me. Just as space has no distinct characteristics, so too all dharmas, in their equality, have no distinct characteristics.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī,
you should know that the Tathāgata is a speaker of truth, for he understands these dharmas according to reality.”
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said: “Brahmā, the Buddha does not engage in any practice regarding any phenomena.”
"Why is this? Even the Tathāgata does not apprehend any dharmas; how much less could there be any cultivation? Brahmā asked.
“Mañjuśrī! How could the Tathāgata not know that all phenomena are conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, mundane phenomena, or supramundane phenomena?”
Mañjuśrī asked: "Brahmā, what do you think?"
"Is there anyone who can practice emptiness and know emptiness? He replied, "No."
He asked, "Brahmā!
Regarding the space you have spoken of, does that space undergo birth or cessation?"
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:

“Brahmā! All phenomena are like space; just as that space has neither arising nor ceasing, so too it is with all phenomena. One should not say that phenomena have arising and ceasing merely because they are spoken of.”
Brahmā! Thus, in this teaching of the Dharma, there is nothing that is taught; yet all dharmas can be taught.

Because all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, there is nothing that can be taught. If that which is taught is neither born nor extinguished and thus cannot be taught, then the act of teaching is likewise a non-dharma that is not taught.
Why is this? Just as those dharmas are explained by means of whichever consciousness explains them, so too is that consciousness.
For this reason, it is said that the *tathatā* (suchness) of all dharmas abides; yet there is no abiding of *tathatā*, nor does *tathatā* not abide.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām-Indra, and Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, were assembled in the gathering; they immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

If any son or daughter of good family hears this Dharma taught by the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī and possesses faith and understanding, you should know that such a person is able to destroy the armies of Māra and all enemies.
Why is this? Because the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī has skillfully expounded all dharmas as being free from all marks.

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing such a profound dharma-gate, are neither startled nor terrified and are able to believe and understand it, you should know that these persons have certainly not come from meager merit.
Wherever this sutra may be located, one should know that it is a place sustained by the Buddha.
Wherever anyone hears such a profound Dharma-gate, one should know that it is a place where the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma.

Wherever this sutra resides—whether in a village, city, town, mountain forest, wilderness, stupa, monastery, monk’s cell, or place for walking meditation—it cannot be frequented by any demons, non-Buddhists, or those who are greedily attached.
"Only those who have made extensive offerings to the Buddhas of the past are able to hear such a sutra as this.
Within this sutra, we have obtained the light of wisdom, yet we are unable to fully repay the great kindness of the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī, and the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin."

We always conceive the thought of the World-Honored One toward the Dharma masters from whom we hear the sutras and teachings; even if we were to offer them our own flesh and blood as an offering, we would still not have repaid their kindness.

We all shall conceive the thought of the World-Honored One toward this Dharma Master; we shall always attend upon and serve this expounder of the Dharma, for this son of good family shall be constantly protected by the devas.
"Bhagavān! If there is a person who writes down such a sutra as this, or reads it, or recites it, or explains it, immeasurable devas will go to that place for the sake of hearing the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-deva-rāja, and the great assembly, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O sons of good family!
It is as you have said; it is so, it is so.

Suppose there were a trichiliocosm filled with the seven treasures, and the merit from giving them away constituted one portion; the merit obtained from hearing this Dharma-gate would surpass that [merit]."
"O sons of good family!

Setting aside this trichiliocosm, suppose there were someone who filled as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River with the seven treasures and offered them in charity; the merit of that act constitutes one part, whereas the merit obtained from hearing this Dharma-gate exceeds even that."
“O sons of good family!

If there are those who wish to attain all merits, they should listen to this sutra; if there are those who wish to attain a handsome and upright physical form, wish to attain wealth, wish to attain a retinue, wish to attain sovereignty, wish to attain the fullness of celestial and human pleasures, wish to attain renown, wish to attain extensive learning, firm mindfulness, correct conduct and deportment, precepts, concentration, and wisdom, thorough understanding of the scriptures, wish to attain virtuous friends, wish to attain the eloquence of joyful speech, wish to attain the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, wish to attain all wholesome dharmas, wish to provide all means of happiness to sentient beings, or wish to attain nirvana—they should listen to this sutra, revere and believe in this sutra, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, practice according to its teachings, and explain it extensively for others.
“O sons of good family!
If there is anyone who can practice this sutra, I do not see that they would not be sustained by all such powers.”
"O sons of good family!

I now tell you: if there is a person from whom one hears this sutra—whether it be one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or an instructor (ācārya)—I have never seen any offering in the world capable of repaying that person's kindness."
This Dharma-gate emerges from the world, and the worldly offerings of worship cannot repay its merit. Why is this?
Because this Dharma-gate transcends the world, and the material wealth of the world cannot repay it.
This Dharma is undefiled; it cannot be requited by defiled things, nor can its debt of gratitude be repaid by means of worldly necessities such as food, drink, or bedding.
“O sons of good family!
There is no other way to repay one who preaches this Dharma; there is only one thing, namely, to practice according to what has been taught.
If anyone is able to practice this Dharma-gate according to what has been taught, that person is said to be able to repay the Buddha’s kindness.”
Such a person is also said to revere their teacher, having purely fulfilled their debt of gratitude;
such a person does not consume the faithful offerings of others in vain; such a person is said to follow the teachings of the Tathāgata;
such a person is said to have crossed over the various torrents.
Such a person is said to have transcended all perilous paths;
such a person is said to have erected the banner of victory;
such a person is said to be able to shatter the enemy's ranks.
Such a person is called the Lion King because he is free from fear;
he is called the Elephant King because he can subdue Māra;
he is called the Ox King because no heterodox teachers can defeat him.
Such a person is called a King of Physicians, because they heal all illnesses;
such a person is called one who has nothing to fear, because they can expound such profound Dharma;
such a person is called one who is able to fulfill relinquishment, because they can relinquish all afflictions.
Such a person is said to uphold pure precepts, because they have brought all wholesome dharmas to ultimate completion;
such a person is said to have attained great forbearance, because they have distanced themselves from the notions of "self" and "mine";
such a person is said to possess the power of great diligence, because their minds never grow weary throughout immeasurable eons.
Such a person is said to be fully endowed with meditative concentration, because their mind is constantly focused and dwells upon a single point;
such a person is said to possess great wisdom, because they skillfully understand all spoken words and scriptural passages;
such a person is said to possess great merit, because they adorn their physical form with immeasurable blessings.
"This person is said to possess great majestic power, for they can eclipse the radiance of the sun and moon;
this person is said to possess great strength, for they uphold the ten powers of the Buddha;
this person is said to be a great cloud, for they can thunder forth the Dharma."
Such a person is called "Great Rain," because they extinguish the dust of afflictions;
such a person is called "Refuge," because they lead others to nirvana;
such a person is called "Great Savior," because they rescue others from the fear of birth and death.
This person is named "Lamp of Light," because they have departed from the darkness of ignorance;
this person is named "Refuge," because they are the one upon whom those terrified by Māra rely for protection;
this person is named "A Being of the Ultimate Great Path."
This person is said to have attained their station because they sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
This person is said to have attained the Dharma-eye;
this person is said to have seen Suchness (tathatā).
Such a person is called one who knows emptiness;
such a person is called one who dwells securely in great compassion;
such a person is called one who establishes great loving-kindness.
Such a person does not abandon any sentient being;
such a person is said to have turned their back on the Hīnayāna;
such a person is said to be heading toward the Mahāyāna.
Such a person is said to have abandoned and relinquished inversion;
such a person is said to have attained equanimity;
such a person is said to have entered the station of the Dharma.
Such a person is said to be securely established in the site of enlightenment;
such a person is said to have destroyed all Māras;
such a person is said to abide in omniscience.
Such a person is able to turn the wheel of Dharma;
such a person is able to perform the work of a Buddha.
"O sons of good family!

Whether for an eon or for the remainder of an eon, were I to extol that person, praise that person, and speak of the merit of their practice according to the teaching, I could not reach its end; the eloquence of the Tathāgata would likewise be inexhaustible, and all such merit would remain inexhaustible.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Avivartika (Non-regressing) seated in the great assembly.
Then, the son of heaven Avivartika addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

“The Blessed One has spoken of practicing in accordance with the Dharma. As for one who practices in accordance with the Dharma, why is such a person called ‘one who practices in accordance with the Dharma’?
The Buddha said, “Devaputra!”
As I have taught, one who practices in accordance with the Dharma is said to not practice any dharmas at all; this is called practicing all dharmas. Why is this?
If a person practices all dharmas, those dharmas are neither performed nor unperformed; if dharmas are neither performed nor unperformed, this is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

A practitioner who acts in this manner does not practice the wholesome nor the unwholesome; does not practice the tainted nor the untainted; does not practice the mundane nor the supramundane; does not practice the conditioned nor the unconditioned; and does not practice birth-and-death nor nirvana. This is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
If one does not practice with regard to any phenomena, this is called "practice," because worldly people who possess the conceptual signs of phenomena do not practice according to reality.

If a person possesses the conceptual signs of phenomena, that person lacks practice according to reality; if a person cannot abide within phenomena and thus does not practice all phenomena according to reality—because all phenomena are without opposition—it is in this way called "practice according to reality."
At that time, the Devaputra Avivartika addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If one can practice in this way according to reality, such a person ultimately practices according to reality."

Why is this? One who practices the true Dharma is called "ultimate"; such a person practices according to reality and does not abide in the path of wrong practice. For one who abides in the right path, there is practice in accordance with the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
For one who practices the right practice, there is no deviant dharma. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas are equal and without differentiation.
At that time, the Brahma Heaven Superior Reflection asked the Non-regressive Devaputra:
"O Son of Good Family!"
"Do you abide in the practice of suchness? He replied, "Brahmā!"
If there were two characteristics within the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, I would abide in the practice of suchness;
however, since all dharmas are without two characteristics, this is what is called the practice of suchness.

Brahmā! I dwell in that practice exactly as it is; because I constantly refrain from action and do not engage in conceptual proliferation, I practice the Dharma of reality in accordance with suchness.
"I abide in those dharmas and act in accordance with those dharmas; for this reason, I say that I abide in practice. Brahmā said:
"O Son of Heaven!"
"I have never seen you before in this buddha-field," the devaputra said.
The Brahmā replied, "O Devaputra!"
"I, too, have never seen myself within this Buddha-field.
The Brahmā said: "O Son of Heaven!"
"This Buddha-land is not a matter of conceptual discrimination; there is no discrimination of 'I see' or 'I do not see.
The devaputra said, "Brahmā!..."
I am also like this; I do not engage in discrimination, nor have I ever discriminated as to whether I have seen or not seen [the Buddha] within a buddha-field.
He asked: “O Devaputra!
"Who is it that can see what has never been seen before? He replied, "Brahmā!"
This means that all ordinary persons have never before seen the stage of the noble Dharma; if one is able to enter it, this is called being able to see what was previously unseen.
This reality-position (*dharmatā*) is suchness; it is not seen by eye-consciousness, nor is it known by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

Only the noble ones see it in accordance with that true suchness. Just as the suchness of the eye and ear, so too is it for the suchness of the mind, up to the suchness of the reality-position; it is likewise in this manner.
"If there is anyone who can form such a view, this is called right view.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

For example, just as a merchant leader who has entered a treasure island perceives only precious jewels with his eyes, so too, for one who has accomplished inconceivable merits, whatever they delight in speaking is all a jewel of the Dharma, and all reveals the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

For this reason, these sons of good family do not cling to the view of a self nor do they cling to the view of sentient beings; therefore, whatever they delight in expounding is entirely non-erroneous.
These sons of good family have eloquent discourse that can purify the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), without perceiving a future limit (*aparākoṭi*) or a present limit (*pratyutpannakoṭi*).
These sons of good family have eloquent discourse that, for those without faith, can engender faith, and for those who already have faith, can bring about liberation.
Whatever these good sons delight in proclaiming, they can cause those who are arrogant to be humbled, and lead those without arrogance to know things as they truly are.
Whatever these good sons delight in proclaiming, no māras whatsoever can find an opportunity; and those who hear it shall transcend all the works of māras.
These good sons possess eloquence such that they can cause any wholesome dharmas not yet arisen to arise, and they can prevent any wholesome dharmas already arisen from perishing.
These sons of good family, in whatever they delight to speak, are able to sever afflictions already arisen in the present and prevent those not yet arisen from arising.

These sons of good family, in whatever they delight to speak, are able to cause those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta to resolve upon it, and to cause those who have already resolved upon it not to regress.
Whatever these good sons delight in expounding is able to ensure that all dharmas are not interrupted and to encompass all dharmas so they do not perish.
Whatever these good sons delight in expounding is able to bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment.
“World-Honored One!
By means of this eloquence, one is able to skillfully subdue all non-Buddhists. Why is this? ”
“World-Honored One!
No jackal can withstand its body before the lion king, let alone utter a sound.
World-Honored One!”
"All the teachers of various non-Buddhist doctrines are likewise unable to endure or perform the unsurpassed lion’s roar of a king.
At that time, the Devaputra Avivartika addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!..."
Regarding what was called "lion’s roar," what is meant by "lion’s roar"?
For what reason is it named "lion’s roar"? He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
If a practitioner preaches the Dharma without any attachment while having something to say, this is called a lion’s roar.
If a practitioner preaches while attached to their own views, this is the howling of a jackal; it cannot be called a lion’s roar, because it gives rise to all manner of false views.”
“Son of Heaven!
You should further explain: what is meant by ‘one who utters the lion’s roar’?
The son of heaven replied:

“Kauśika! If a practitioner preaches the Dharma and does not even become attached to it—let alone to other dharmas—even as much as the Tathāgata himself would not be attached, this is called a lion’s roar.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a practitioner practices according to what has been taught, such preaching of the Dharma is called the lion’s roar; teaching the Dharma with certainty is called the lion’s roar; teaching the Dharma without fear is called the lion’s roar."
“Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a practitioner, for the sake of attaining the non-arising and non-ceasing of all dharmas, does not act for the arising of dharmas nor for the ceasing of dharmas, such preaching of the Dharma is called the lion’s roar.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a practitioner is without defilement, without purity, without conjunction, and without dispersion, for this reason the teaching of the Dharma is called the Lion’s Roar."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
That which is called the 'lion's roar' is the definitive teaching that all phenomena are entirely without self, without sentient beings, and so forth; this is termed the lion's roar."
To definitively teach that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless is called the lion’s roar.
To speak for the sake of guarding the Dharma is called the lion’s roar.
"To bring liberation to all sentient beings, one resolves upon bodhicitta and speaks these words:
'I shall become a Buddha.
To teach the Dharma in this manner is called the lion's roar."
If one can purify the necessities of life and be content, preaching the Dharma in such a manner is called the lion’s roar.
If one can always refrain from abandoning the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), preaching the Dharma in such a manner is called the lion’s roar.
If one practices giving oneself and transforms others to give, preaching the Dharma in this way is called the lion’s roar.
If one is able not to abandon the accomplishment of dignified deportment, preaching the Dharma in this way is called the lion’s roar.
To regard enemies and kin with an equal mind—teaching the Dharma in this way is called the lion’s roar.
To constantly cultivate diligence without forsaking one's original vow—teaching the Dharma in this way is called the lion’s roar.
To be able to eliminate afflictions—such preaching of the Dharma is called the lion’s roar.
To be able to skillfully know one's conduct through wisdom—such preaching of the Dharma is called the lion’s roar.

When this lion’s roar was thus proclaimed, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments spontaneously produced sounds, and a great radiance was emitted, universally illuminating heaven and earth.
Hundreds of thousands of devas leaped for joy and exclaimed:
"We have heard this lion’s roar of the Dharma spoken by this non-retrogressive devaputra; for Jambudvīpa, it is as if the Wheel of Dharma has been turned once again."

At that time, the Buddha smiled. It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, and so forth—issue from their mouths, universally illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds. They pass upward beyond the Brahma world, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon; having shone, they return and encircle the body three times before entering through the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin joined his palms toward the Buddha and praised him with verses, requesting:
"O Most Victorious Honored One, whose wisdom transcends all, You fully know the conduct of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding your wisdom, merit, and liberation, I pray that you will explain the cause and condition for your smile."
The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and inconceivable; he knows the minds of sentient beings without obstruction.
He preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, in accordance with their capacities, something that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot attain.
We pray only that the Most Victorious, Unsurpassed Honored One, will explain for us the cause and conditions of his smile.

Your tongue is pure and stainless, with the radiance of the moon; like Śakra, the King of Devas, or Brahmā, it shines universally upon gods and humans, Mount Sumeru, and all mountains such as Cakravāḍa.
I pray that you, the most supreme and peerless Honored One, will explain for me the cause and condition of your smile.
The Great Sage is serene and free from anger; gods and humans gaze upon him without weariness.
All beings receive his grace and attain happiness; we pray that you will explain the causes and conditions of your smile.
Thoroughly penetrating all phenomena as being like space, Like foam, lightning, clouds, illusions, dreams, reflections, And the moon in water—
having the characteristics of space— I pray that you will explain the cause of your smile with your wondrous voice.
Free from the marks of conceptualization and all false views, Thoroughly realizing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
Always delighting in meditative concentration and the quiescent Dharma— I pray you will explain the causes for emitting this pure light.
Unattached to words, language, or sounds, you constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings;
unattached to self or dharmas, your wisdom is stainless. Every single phrase of the Dharma has been spoken by the Tathāgata;
your wisdom-penetration and faculties are fully perfected—O Flower-Light Wisdom, speak for me!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is able to extinguish forever All sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
With the power of Nārāyaṇa and heroic vigor, He subdues all the powers of Māra.
To sentient beings who have no refuge, He acts as a refuge, a Dharma-lamp, and a light.
"I only pray that the Valiant Teacher of Gods and Humans will explain for me the cause of your smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Brahma Heaven King, Viśeṣacintin, saying: "Brahma!..."
“Is this the Non-regressing Devaputra, whom you have seen?
Mahābrahmā replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One!”
"Yes, I have indeed seen it.
The Buddha said, "Brahmā!"

This non-retrogressive devaputra, from this day forward, after the passing of three million two hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sumerupradīparāja, and so forth up to Buddha Bhagavān; his world shall be named Suvinīta, and the kalpa shall be named Brahmastava.

That Buddha-land has Jāmbūnada gold and lapis lazuli for its ground, and consists solely of a community of bodhisattvas who are valiant in subduing all māras and enemies. Whatever they require arrives instantly upon thought, just as in the Tuṣita Heaven. The Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and incalculable, and his preaching of the Dharma is beyond reproach.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Devaputra Avaivartika, saying:
"Devaputra! The Tathāgata has now bestowed upon you the prediction of enlightenment."
The devaputra said: "Brahmā!
Just as one receives a prediction of enlightenment regarding the *tathatā* (suchness) and the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), my receiving of a prediction is likewise so."
The Brahmā said: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) cannot be given a prediction of enlightenment.
The devaputra said:
"Just as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) cannot be prophesied, you should know that the prophecy for all bodhisattvas is likewise.
Brahmā said: "O Son of Heaven!"
"If the Buddha-Tathāgata does not grant you this prediction, then your cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya) under all the Tathāgatas of the past would have been in vain.
The Devaputra said: "Brahmā!..."
"If there is no abiding, this is abiding in the holy life. He asked: "O Devaputra!"
"How does one dwell in the holy life (brahmacarya) while dwelling in non-abiding? He replied: "Brahmā!"
If one does not dwell in the desire realm, does not dwell in the form realm, and does not dwell in the formless realm, this is dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, O Brahmā!
If one does not dwell in a self, does not dwell in sentient beings, does not dwell in a life-span, and does not dwell in a person, this is dwelling in the holy life.
To put it briefly, if one does not abide in dharmas nor abide in non-dharmas, this is abiding in the holy life. He asked: “O Devaputra!
"What is the meaning of the Brahma-conduct you have described? He replied, "Brahmā!"
"To abide in the path of non-duality is the meaning of the holy life (brahmacarya). He asked: "O Devaputra!"
"If one dwells in the path of non-duality,
in what does one dwell? He replied, "Brahmā!"
To abide in the path of non-duality is precisely to not abide in any phenomena whatsoever. Why is this?
Because all noble sages abide nowhere; they do not grasp at dharmas, nor do they cross over the various torrents.
He asked: "Devaputra, how does one cultivate the path?"
He replied, “Brahmā!

Because one does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence, one does not discriminate between ‘it exists’ and ‘it does not exist. To practice in this manner is called the cultivation of the path.”
He asked: "Devaputra! By means of what dharma do you cultivate the path?"
He replied: "Brahmā!

It is not by means of the dharmas of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor by attainment, nor by realization; that which, regarding all dharmas, is without marks and without demonstration, is called the cultivation of the path."

At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin asked the non-regressive devaputra:
"Devaputra, what is meant by the firm diligence of a bodhisattva? He replied:
“Brahmā! If a bodhisattva perceives neither a single characteristic nor a diverse characteristic in all phenomena, this is called the firm diligence of a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva, because they do not destroy the dharma-nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena, remains without attachment, without cessation, without increase, and without decrease regarding all phenomena; and if they perceive neither defilement nor purity, transcending the dharma-nature—this is called the foremost firm diligence, namely, that the bodhisattva’s body does not arise and the mind does not arise.”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the Devaputra Avivartin, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Having praised the devaputra, he addressed the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying: "O Devaputra!
That which you have just described—the non-arising of body and the non-arising of mind—is the foremost firm diligence."

“Brahmā! I recall that in the past, I practiced all deeds with firm diligence, maintained the precepts and dhūta austerities, and made offerings to and reverently honored all Buddhas; yet those Buddhas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Having thus made offerings, paid homage, and shown respect to those Buddhas, I dwelt in secluded places practicing meditation and cultivating wisdom through extensive learning; out of compassion for sentient beings, I provided them with their necessities, and I diligently practiced all forms of difficult and arduous austerities with great vigor. Yet, those Buddhas did not bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because at that time, I dwelt in body, speech, and mind, giving rise to diligence. "Brahmā!
It was only later, after I had attained the firm and resolute diligence as described by the Devaputra above, that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."

"Therefore, Brahmā! If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to receive the Tathāgata’s swift prediction of enlightenment, they should practice the firm diligence as spoken by the Devaputra—namely, not giving rise to diligence toward any phenomena."
The Brahmā said: “World-Honored One!
What is the diligence that is equal throughout the three periods of time?”
The Buddha said:
"Brahmā! The past mind has already ceased; the future mind has not yet arrived; the present mind abides nowhere."

If a phenomenon has already ceased and does not arise again, if a phenomenon has not yet arrived and thus lacks the characteristic of arising, and if a phenomenon has no abiding and thus abides in the true mark (dharmatā),
then such a phenomenon is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present.
That which is neither past, nor future, nor present is called intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Such intrinsic nature is non-arising, O Brahmā!
This is called the diligence of the equality of the three periods of time, which enables a bodhisattva to swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment. "Brahmā!

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such patience in dharmas (dharmakṣānti), because they believe that all dharmas are nothing to be relinquished, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of giving (dānavīrya)."
Because one has faith that all phenomena are free from outflows, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of upholding the precepts;
because one has faith that all phenomena are incapable of causing injury, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of patience;
because one has faith that all phenomena are without arising, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of diligent practice.
Because one has faith that all phenomena are entirely equal, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence in meditative concentration;
because one has faith that all phenomena are without discrimination, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence in wisdom.

Brahmā! Thus, a bodhisattva has faith that all phenomena neither increase nor decrease, and are neither deviant nor incorrect; yet they constantly practice giving without seeking karmic retribution, constantly maintain the prohibitive precepts without attachment, cultivate patience while knowing the emptiness of the internal and external, cultivate diligence while knowing there is nothing to arise, cultivate meditative concentration without any point of reliance, and cultivate wisdom without grasping at signs.

“Brahmā! When a bodhisattva accomplishes such patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), although they manifest as practicing within all dharmas, they remain undefiled. Such a person is said to have attained the equality of all dharmas; they are not shaken by worldly dharmas—gain or loss, defamation or praise, fame or insignificance, suffering or pleasure—because they have transcended all worldly dharmas. Furthermore, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage themselves; they are without joy or sorrow, unmoved and undistracted, free from dualistic thought, having abandoned all views and attained the non-dual dharma.”

“Vasava! Toward all sentient beings who have fallen into the two views, he gives rise to great compassion; for the sake of teaching and transforming those sentient beings, he manifests the taking on of a body.”

"This is called the first kind of firm and steadfast diligence: namely, attaining the patience of non-self and enduring toward sentient beings, giving rise to great compassion, and gathering in sentient beings.

While this great diligence was being taught, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The Buddha conferred upon them the prediction that they would all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, each realizing the Way of the Buddha in a different land, all bearing the same name: Firm Diligence (*Dṛḍhavīrya*).
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was seated in the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

For example, when a great dragon wishes to send down rain, it rains upon the great ocean and not elsewhere; this bodhisattva is also like this, for he uses the rain of the Great Dharma to preach for the bodhisattvas who are like the heart of the great ocean, and not for others."
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Kāśyapa!”
As you have said, the reason the great dragon kings do not send rain upon Jambudvīpa is not out of stinginess or envy, but simply because that place is incapable of receiving it.

Why is this? The rain poured by the great dragon falls in torrents as thick as chariot axles; Jambudvīpa cannot contain it. If such rain were to fall, the cities, towns, villages, mountains, forests, ponds, and pools of Jambudvīpa would all be swept away like drifting jujube leaves. For this reason, the great dragon does not rain upon Jambudvīpa with such heavy downpours.

In this way, Kāśyapa, these bodhisattvas do not rain down the Dharma-rain upon other sentient beings, nor do they harbor stinginess or envy; it is simply that those beings lack the vessels capable of receiving such teachings as these.

For this reason, these bodhisattvas rain down such inconceivable, unsurpassed Dharma rains only within the hearts of those bodhisattvas who are like a vast, profound, immeasurable, and boundless ocean of wisdom.
“Kāśyapa! It is like the great ocean, which can receive heavy rains falling as thick as chariot axles without increasing or decreasing.

These bodhisattvas are also just like this: whether for one kalpa or even for a hundred kalpas, whether listening to or expounding the Dharma, their realization remains profound, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
“Kāśyapa! It is like the great ocean: among the four continents, all the hundreds of rivers that flow into it become of one single salty taste.

These bodhisattvas are also like this; hearing various teachings and various discourses on the meaning, they are able to believe and understand them all as being of one single taste—namely, the taste of emptiness.”
“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean is pure and free from defilement, such that even turbid water flowing into it becomes entirely clear and pure, so too are these bodhisattvas;
they are able to purify all stains of anger, hatred, and malice.”
“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean is profoundly deep and bottomless, beyond measure, so too are these bodhisattvas;
they are all able to enter the profound characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), which cannot be measured by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean collects immeasurable water and collects immeasurable jewels, so too do these bodhisattvas collect immeasurable dharmas, immeasurable wisdom, and immeasurable dharma-jewels. For this reason, it is said that the minds of bodhisattvas are as vast as the ocean.”
“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean accumulates all manner of immeasurable precious treasures, so too it is with these bodhisattvas:
they all enter into various gateways of the Dharma, gather the various treasures of the Dharma through diverse practices, and give birth to an immeasurable accumulation of Dharma-treasures.”
“Kāśyapa! It is like the great ocean, which produces three kinds of jewels:
first, those of little value;”
Second, those of great value;
third, those of priceless value.

The Dharma taught by these bodhisattvas is likewise: according to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings, they enable them to attain liberation—some through the Small Vehicle, some through the Middle Vehicle, and some through the Great Vehicle.
“Kāśyapa! For example, the great ocean never exists for the sake of a single sentient being alone.
These bodhisattvas are likewise; they do not resolve their minds toward enlightenment solely for the sake of a single sentient being.”
“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean gradually deepens and gradually becomes more expansive, so too it is with these bodhisattvas:
they gradually deepen toward omniscience (sarvajñatā) and gradually become more in accord with their aspirations.”
“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, so too it is with these bodhisattvas:

they do not harbor the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; nor do they harbor such minds as stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distracted mindfulness, or ignorance; nor do they harbor such views as those of a self, a person, or a sentient being.”
“Kāśyapa! It is like when the world is consumed by fire at the end of a kalpa: first the small ponds, rivers, streams, and springs dry up, and only then does the great ocean finally vanish.”

It is likewise when the True Dharma is extinguished: the True Dharma of those who practice the minor paths perishes first, and only thereafter does the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvas’ great ocean-like mind come to an end.
Kāśyapa! These bodhisattvas would rather lose their bodies and lives than abandon the true Dharma. Kāśyapa!
"The waters of the great ocean may eventually reach exhaustion, yet the profound and true Dharma of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is neither exhausted nor extinguished. Kāśyapa!"
Do you think that the Bodhisattva has lost the True Dharma?
Do not hold such a view, Kāśyapa!
Just as there is a vajra-gem in that great ocean called "Gatherer of All Jewels," which, within the great oceans of a thousand worlds, transforms into a vajra-maṇi jewel.
When even the seventh sun rises, its fierce flames reach as high as the Brahma-world, yet this precious jewel is neither burned nor lost; it moves on to another great ocean in a different direction.
If this precious jewel were in this world, it would be impossible for the world to be consumed by fire.
These bodhisattvas are also like this: when the True Dharma is extinguished and the seven types of false dharmas emerge, they will even go to other worlds.
What are the seven?
First, the treatises of non-Buddhists;
second, evil associates.
Third, the wrongful application of the Dharma;
fourth, mutual affliction and disturbance;
fifth, entering the thorny forest of false views.
Sixth, they are unable to destroy the roots of unwholesomeness;
seventh, there are none who realize or witness the Dharma.

When these seven evils appear in the world, these bodhisattvas, knowing that sentient beings cannot be saved, even go to other Buddha-lands, where they never cease to see Buddhas and hear the Dharma, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that their roots of goodness increase.
“Kāśyapa! Just as the great ocean is the place where immeasurable sentient beings rely upon for their peace and happiness, so too it is with these bodhisattvas;
sentient beings rely upon them and obtain three kinds of happiness: the happiness of humans, the happiness of devas, and the happiness of nirvāṇa.”
“Kāśyapa! For example, the water of the great ocean is extremely salty, and the sentient beings of other places cannot drink it because of its saltiness.
These bodhisattvas are also like this; they cannot be swallowed up or extinguished by any māras or non-Buddhists.”
“Kāśyapa! For example, just as sentient beings within the waters of the great ocean do not seek water for drinking elsewhere, but drink this very salt water of the great ocean.”
These bodhisattvas are likewise; they do not seek out the flavor of the Dharma from elsewhere to drink and consume, but only drink and consume the flavor of the Buddhas' Dharma themselves.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Although the great ocean is deep, it can still be measured; yet these bodhisattvas cannot be measured by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others. For this reason, it is said that the minds of these bodhisattvas are like space."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"In as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, the waters of the great oceans may still be measured; yet this great ocean of the wisdom of these bodhisattvas cannot be measured."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Just as the great ocean can receive all waters, Yet never reaches a point of fullness, So too are these bodhisattvas:
They constantly seek the benefit of the Dharma without ever being satiated."
Just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams, Taking them all in without increasing or decreasing, So too it is with these bodhisattvas:
They hear and receive the profound Dharma without increase or decrease.

Just as the nature of the great ocean is not turbid, and all turbid waters that flow into it become completely clear, so too are these bodhisattvas; they are able to purify the defilements of all afflictions.
Just as the great ocean is deep and bottomless, so too are these bodhisattvas;
their merit and wisdom are immeasurable, such that no outsider can fathom them.
Just as the great ocean has but a single flavor, and the hundred rivers that flow into it do not differ in taste, so too are these bodhisattvas:
all the dharmas they hear and receive have the single flavor of emptiness.
Just as the great ocean exists throughout the world, not for the sake of a single sentient being alone,
so too are these bodhisattvas, universally giving rise to the mind of enlightenment for the sake of all.

Just as there is a sea jewel named "Gatherer of Jewels," and because of this jewel all other jewels exist, so too is the mass of jewels that is the Bodhisattva; from the Bodhisattva-jewel, the Three Jewels emerge.
Just as the great ocean contains three treasures, yet that great ocean is without discrimination, so too is the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma:
by means of the three vehicles he delivers beings, without distinction between self and other.
Just as the great ocean gradually deepens, so too do these bodhisattvas;
for the sake of sentient beings they cultivate merit, and thus gradually enter the profound *sarvajñā*.
Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, so too are these bodhisattvas:
having given rise to the pure mind and the vow for enlightenment, they do not harbor the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Just as there is a precious jewel in the great ocean that is not burned when the kalpa ends in fire,
so too, when the Dharma is about to perish, the Bodhisattva protects and sustains it with great wisdom so that it does not vanish.
Just as that precious jewel is not consumed or lost, but travels on to another great ocean,
so too does the wise Bodhisattva go to other lands, knowing that certain sentient beings are not vessels for the Dharma.

When the three-thousandfold world system is about to burn, and the kalpa-fire is about to arise and consume heaven and earth, the myriad streams of the hundred rivers dry up first; only then does the king of waters exhaust itself thereafter.
It is the same for those who practice the Lesser Vehicle: when the Dharma is about to perish, they are extinguished first.
The Bodhisattva is courageous and does not begrudge his own body; in upholding the True Dharma, he never comes to an end.
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has passed into extinction, this jewel within the mind truly does not perish.
Dwelling in this Dharma with a profoundly pure mind, one practices the Path through these wholesome dharmas.
Hundreds of thousands of sentient beings rely upon the ocean, yet the ocean does not exist for the sake of a single being;
so too is the Bodhisattva’s resolve: it is for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
The vast oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions may still have their measure fathomed,
But the path traversed by these bodhisattvas cannot be measured by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Throughout the world-systems of the ten directions, the realm of empty space may yet be measured;
but the realm of these bodhisattva practices, which traverse the realm of empty space, cannot be measured.
Kāśyapa, you should know that all bodhisattvas, with courageous diligence and a firm resolve, aspire to become Buddhas to deliver sentient beings; there is none equal to them, let alone superior.
This mass of precious virtues is like the great ocean; they are a worthy field of merit to be honored and supported.
This is the supreme Great King of Physicians, Able to heal the illnesses of all sentient beings;
This is the refuge that provides protection, The island, the lamp, and the ultimate path.
It can grant the eye to the world of ignorance; Having gained this eye, one can then partake of the nectar of immortality.
He is the King of Dharma among all those in the world; he is Śakra’s wisdom of decisive judgment;
he is Mahābrahmā practicing the four dhyānas; he is the one capable of turning the Brahma-wheel of Dharma;
he is the Greatly Wise Teacher who guides the world, showing the true and correct path amidst the false paths upon which others are stuck.
Courageous, they are able to abide in great enlightenment; this is the purification that eliminates defilement and affliction.
This is the cultivation of pure dharmas like the full moon, its radiance lofty and manifest like the sun.
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom arises and increases; Like the great roar of thunder, he rains down the Dharma rain.
He is fearless like a lion; His mind is tamed and supple like a king of elephants.
The Bodhisattva is as firm and solid as Mount Sumeru; None of the various Māras can subdue him.
Detached from turbidity and pure, they are like water; possessing fierce majesty, they are like fire;
being without obstruction, they are like wind; being immovable, they are like earth.
Because this bodhisattva has abandoned the limited mind, having uprooted the roots of self-conceit, greed, jealousy, and the like,
they are free from discrimination like the king of medicinal trees; unstained by the eight worldly dharmas,
the bodhisattva is like the udumbara flower, visible only once in ten million billion kalpas.
This is knowing how to repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is ensuring that the lineage of all Buddhas is never severed;
this is firmly establishing the practice of great compassion; this is transcending by means of joyful relinquishment;
this is being able to abandon the mind of the five desires; this is constantly seeking the precious wealth of the Buddha-dharma.
This practice of giving is supreme; dwelling well in the precepts, they have no equal.
Dwelling well in the power of patience, they are peerless in vigor; this diligent application of energy is free from weariness.
This practice of meditative concentration possesses supernormal powers, enabling them to reach immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Constantly seeing the Buddhas and hearing their teachings, they explain what they have heard for the sake of others.
Skillfully knowing the conduct of sentient beings, they act according to their inclinations, dispositions, and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties;
this is called the power of skillful means. This is the place where the lamp of wisdom is lit to achieve salvation.
This one is able to skillfully know all phenomena; this one knows that sentient beings attain liberation.
With firm practice and knowing according to reality, they know according to reality how such causes give rise [to results].
This is the correct contemplation of all phenomena: from where they come and to where they go.
Skillfully knowing that all phenomena have no coming or going, one abides eternally in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without wavering.
Seeing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are empty, one increases great compassion to rescue sentient beings.
Due to deluded thoughts and afflictions, they undergo suffering; to deliver them, one practices the Path.
Ordinary people discriminate between "self" and "what belongs to the self," practicing various kinds of false views.
One who can clearly understand the true nature of phenomena preaches the Dharma to sever all such views.
Taking the impermanent for permanent, the impure for pure, The non-self for self, and suffering for pleasure—
Because ordinary beings are thus inverted and greedily attached, The prior limit of birth and death cannot be known.
Able to know such inverted dharmas— That there is no self, no person, and no sentient being—
the Bodhisattva thus cultivates the true path, [Seeing] impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
Kāśyapa, you should know that these bodhisattvas possess the various merits I have praised;
their practice is inexhaustible, like taking up a single speck of dust from the great earth.
If one who has resolved for bodhicitta does not regress, even with the three thousandfold world-system as an offering,
or if there should be an offering superior to this, such a person is worthy of receiving this offering.
If a person resolves their mind to become a Buddha, they are thereby honoring and making offerings to me;
they have likewise honored and made offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!

What are the ten? First, attaining the power of mindfulness, because one does not forget any dharmas;
second, attaining the power of intention, because one skillfully discerns all dharmas through expedient means.
Third, one attains the power of the Dharma, because one is able to skillfully awaken to and understand the intent of the sūtras;
fourth, one attains the power of firmness, because one never abandons practice according to reality;
fifth, one attains the power of shame and remorse, because one protects both others and oneself.
Sixth, they attain the power of great learning, because they are fully endowed with wisdom;
seventh, they attain the power of dhāraṇī, because they are able to retain everything they have heard;
eighth, they attain the power of eloquence in joyful speech, because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

the eleventh is the treasury of wisdom, because it attains all the Buddha-dharmas.

When the Buddha had spoken this sūtra, seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and countless sentient beings, no longer grasping at any dharmas, were liberated through the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya).
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and said: “World-Honored One,
by what name should this Dharma-gate be called, and how should it be upheld?”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
This Dharma gate is called ‘The Equal Encompassment of All Dharmas’; you should receive and uphold it thus.”
It is to be upheld as "The Adornment of All Buddha-Dharmas";
it is to be upheld as "The Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin";
it is to be upheld as "The Treatise on the Meaning by Mañjuśrī."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this Dharma-gate, Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King; the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin; the noble youth Samatācārin; the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha; the Elder Mahākāśyapa; the Venerable Ānanda; and all the bodhisattvas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharva kings, asuras, and others, received and upheld the Buddha’s words and were all greatly filled with joy.
